People can live a healthy life with just one, which is why living kidney donation works. Because you can lose a lot of kidney function before you feel anything, problems are often found late. A blood test and a urine test are the way to catch them early, especially if you have diabetes or high blood pressure.

An adult has 206 bones, but a newborn has around 300. Many of a baby's bones fuse together as it grows, such as the separate plates of the skull and the bones at the base of the spine.
Bone isn't dead. It's living tissue that constantly rebuilds itself, with old bone absorbed and new bone laid down, and it gets stronger with weight-bearing exercise. Over about a decade, most of the adult skeleton is replaced. That's why walking, lifting and jumping help keep bones dense, and why people who don't use their bones lose them. The skeleton is less like a scaffold and more like a garden that needs tending.

A muscle can only contract. It can pull, but it can never push. That's why muscles work in pairs on either side of a joint: one bends your elbow and its partner straightens it.
The body has more than 600 muscles. The heart is a special kind, which works without ever stopping. Moving the body well is a matter of timing and coordination between them. A simple step involves dozens of muscles switching on and off in order. When you train, you're improving the strength of the muscles, and also the way the brain directs them, which is why beginners often get stronger quickly, before their muscles have grown at all.

The human body hosts trillions of microbes, mostly bacteria in the gut. For years, it was said that they outnumbered our own cells ten to one. In 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo recalculated and found about 38 trillion bacteria and about 30 trillion human cells, closer to even.
They help digest food, make some vitamins and train the immune system, and scientists are still learning how much they affect health. A varied diet with plenty of fiber seems to support a varied community of bacteria. The old ten-to-one figure is a good example of a "fact" that was repeated for decades without being checked, and it was corrected when someone did the arithmetic.

Your gut and your brain are in constant conversation, mostly along the vagus nerve, a long nerve that runs between them. It's why stress can upset your stomach and why anxiety can make your gut feel tight.
In animal studies, changes in gut bacteria change behavior. How much this affects human mood is still being worked out, and claims made for probiotics are ahead of the evidence. The link is real, but the practical advice is not yet clear. For now, what's well supported is the simple things: eating regular meals, getting enough fiber and sleep, and noticing how stress shows up in your stomach.

The immune system has two parts. The innate part is fast and general. Within hours, cells such as macrophages attack anything that looks foreign. They don't need to have met it before.
The adaptive part is slower but precise. T cells and B cells learn the particular shape of a germ over days, and make antibodies that fit it. Afterward, memory cells remember it, sometimes for decades, which is the principle behind vaccines. A vaccine shows the adaptive system a harmless piece of a germ, so that when the real one arrives, the response is quick. It's a bit like giving a guard a photograph of a burglar.

A fever feels miserable, but it's part of the body's defense. A higher temperature slows the growth of many germs and helps your immune cells work faster. It isn't the illness itself. It's the body's response to it.
Treating a mild fever is mainly for comfort, and it isn't always necessary. If you feel better with a fever reducer, that's fine, but the fever is rarely dangerous by itself. A very high fever, or any fever in a young infant, is a reason to see a doctor, since it can signal a serious infection. How the person looks and acts is often more important than the number on the thermometer.

You see "immune boosting" on supplement labels, but scientifically it isn't a meaningful idea. The immune system isn't a muscle that gets stronger the more it's stimulated. It's a balance, and an overactive one is what causes allergies and autoimmune diseases.
What actually supports it is plain: enough sleep, regular exercise, a balanced diet, vaccination, not smoking and managing stress. None of those is exciting, and none of them can be bottled. If a product claims to boost your immunity, it's reasonable to ask what that would mean, and what evidence there is. The honest answer is usually that nobody knows, and that the money would be better spent on food and a good pair of walking shoes.

An allergy is when the immune system treats something harmless, such as pollen or peanut, as a threat and produces antibodies called IgE against it. The next exposure triggers sneezing, itching or, in serious cases, anaphylaxis.
For years parents were told to keep peanuts away from babies. In 2015 the LEAP trial showed the opposite. Giving peanut foods early to infants at high risk cut their chance of a peanut allergy by about 80 percent. The old advice, though well meant, had probably made the problem worse. It's an example of how medical advice changes when it's properly tested, and why it's worth asking a doctor what the current guidance is.

Insulin is the hormone that tells your cells to take up sugar from the blood. In 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working in a Toronto lab, isolated it. In January 1922 a 14-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson, who was dying of type 1 diabetes, got the first injection.
Within a year, people who would have died within months were being kept alive. Before that, the treatment for type 1 diabetes was a near-starvation diet that only prolonged life for a short time. Banting sold the patent for one dollar, saying that insulin belonged to the world. It's one of the great stories of modern medicine, and it happened not so long ago.

In 1994 Jeffrey Friedman's team at Rockefeller University discovered leptin, a hormone made by fat cells that signals to the brain how much energy is stored. It tells the brain how well-fed the body is.
Mice that lack it eat constantly and become very obese, and so do rare people with the same genetic fault. Most people with obesity, however, have high levels of leptin, and the brain has become less responsive to it. So it isn't a simple cure. The discovery showed that body weight is regulated by hormones, and not only by willpower, which changed how researchers think about weight. Hunger and fullness are chemical signals, and they can be disrupted.

The human genome is about 3 billion letters long, and any two people share about 99.9 percent of them. There are around 20,000 genes that code for proteins, but they make up only 1 or 2 percent of the sequence.
The rest includes regulatory regions that switch genes on and off, and a lot that we're still learning about. Small differences in those letters help explain why people differ in traits and in disease risk. It's humbling that the first full sequence took 13 years and billions of dollars, and that today it can be done in a day for a few hundred. Those few differences between us are tiny, compared with all that we share.

Light in empty space travels at exactly 299,792,458 meters per second. It's exact because we define it that way. Since 1983 the meter has been defined as the distance light covers in 1/299,792,458 of a second, so the speed fixes the length, and not the other way around.
It's also the same for every observer, however fast they're moving, and that is the strange fact that Einstein built relativity on. If you chase a beam of light at half its speed, it still races away from you at the full speed. Nothing that has mass can ever reach it, because the closer you get, the more energy it takes to speed up even a little more. It acts as a cosmic speed limit.

Light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to get from the Sun to Earth. So when you look at the Sun, which you shouldn't do directly, you're seeing it as it was a little over eight minutes ago. If the Sun suddenly disappeared, we wouldn't know for those eight minutes.
The next-nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is just over four light-years away, so its light shows you the star as it was more than four years ago. Looking at the night sky is a way of looking into the past, and the farther the star, the older the picture. Some of the points of light you can see now are from stars that may no longer exist, though their light is still on its way.

In 1687 Isaac Newton published three rules of motion in his book Principia. An object keeps doing what it's doing, staying still or moving in a straight line, unless a force acts on it. A force makes an object accelerate, more for a lighter object than for a heavy one. And forces come in pairs: when you push on something, it pushes back on you equally.
A rocket works through the third law. It throws gas backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward. It doesn't need air to push against, which is why rockets work in space. That surprised people for a long time, since many assumed that a rocket would have nothing to push on. The same law is at work when you jump from a small boat and feel the boat slide away behind you.

Galileo is said to have shown that heavy and light objects fall together. On Earth, we don't see this with a feather, because air resistance holds it back. In 1971, astronaut David Scott tested it on the Moon, where there's no air.
He held a geologist's hammer and a falcon feather at shoulder height, let go, and both hit the lunar dust at the same moment, on live television. Without air, gravity treats everything the same. A heavier object is pulled harder, but it also takes more force to move it, and the two effects cancel out exactly. It's a very clean demonstration, and it's still a pleasure to watch the video.

Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. A pendulum swaps motion for height and back. A battery turns chemical energy into electricity and then into light or motion. A candle turns the energy stored in wax into heat and light.
Several scientists reached the idea in the 1840s, and Hermann von Helmholtz set out the law in its general form in 1847. It's one of the most reliable rules in physics, and no machine that gets energy from nothing has ever worked. That's why the patent offices turn away perpetual motion machines. Energy can seem to disappear, as it does when a ball stops bouncing, but it has only been turned into heat, in tiny amounts, spread everywhere.

The lowest temperature there could be is about minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, or zero on the Kelvin scale. At that point, the particles in a substance would have as little motion as physics allows. Nothing can be colder, since temperature is a measure of how much the particles move.
Scientists have cooled atoms to within a billionth of a degree above it, but the laws of thermodynamics say you can't reach it exactly. The coldest natural place we know of, the Boomerang Nebula, is about one degree above. At very low temperatures, strange things happen. Some materials lose all electrical resistance, and some fluids flow without any friction, and they can climb up the walls of their container.

In 1827 the German schoolteacher Georg Ohm published what became the first rule of electrical circuits. The current through a conductor equals the voltage across it divided by its resistance. Double the voltage across a fixed resistor, and the current doubles. Double the resistance, and the current halves.
It was dismissed at first, and Ohm struggled for years in poorly paid teaching jobs. Now every electrician uses it, and the unit of resistance carries his name. A helpful picture is a water pipe: voltage is the pressure, current is the flow, and resistance is how narrow the pipe is. With any two of the three numbers, you can find the third, and the arithmetic is simple enough to do in your head.
Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface

A bolt of lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 kelvin, roughly five times hotter than the visible surface of the Sun, which is about 5,800 kelvin. The heating is so sudden that the air expands faster than the speed of sound, producing a shock wave.
That's the thunder you hear. You can estimate how far away a strike was by counting the seconds between the flash and the sound, and dividing by five to get the distance in miles. The flash arrives almost at once, and the sound takes much longer. A strike that you can hear is close enough to be dangerous, so the old advice stands: when thunder roars, go indoors.

Earth's core acts like a giant magnet, and its field deflects charged particles from the Sun, which helps protect life. It's why we have auroras, where some of the particles are funneled toward the poles and make the air glow.
The field isn't fixed, though. Rocks record that its direction has reversed many times. The last full flip was about 780,000 years ago, and after one, a compass needle would point south. A reversal takes thousands of years, and nothing suggests one would be a catastrophe, but nobody knows when the next will be. The north magnetic pole is also wandering, and it has been moving toward Siberia at a good pace in recent decades.

In air at 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels at about 343 meters per second, roughly a kilometer every three seconds. It moves faster through liquids and solids: about 1,480 meters per second in water, and over 5,000 in steel.
The reason is that denser, stiffer materials pass vibrations along more quickly, since the particles spring back faster. It's why you can hear an approaching train by putting an ear to the rail before you hear it in the air. It's also why whales can communicate over great distances, since sound carries so well in water. Sound can't travel in a vacuum at all, because it needs something to push on.

When a source of sound moves toward you, the waves are squeezed together and the pitch sounds higher. When it moves away, the waves are stretched and the pitch drops. You hear it when an ambulance passes, with that falling "neeee-yow."
Christian Doppler proposed the idea in 1842, and in 1845 the Dutch scientist Buys Ballot tested it with trumpeters playing a steady note on a moving train. Astronomers use the same effect with light to measure how fast distant galaxies are moving. If a star is moving away, its light shifts toward the red, and if it's coming toward us, it shifts toward the blue. It's a simple idea that lets us measure the motion of things that are billions of miles away.
Why the Tacoma Narrows Bridge fell

In November 1940 a new suspension bridge in Washington state twisted wildly in a moderate wind and collapsed. A film of the event is still shown in engineering classes. Many physics textbooks used to call it a simple case of resonance.
Later analysis showed it was something more subtle, called aerodynamic flutter. The twisting motion of the deck changes how the wind pushes on it, which feeds more energy into the motion, and the twisting grows. Engineers have designed bridges to avoid it since, using wind tunnels to test models. The story is a good example of how an explanation can be repeated for decades before someone checks it, and of how failures teach engineers more than successes do.

Before Newton, many people thought that a prism added colors to white light, staining it as it passed through the glass. In 1666 he showed otherwise. He sent a beam of sunlight through one prism, and it spread into a rainbow.
Then he sent the colors through a second prism turned the other way, and they came back together as white. So white light is a mixture of all the colors, and the prism only separates them. A rainbow does the same thing using raindrops. Each color bends by a slightly different amount, and so they come out in order. It was a neat experiment that needed only two pieces of glass and a small hole in a window shutter.

In 1801 Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw a pattern of bright and dark stripes on a screen behind them, which is what waves do when they overlap. It seemed to settle the matter: light is a wave.
A century later, scientists found that light also comes in particles. Then in 1927 Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer found that electrons behave like waves too. Later experiments sent single electrons, one at a time, through the slits, and the stripes still built up, one dot at a time. Each electron seems to go through both slits and interfere with itself. It's one of the strangest experiments in physics, and physicists have lived with the puzzle for a hundred years.

In 1927 Werner Heisenberg showed that you can't know both the exact position and the exact momentum of a particle at the same time. The more precisely you pin down one, the fuzzier the other becomes.
It's often described as the effect of measuring disturbing the thing measured. But the deeper point is that it's built into nature. A particle simply doesn't have a perfectly sharp position and a perfectly sharp velocity together. The limit is tiny and doesn't matter for a baseball or a car, so you aren't going to be uncertain where you left your keys. But for electrons and atoms, it's a basic fact of how the world works.

In quantum mechanics, a particle can be in a combination of states at once, until it's measured. It isn't that we don't know which state it's in. The particle really is in a blend of both.
Erwin Schrödinger found this so strange that in 1935 he made up a thought experiment in which a cat in a box is linked to a quantum event, so that it's both alive and dead until someone opens the box. He meant it as a criticism, to show how odd the idea gets when scaled up. Physicists still debate what a measurement actually does. The experiments agree with the theory to remarkable accuracy, even though nobody agrees on what it means.

Two particles can be linked so that measuring one instantly tells you something about the other, however far apart they are. Einstein didn't like it and called it "spooky action at a distance."
But experiments, from Alain Aspect's in the early 1980s to tests with no loopholes in 2015, have confirmed that it's real. Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work. It doesn't let you send messages faster than light, because the results of each measurement look random until the two sides compare notes. But it's the basis for new technologies, like quantum cryptography, and it shows that the world is stranger than our everyday experience suggests.

In everyday life, a ball can't roll through a hill that's higher than its energy. In the quantum world, particles sometimes can. This is called tunneling, and it happens because a particle's position is spread out, with a small chance that it turns up on the other side.
It's how the Sun shines. Protons in its core don't have quite enough energy to overcome their mutual repulsion and fuse, but a few tunnel through, enough to keep the Sun burning for billions of years. The effect is also used in scanning tunneling microscopes, which can see individual atoms, and in the flash memory in phones. Without tunneling, there would be no sunlight and no smartphone storage.

When light hits a metal surface, it can knock electrons loose, but only if its frequency is high enough. A dim blue light does it, while a very bright red light doesn't. Physicists couldn't explain that with waves, since a brighter wave should have more energy.
In 1905 Einstein proposed that light comes in packets of energy, later called photons, and each must carry enough energy to free an electron. A red photon doesn't have enough, however many you send, and a blue one does. This, and not relativity, won him the 1921 Nobel Prize. It's the principle behind solar panels and the sensor in a digital camera, and it was one of the first steps toward quantum theory.

In 1911 Ernest Rutherford's team fired particles at thin gold foil and found that most went straight through, but a few bounced right back. He later said it was as surprising as firing a shell at tissue paper and having it come back at you.
He concluded that an atom has a tiny, dense nucleus with mostly empty space around it. The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller than the atom. If the atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a pea at the center. Things feel solid because of the electric forces between atoms, and not because they're packed with stuff. When you lean on a table, your atoms never touch the table's atoms. They only repel one another.

In 1915 Einstein published a new theory of gravity. Instead of a force, he described it as the bending of space and time by mass and energy. Matter tells space how to curve, and curved space tells matter how to move.
In 1919, during a solar eclipse, Arthur Eddington's expeditions measured starlight bending as it passed the Sun, by an amount consistent with Einstein's prediction. The reports made him world-famous overnight. A century later, the theory has passed every test. It describes the orbits of planets and the behavior of black holes, and it's built into the GPS in your phone, which wouldn't work without it.

Einstein predicted in 1916 that moving masses would send out ripples in spacetime. They're incredibly faint, and for a century they could not be detected. Einstein himself doubted that anyone ever would.
On September 14, 2015, the LIGO detectors in Louisiana and Washington picked up a signal from two black holes that had merged 1.3 billion light-years away. The stretching of space they measured was thousands of times smaller than the width of a proton. Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish won the 2017 Nobel Prize for it. Since then, many more have been found. It opened a new way to observe the universe, by feeling it as well as seeing it.

A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from inside its boundary, called the event horizon. They form when very massive stars collapse, and some, in the centers of galaxies, are millions or billions of times the mass of the Sun.
The first image of one, in the galaxy M87, was released in 2019 by the Event Horizon Telescope. In 2022 the same team showed the black hole at the center of our own galaxy, which is about four million times the mass of the Sun. The images show a bright ring of glowing gas around a dark center. They are blurry, but they are real pictures of something that was once only a prediction of the mathematics.

In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that, thanks to quantum effects near the event horizon, black holes should slowly lose mass by emitting a faint glow of radiation. It means that they aren't completely black, and that they can eventually evaporate.
For a black hole of the size we know, the process would take far, far longer than the current age of the universe. No one has ever detected the radiation, since it's far too weak. It's a prediction that's accepted by most physicists because it comes from putting together two of the best theories, quantum mechanics and gravity. It's a clue to what a deeper theory might look like.

General relativity predicts that time passes more slowly in stronger gravity. A clock at sea level ticks slightly slower than one on a mountaintop. It isn't that the clock is broken. Time itself runs at a different rate.
In 2010 researchers at NIST measured it with extremely precise atomic clocks that were only about 33 centimeters, a foot, apart in height. The difference was tiny but real. It also matters in practice. GPS satellites orbit high above the surface, where time runs faster, and they need to correct for it, or they'd drift by kilometers each day. Every time your phone finds your location, it's using Einstein's theory.

The evidence says that the universe began as an incredibly hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago, and has been expanding and cooling since. The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître first proposed it in 1927.
Three main things support it. Galaxies are moving apart, the whole sky glows with leftover radiation, and the proportions of hydrogen and helium match the predictions. It describes what happened after the beginning, not what caused it, and not where it happened. There was no center and no outside. Space itself was small and has grown. The name "Big Bang" was coined in 1949 by the astronomer Fred Hoyle, who favored a rival theory, and it stuck.

In 1964 two radio astronomers at Bell Labs, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, were bothered by a faint hiss in their big horn antenna. They even cleaned out pigeon droppings, thinking they might be the cause. The hiss didn't go away.
It turned out to be the afterglow of the Big Bang, light released when the universe was about 380,000 years old and had cooled enough to become transparent. It has been stretched by the expansion of space into microwaves, and it comes from every direction. They won the 1978 Nobel Prize. An old analog television that isn't tuned to a channel shows a small part of it as static, so you've perhaps seen the afterglow of the beginning of time.

In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that galaxies are moving away from us, and that the farther away they are, the faster they're receding. This built on the 1927 work of Georges Lemaître, who had reached a similar result from the theory.
It doesn't mean we're at the center. Space itself is stretching, so every galaxy sees the others moving away, like dots on the surface of an inflating balloon. It was the first key observation behind the Big Bang model, and it changed our view of the cosmos from a fixed, eternal stage to an evolving one. If everything is moving apart today, then in the past, everything must have been closer together.

In the 1970s the astronomer Vera Rubin measured how fast stars orbit at the edges of galaxies. They moved as fast as the stars near the center, which didn't match the visible matter. If only the visible matter were there, the outer stars should have been flung away.
The best explanation is that there's an unseen halo of matter whose gravity holds everything together. It makes up about 27 percent of the universe. We don't know what it's made of, and experiments around the world are trying to find out. The name is a little misleading, since it isn't dark so much as invisible. It doesn't give off or absorb light, and we only know it through its gravity.

In 1998 two teams studying distant exploding stars expected to find that the expansion of the universe was slowing down because of gravity. Instead, they found that it was speeding up.
Something is pushing space apart, and it's been named dark energy. It makes up about 68 percent of the universe, and nobody knows what it is. The leaders of the two teams shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. It's one of the biggest open questions in science. We have a name and a measurement, but not an explanation, and it might be a property of space itself or something else we haven't thought of.

Everything you can see, from the Earth to the stars to you, is made of ordinary atoms, and all of that is only about 5 percent of the universe. The other 95 percent is dark matter, about 27 percent, and dark energy, about 68 percent.
The measurements come mainly from satellites studying the cosmic microwave background. We've learned that most of the universe is something we don't yet understand. It's humbling. After centuries of science, the stuff we know best, and are made of, turns out to be the minority. The numbers may shift with new measurements, but the point is that we have a lot left to discover.

The part of the universe we can see is about 93 billion light-years across. That may sound odd, since the universe is only 13.8 billion years old, and nothing should have been able to travel farther than that. But space has been stretching all the while the light was traveling to us.
So the distance to the places that sent us the oldest light is much larger now. There may well be more beyond the edge, but its light hasn't had time to reach us. We can never see it, because the stretching carries it away faster than light can cross the gap. The observable universe is the region we can see from here, and it doesn't have to be all there is.

Our galaxy is a spiral of somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. We live in one of its arms, about halfway out from the center. From the inside, it looks like a faint band of light across the night sky.
The Sun takes about 230 million years to go once around, so it has made about twenty trips since it was born. In roughly four to five billion years the Milky Way will merge with its nearest large neighbor, the Andromeda galaxy, which is heading our way. The stars are so far apart that few will actually collide. The two galaxies will pass through one another and settle into a new shape.

The Sun is a middle-aged star, about 4.6 billion years old. Every second, in its core, it turns about 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium, and the small amount of mass that vanishes in the process becomes the energy that warms us.
It has enough fuel for roughly another five billion years. After that it will swell into a red giant, and then shrink into a white dwarf. The energy that you feel as warmth on your face started in the core, and took tens of thousands of years to work its way to the surface, and then eight minutes to reach you. It's a very old gift, and we're lucky that the Sun burns so steadily.

A star's life is decided mainly by its mass. Small ones, called red dwarfs, burn their fuel slowly and can last trillions of years. Massive stars burn fast and bright, lasting only millions of years, and end in a supernova explosion that leaves behind a neutron star or a black hole.
Our Sun, in the middle, will end more quietly as a white dwarf, a small, dense, cooling ember. It's a strange rule that the bigger the star, the shorter its life, but it follows from the way they burn. A larger star has more fuel, but it's squeezed harder, so it uses it up at a furious pace. Stars are born, live and die, and the universe has been recycling their material for billions of years.

Just after the Big Bang, the universe was almost entirely hydrogen and helium. Every heavier element, including the carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe and the iron in your blood, was made later inside stars, and was scattered into space when stars died.
Some heavy elements also come from the collisions of neutron stars. The 1957 paper by Margaret and Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle worked out how stars make the elements. In a real sense, you're made of material that was cooked in stars, and has been through more than one. It's a fact that can make an ordinary day feel a little less ordinary, since every atom of you has a long history.

When a massive star explodes as a supernova, its core can collapse into a neutron star, a ball only about 20 kilometers across but with more mass than the Sun. The atoms are crushed so that the protons and electrons merge into neutrons.
A teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons. Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times a second, and they send out beams of radio waves that sweep across space like a lighthouse. We detect those beams as pulses, and the objects are called pulsars. Neutron stars are among the densest things in the universe, short of black holes, and they're a natural laboratory for physics under extreme conditions.

In 1967 a graduate student at Cambridge, Jocelyn Bell, noticed a strange signal in her radio telescope data. It was a pulse repeating every 1.337 seconds, as regular as a clock. Nothing natural was known to behave that way, and the team half-jokingly named it LGM-1, for "little green men."
It turned out to be a rapidly spinning neutron star, sweeping a beam of radio waves past Earth like a lighthouse. Her supervisor, Antony Hewish, shared the 1974 Nobel Prize for the discovery. She was not included, and many people have thought that this was unfair. Bell Burnell has handled it with grace, and she later donated a large prize of her own to help students from groups that are underrepresented in physics.

On February 23, 1987, astronomers saw a star explode in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy next to ours, about 168,000 light-years away. It was the closest supernova in about four centuries, and it could be seen without a telescope in the southern sky.
A few hours before the light arrived, detectors deep underground in Japan and the US caught a burst of neutrinos, ghostly particles produced in the explosion. The neutrinos had left the dying star's core before the shock wave had broken through to the surface. The two signals confirmed how such stars die, and the observation helped begin a new kind of astronomy, which looks at the universe by catching its particles.

In August 2017, detectors picked up gravitational waves from two neutron stars spiraling into each other 130 million light-years away. Telescopes around the world turned toward the spot and watched the glow that followed. It was the first time that a collision had been seen in both gravitational waves and light.
The glow showed signs of heavy elements being created, including gold and platinum. It helped answer a long-standing question about where the heaviest elements come from. Calculations suggest that one such merger can make heavy elements amounting to many times the mass of the Earth. If you're wearing a gold ring, its atoms were probably forged in the collision of two dead stars, long before the Sun was born.

The closest planet to the Sun is also the smallest, a little bigger than our Moon. A year there lasts just 88 days. With almost no atmosphere to hold in heat, its temperature swings wildly, from about 430 degrees Celsius in the day to about minus 180 at night.
Even so, scientists have found water ice in permanently shadowed craters near its poles, where sunlight never reaches. It's a surprise to find ice on the planet nearest to the Sun, and it shows how much a bit of shade can matter. Mercury also moves faster than any other planet, at about 47 kilometers per second, which is why the Romans named it after the swift messenger of the gods.

Venus is a strange world. It spins backward and so slowly that a day, which lasts 243 Earth days, is longer than its year of 225 days. If you could stand on its surface, the Sun would rise in the west.
Its thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, making it the hottest planet at about 465 degrees Celsius, hotter than Mercury, even though it's farther from the Sun. The pressure at the surface is about 90 times Earth's, similar to being almost a kilometer under the sea. The Soviet probes that landed there in the 1970s lasted only an hour or two before they were crushed and cooked. Venus is sometimes called Earth's twin because of its size, but it's a very unfriendly twin.

You're sitting still, but you're traveling. Earth orbits the Sun at about 30 kilometers per second, nearly 70,000 miles per hour. At the equator, the planet's spin carries you eastward at about 1,670 kilometers per hour.
You don't feel any of it, because the speed is smooth and steady and everything around you is moving along with you. We notice only changes in motion, such as speeding up, slowing down or turning, and not the motion itself. That's the same reason you can't tell that you're moving at all when you are on a smooth flight. Galileo made the argument four centuries ago, when people asked why we don't feel the Earth move. The answer is that nothing about being at rest is any different from moving steadily.

Mars looks red because its surface is rich in iron oxide, which is rust. It has the biggest volcano known in the solar system, Olympus Mons, about 22 kilometers high, roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.
Billions of years ago, Mars had rivers and lakes of liquid water, and rovers have found signs of old streambeds and lake sediments. Today it's cold and dry, with a thin atmosphere that can't hold much heat. The planet lost most of its air over time, perhaps because it's smaller than Earth and has no global magnetic field to protect it. Whether it ever had life is one of the biggest open questions in science, and rovers are collecting samples to bring back and study.

Jupiter is by far the largest planet, with enough volume to hold more than 1,300 Earths. It's made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface to land on. If you tried to descend, the atmosphere would just get denser and hotter.
Its Great Red Spot is a giant storm, wider than Earth, that has been observed for at least 150 years, though it has been shrinking in recent decades. Its strong gravity has probably shaped the solar system, and it has pulled in comets and asteroids. In 1994, pieces of the comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crashed into it, and left dark scars that were visible from Earth. It spins faster than any other planet, completing a rotation in under ten hours.

Saturn is the least dense planet in the solar system, with an average density lower than water. In theory, it would float if you could find a bathtub big enough. It's a ball of gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, with a small, dense core.
Its famous rings are made mostly of water ice, in pieces from dust to house-size boulders, and they spread out over hundreds of thousands of kilometers, yet in places they're only about ten meters thick. If the rings were scaled down to the width of a football field, they'd be only a few millimeters thick. They may also be young, only a few hundred million years old, though scientists don't agree on that.

Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so it spins almost on its side, like a rolling ball. As a result, each pole gets 42 years of constant sunlight, followed by 42 years of darkness. It's the only planet whose seasons are that extreme.
William Herschel found it in 1781, the first planet discovered with a telescope. At first, he thought it was a comet. A giant collision early in the planet's history may have knocked it over, though no one is sure. Only one spacecraft, Voyager 2 in 1986, has ever visited it, so there's a great deal that we still don't know. It's a pale blue-green world, and the color comes from methane in its atmosphere.

Neptune was found with mathematics before anyone saw it. After Uranus was discovered, astronomers noticed that its orbit wasn't quite as predicted, as if something were tugging on it. In 1846 Urbain Le Verrier in France, and John Couch Adams in England, each calculated where an unseen planet must be.
Johann Galle in Berlin pointed his telescope at the spot Le Verrier gave and found it that very night. It was a triumph for Newton's laws, since a planet had been found with pencil and paper. Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, over 2,000 kilometers per hour, even though it receives very little sunlight. It takes 165 years to go around the Sun, and it completed its first orbit since discovery in 2011.

Pluto was called the ninth planet from its discovery in 1930 until 2006, when the International Astronomical Union voted to define a planet as something that has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit. Pluto hasn't, so it became a dwarf planet.
Many people were upset, and the debate still comes up. But the new definition arose because astronomers were finding other icy worlds out there, some almost as big as Pluto. In July 2015 NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew by it and showed a surprisingly active world, including a large heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen. Pluto turned out to be more interesting than anyone had expected, whatever we call it. The name was suggested by an eleven-year-old girl in England.

The leading explanation, developed in the 1970s, is that about 4.5 billion years ago a planet-sized body, which has been called Theia, struck the young Earth. The debris from the collision orbited the planet and gradually came together as the Moon.
Moon rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts have a chemistry very close to Earth's outer layers, which fits the idea. It's called the giant-impact hypothesis. It also explains why the Moon is so large compared with its planet, and why it has such a small iron core. Not every detail is settled, and the details are still being worked out, but most scientists consider it the best account that we have.

The Moon's gravity pulls more strongly on the side of Earth nearest it and less on the far side. That stretches the oceans into two bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side, and as Earth turns, coastlines pass through both, giving most places two high tides a day.
The Sun adds its own pull, about half as strong as the Moon's. When Sun and Moon line up, at new and full moon, the tides are higher, called spring tides, and the name has nothing to do with the season. When they pull at right angles, at the quarter moons, the tides are weaker. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the difference between high and low tide can exceed fifty feet.

The Moon is moving away from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters a year, roughly the speed at which your fingernails grow. Scientists know this because Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the surface, and lasers fired from Earth bounce off them, letting us measure the distance to within a few millimeters.
As it recedes, Earth's rotation slows slightly, so our days get gradually longer. Long ago, a day was much shorter than it is now. Fossil corals show that 400 million years ago, the year had about 400 days. The effect is tiny from one year to the next, but it has added up over billions of years. It's a quiet reminder that the Earth and Moon are a connected system.
Why we only see one side of the Moon

The Moon spins exactly once for every trip it makes around Earth, so the same face always points toward us. It's called tidal locking, and it happened because Earth's gravity slowly slowed the Moon's spin until the two matched.
It's not a "dark side," though. The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side, and so it goes through the same cycle of day and night. It was first photographed by a Soviet spacecraft in 1959, and humans first saw it with their own eyes when Apollo 8 flew around the Moon in 1968. The two sides are surprisingly different, with the far side having far fewer of the large dark plains.

By a remarkable coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look nearly the same size in our sky. When the Moon passes exactly in front of the Sun, it can cover the disk completely and reveal the Sun's faint outer atmosphere, the corona.
During the brief darkness, the temperature drops, birds go quiet and the stars come out. Because the Moon is slowly drifting away, in about 600 million years it will be too small to cover the Sun fully, and total eclipses will end. We happen to live at the one time when they're possible. Ancient peoples feared them, and some used the records of eclipses to date historical events.

Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active place in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes. The reason is tidal heating. Jupiter and its other big moons tug on Io, squeezing and flexing it constantly, which heats the interior.
Its volcanoes spray sulfurous material hundreds of kilometers into space, and the surface is painted in yellows, oranges and reds. Voyager 1 spotted the first plumes in 1979, and an image analyst, Linda Morabito, noticed them. She saw a strange crescent at the edge of the moon in a picture that had been taken to help navigate the spacecraft. It was the first time that active volcanoes had been found anywhere beyond Earth.

Europa, a moon of Jupiter, has a surface of ice, and under it is an ocean of salty liquid water, kept warm by tidal flexing. It may contain twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans, even though the moon is smaller than our own.
Because liquid water is one ingredient of life as we know it, scientists are very interested. The ice shell may be many kilometers thick, so any life would be hidden from view. NASA launched the Europa Clipper spacecraft in 2024 to fly past it dozens of times and study whether it could be habitable. It isn't built to search for life directly. It's meant to find out whether the conditions are right.

Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, and the only other place in the solar system where we've seen stable liquid on the surface. But it's not water. It's lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane, at about minus 180 degrees Celsius.
In 2005 the Huygens probe landed there, and sent back pictures of a landscape that looks eerily like a shoreline, with rounded pebbles that are probably made of ice. It rains methane, and the weather creates channels and dunes. It's a world that works like Earth, but with different materials. NASA plans to send a helicopter called Dragonfly to explore it in the 2030s.

Enceladus is a small, icy moon of Saturn, only about 500 kilometers across. In 2005 the Cassini spacecraft discovered jets of water vapor and ice particles shooting from cracks near its south pole.
Later flybys found salt, organic molecules and hydrogen in the spray, which suggests that there's a liquid ocean beneath the ice and active chemistry. Hydrogen could be a source of energy for life, in the same way as it is around some vents on Earth's sea floor. Enceladus is among the most promising places to look for life beyond Earth. Cassini even flew through the plumes, so scientists could taste the ocean without landing.

In movies, the belt between Mars and Jupiter is crowded with rocks, and ships weave between them. In reality it's mostly empty space. There are millions of asteroids, but they're spread so far apart that spacecraft have passed through without any close calls.
The total mass of the belt is less than that of our Moon, and about a third of it is in the largest body, the dwarf planet Ceres. The belt is the leftover material of a planet that never formed, probably because Jupiter's gravity stirred it up. Most asteroids are small, rough chunks of rock or metal, and a few have been visited by spacecraft, some of which have returned samples to Earth.

About 66 million years ago, an asteroid roughly 10 kilometers wide struck what is now the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. In 1980 the father-and-son team of Luis and Walter Alvarez noticed a thin layer of clay around the world rich in iridium, a metal common in asteroids, and suggested that it came from an impact.
In the 1990s, the buried Chicxulub crater was identified as the site. About three-quarters of species died, including all the large dinosaurs, though birds, which descend from small dinosaurs, survived. The impact threw dust and soot into the sky, and the world was cold and dark for a long time. It's a vivid example of a scientific idea that was doubted at first and then confirmed by new evidence.

Halley's comet comes back about every 76 years. It was last seen in 1986, and it's due again in 2061. For most of history, comets were seen as unpredictable omens that appeared from nowhere.
In 1705 Edmond Halley noticed that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had similar orbits, and he used Newton's new laws to predict that it would return in 1758. It did, after his death, and it was the first comet shown to travel in a regular orbit. It was a major triumph for Newtonian physics. A person who is lucky enough to live a long life may see it twice, as Mark Twain famously did, being born and dying in the years when it was visible.

Launched in 1977 to study the outer planets, Voyager 1 is now the most distant human-made object, and it entered interstellar space in 2012. It's still sending data from over 24 billion kilometers away, on only a couple of hundred watts of power.
Attached to its side is a gold-plated record containing greetings in 55 languages, music and sounds from Earth, in case anyone ever finds it. The spacecraft's power is slowly fading, and engineers have been turning off instruments one by one to make it last. Its signal takes more than 22 hours to reach us. Even so, it will keep drifting through the galaxy long after the Sun has changed.

In 1990, as Voyager 1 was leaving the solar system, Carl Sagan asked NASA to turn its camera back for one last look. In the resulting picture, from about 6 billion kilometers away, Earth is less than a single pixel, a tiny speck in a ray of sunlight.
Sagan wrote of it that everyone you love, everyone you know, and everyone who ever lived, lived their lives on that dot. It's become a symbol of our place in the universe, small and shared. Some people find it humbling, and others find it comforting, since our troubles look so small from there. It's worth a few minutes to look at the picture and think about it.
The first humans on the Moon

On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle on the Moon, while Michael Collins stayed in orbit above in the command module. The landing site was nearly missed, and Armstrong had to fly manually past some boulders with little fuel to spare.
They spent about two and a half hours walking on the surface, collecting samples and setting up experiments, and brought back 21.5 kilograms of lunar rock and soil. About 600 million people watched on television. Twelve people have walked on the Moon in all, the last in 1972. It was one of the most difficult engineering feats ever undertaken, and it was done with computers less powerful than a modern calculator.

On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a polished metal ball that beeped as it orbited Earth. It was the first artificial satellite and it started the Space Race.
Less than four years later, on April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, and completed one orbit in 108 minutes. Many people in the US were shocked, and it spurred major investment in science education. Within a few years, the country had created NASA's Apollo program and a generation of new engineers. The race had its dark side, since the same rockets could carry weapons, but its effects on science and technology were large.

Launched in 1990, Hubble orbits above the atmosphere, which blurs the view from the ground. Its first mirror was ground to the wrong shape, giving blurry images, until astronauts installed corrective optics in 1993.
After that it transformed astronomy. It helped measure how fast the universe is expanding, and its "Deep Field" images revealed thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length. Each of those galaxies has billions of stars. Hubble has now been operating for more than thirty years, in large part because astronauts could visit it to repair and upgrade it five times.

The James Webb telescope launched on Christmas Day 2021 and began science work in 2022. It's an infrared telescope with a mirror 6.5 meters across, made of 18 gold-coated segments, and it sits about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
A sunshield the size of a tennis court keeps it cold enough to detect faint heat. Because infrared passes through dust, it can see galaxies that formed in the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang, and it can study the atmospheres of planets around other stars. Its mirror folded up like origami to fit in the rocket, and then unfolded in space. It all had to work on the first try, and it did.

Until 1995, we didn't know whether any other stars had planets. That year Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced a planet orbiting the Sun-like star 51 Pegasi, a gas giant that circles its star in just four days. They shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Since then, astronomers have confirmed more than 5,000 exoplanets, and it appears that most stars have planets. Many are very unlike anything in our own solar system, such as giant planets that orbit closer than Mercury does, and worlds somewhere between the sizes of Earth and Neptune. It's an astonishing change in thirty years. A question that was only speculation is now a catalog of thousands of worlds.

The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface, not too hot and not too cold. It's sometimes called the "Goldilocks zone."
Being in it doesn't guarantee life or even water. Venus and Mars both lie close to the edges of the Sun's zone, and their very different atmospheres have made them hostile to life as we know it. The zone depends on the star, too. Around a dim red star, it's much closer in. It's a useful guide when deciding where to point our telescopes, but it's a starting point and not an answer.

In 1961 the astronomer Frank Drake wrote a formula to organize the question of how many civilizations in our galaxy might be able to communicate with us. It multiplies factors like the rate of star formation, the fraction of stars with planets, the fraction of those where life arises, and how long civilizations last.
We know a few of the numbers and have to guess the rest, so answers range from "we're alone" to "millions." It's not a prediction so much as a way of seeing what we'd need to know. As we learn more, for example that planets are common, some of the factors become clearer. The most uncertain are still the ones about life itself, and how long a civilization lasts.

Around 1950 the physicist Enrico Fermi was having lunch with colleagues, discussing extraterrestrial life, when he asked, "Where is everybody?" If the galaxy is so old and so large, and life is common, why haven't we seen any sign of it?
Suggested answers include that life is rare, that civilizations destroy themselves, or that we haven't looked in the right way. No one knows which, if any, is right. It's a puzzle, not a proof, since the premises are uncertain. Still, it's a good prompt for thought. Either we're surprisingly early, surprisingly rare or surprisingly careless about looking, and each of those would be interesting.

In 1956 the geochemist Clair Patterson measured the ratios of lead isotopes in a meteorite and calculated that the Earth is about 4.55 billion years old. His reasoning was that meteorites formed at the same time as the planets.
Later methods have refined the number slightly, to 4.54 billion, and it has held up. Patterson went on to discover that leaded gasoline was spreading lead around the planet, and he campaigned successfully to end its use. His careful work in a clean laboratory led him to find that lead was everywhere, and the discovery changed public health. A question about the age of the planet led to a safer world.

Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, published his table in 1869. He arranged the known elements by weight and noticed that their properties repeated in a pattern, so that every so often a new row began with an element much like one from the row before.
Where the pattern broke, he did something bold. He left a gap and predicted that an element would be found to fill it, along with what it would be like. Gallium, scandium and germanium were discovered over the next seventeen years, and each matched his descriptions closely. That's what convinced chemists that he was right. A table that had begun as a way of organizing facts had turned into a tool for predicting new ones.

What makes an element what it is? Not its weight, as early chemists thought, but the number of protons in its nucleus. That number is called the atomic number, and it's the real address of an element in the table.
In 1913 the young English physicist Henry Moseley measured the X-rays given off by different elements and found that their frequencies followed a neat series of whole numbers. That fixed the true order of the table, and showed exactly where the gaps were. Change the number of protons in an atom and you've changed the element. Moseley was killed at Gallipoli two years later, at the age of 27, and many consider his death a great loss to science.

Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon sit in the last column of the table, and they hardly react with anything. Their outer shells of electrons are full, so they have no reason to take part in chemistry. Each atom is happy alone.
That's why airships and balloons now use helium instead of flammable hydrogen, and why the glowing gas in a neon sign doesn't burn or wear out. They were nicknamed "noble" because they keep to themselves, like aristocrats who won't mix with the common crowd. In fact, chemists did make a few compounds of the heavier ones, starting with xenon in 1962, so the name isn't completely true. But "hardly ever reacts" is a good rule.

The metals in the first column, lithium, sodium, potassium and the rest, are soft enough to cut with a knife and react strongly with water. Lithium fizzes, sodium skates around and burns, and potassium bursts into a lilac flame.
Each atom has a single loose electron on the outside that it's eager to give away. The further you go down the column, the looser the electron and the more violent the reaction. Cesium and rubidium can explode on contact with water. That's why these metals are stored under oil and never found in nature in a pure form. They've always been combined with something, like sodium in table salt.

Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine are one electron short of a full outer shell, so they're eager to grab one from another atom. That makes them very reactive, and they readily form salts. In fact, "halogen" comes from Greek words meaning "salt-former."
Fluorine is the most reactive of all the elements, and will even react with glass. Chlorine and iodine are used as disinfectants. The halogens are the mirror image of the alkali metals. One group gives away an electron, and the other takes one. When a metal like sodium meets a halogen like chlorine, each gets what it wants, and you get table salt.

The fifteen elements called the lanthanides, plus two relatives, are known as the rare earths, but the name is misleading. Cerium is about as common in Earth's crust as copper. What's rare is finding them concentrated in a spot where mining is worthwhile.
They're also hard to separate from one another, because their chemistry is so alike. They're in many things we use daily: magnets in headphones and electric motors, phone screens, lasers and lighting. The name comes from the 1700s, when chemists found them in unfamiliar minerals and thought they were scarce. Today the bottleneck is less about how much there is than about who is able to refine it.

Hydrogen has one proton and one electron, the simplest atom there is. It accounts for about three-quarters of all ordinary matter by mass, and it's what stars burn to make light. Almost everything else in the universe came later.
The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier gave it its name in 1783, from the Greek words for "water-former," because when hydrogen burns, it makes water. It's also being developed as a clean fuel, since burning it produces only water. It's the lightest of all gases, which is why it was used to lift airships until the Hindenburg disaster in 1937 ended that era. Today it's mostly used to make fertilizer and to refine oil.

In 1868, during a solar eclipse, astronomers saw a bright yellow line in the Sun's spectrum that didn't match any known element. They named the new element after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun. For nearly thirty years, it was known only from the sky.
Only in 1895 did the chemist William Ramsay find it on Earth, in a uranium mineral. On Earth it forms from radioactive decay deep underground and gets trapped in natural gas, from which we collect it. Once it escapes, it floats off to space, so it's not renewable in any practical way. It's used to cool the magnets in MRI scanners, and it's a bit sad to let it go in a party balloon.

The lightest metal is so soft that you can cut it with a knife, and it floats on water. A Swedish chemist, Johan Arfwedson, found it in 1817 while analyzing a mineral. Its name comes from the Greek word for stone.
Today most people carry some in their pocket, in the lithium-ion battery that powers a phone. Lithium salts have also been used since the mid-twentieth century to treat bipolar disorder, as a mood stabilizer. It was an Australian psychiatrist, John Cade, who first reported the effect in 1949. It's an odd thing that the same element helps run our phones and steadies the moods of many people.

Beryllium is a light, stiff metal that is toxic as dust, so it's handled with care. Breathing the dust can cause a serious lung disease. But once it's shaped into solid parts, it's safe to use.
Its qualities make it ideal for space. The 18 mirror segments of the James Webb Space Telescope are made of beryllium, coated with a thin layer of gold to reflect infrared light. It stays stable even at extremely low temperatures. In nature it also colors gems. Emerald and aquamarine are both forms of the mineral beryl, and the green of an emerald comes from a trace of chromium within it.

Boron compounds are in more everyday things than you might guess. Borosilicate glass, the type used for lab glassware and some oven-safe dishes, can handle sudden changes in temperature without cracking.
Borax, a boron mineral, has been mined for thousands of years and was used in ancient times for soldering gold. It's now an ingredient in some laundry products and in fiberglass. Plants also need a trace of boron to build healthy cell walls. It's a quiet element that rarely makes the news, but you'd miss it if it were gone, since it holds up your cookware and helps your garden grow. Boron is also the element that makes green flames in some fireworks, and it turns up in the control rods of nuclear reactors, where it soaks up stray neutrons.

Carbon atoms can link up in an astonishing variety of ways, which is why the chemistry of life is built on it. About 18 percent of your body's mass is carbon. Every living thing, from bacteria to blue whales, has a skeleton of carbon chains and rings.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, differently arranged. In 2004 Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov peeled single-atom-thick layers of graphite from a lump using sticky tape, making graphene, and they won the 2010 Nobel Prize for it. A sheet of graphene is only one atom thick and yet stronger than steel. It shows that even the humblest tools can lead to big discoveries.

Nitrogen makes up 78 percent of the air, but plants can't use it in that form. The two atoms in each molecule are held together so tightly that most living things can't break them apart. For centuries, farmers depended on manure and natural deposits to feed their crops.
Between 1909 and 1913 the chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch worked out how to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia on a large scale, making artificial fertilizer possible. Roughly half the nitrogen atoms in your body were fixed by the Haber-Bosch process. It's one of the most important inventions in history, and it let the world's population grow to many times what it could have been. The same chemistry also made explosives, which is a sobering part of the story.

Oxygen is about 21 percent of the air, and about 65 percent of your body's mass, mostly as the oxygen in water. The Swedish chemist Carl Scheele and the English minister Joseph Priestley each found it independently in the 1770s, and Antoine Lavoisier worked out that it was what made things burn.
Most of the oxygen in the air was produced by photosynthesis, by plants, algae and bacteria, over billions of years. About 2.4 billion years ago, it began to build up in the atmosphere, which was a disaster for many of the microbes of the time. For us, it's the reverse. Every breath you take draws on that long labor of tiny green organisms, and every cell of your body uses it to release energy from food.

Fluorine is the most chemically reactive of all the elements, so it's hard to isolate. For decades, chemists were injured, and some were killed, by the poisonous fumes while trying. It attacks nearly everything it touches, including most containers.
The French chemist Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886 and won a Nobel Prize for it. Fluoride, a compound of fluorine, is added to many toothpastes and water supplies because it strengthens tooth enamel and reduces cavities. It's an example of how a dangerous element can have a benign side. In small amounts, as fluoride, it's a protector of teeth, though the pure gas is among the nastiest substances known.

Neon was found in 1898 by William Ramsay and Morris Travers, who chilled air until it turned liquid and then let it boil off piece by piece. They watched the gases come off one at a time, and each had its own color when electricity passed through it.
Neon itself glows a bright red-orange. It's not used in all signs called neon, though. Many use other gases, such as argon, or coatings inside the glass tubes, to produce other colors. The name comes from the Greek word for "new." When Travers saw the brilliant red glow of the new gas, he said later that it was a sight to be remembered, and it still lights up many a city street.

Sodium is a soft, silvery metal that reacts violently with water. In 1807 Humphry Davy was the first to isolate it, by passing an electric current through molten sodium hydroxide. He did the same with potassium a few days earlier.
Table salt is sodium combined with chlorine, a gas that's poisonous by itself. It's a striking example of how two dangerous substances can join to make something we eat every day. Your nerves also use sodium to carry signals, which is one reason the body needs a regular supply. Almost all the sodium on Earth is in the form of salt, and the sea is full of it.

Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame, which is why it was used in the old camera flashes and in fireworks. Once lit, it's very hard to put out, and it can even burn in carbon dioxide.
It's also at the center of every chlorophyll molecule, the green pigment plants use to catch sunlight. In your body, it helps more than 300 enzymes work, and it's found in foods like nuts, seeds and leafy greens. So the same element that makes a brilliant flash in a firework is quietly at work in every green leaf. It's a light, strong metal too, and is used in some car parts and laptop cases.

Aluminum is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, but it's always combined with other elements, and was very difficult to extract. For a time in the 1800s it was more valuable than gold. Napoleon III is said to have served his most honored guests with aluminum cutlery while the rest used gold.
In 1886 two young inventors, Charles Hall in the US and Paul Héroult in France, independently found a way to extract it using electricity, and the price collapsed within a few years. Hall and Héroult were both in their early twenties, and were born in the same year. Today aluminum is in everything from soda cans to airplanes. It's a good example of how a cheaper process can turn a luxury into an everyday material.

Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust after oxygen. Sand and most rocks are silicon compounds. If you've been on a beach, you've walked on silicon dioxide.
In its ultrapure crystal form it's a semiconductor, meaning it can be made to conduct electricity or not, which makes it the foundation of computer chips. California's "Silicon Valley" is named for it. A modern chip has billions of tiny switches etched into a thin slice of silicon. It's remarkable that the stuff of sand, with a lot of purification and cleverness, has become the brain of our machines. The silicon used for chips has to be purified until fewer than one atom in a billion is something else, which is cleaner than almost anything else people make.

Phosphorus is essential to life. It's in DNA, in cell membranes and in ATP, the molecule that carries energy within cells. Your bones and teeth also contain a lot of it, as calcium phosphate.
It was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand, a German alchemist who was searching for the philosopher's stone and boiled down enormous quantities of urine. He ended up with a white substance that glowed in the dark. The name means "light-bringer" in Greek. Today, much of it goes into fertilizer, and the supply of phosphate rock is an important concern for farming. It's an element that links the kitchen of an alchemist to the cells of every living thing.

Sulfur is a yellow solid that has been known since ancient times. The "rotten egg" smell we associate with it comes from hydrogen sulfide gas, not from pure sulfur, which has hardly any smell.
In 1839 Charles Goodyear discovered that heating rubber with sulfur made it stronger and less sticky, a process called vulcanization. It made possible things like tires, shoe soles and rubber hoses. Goodyear spent years in poverty and debt before his discovery paid off, and he died with large debts. The tire company that bears his name was founded after his death, and had no connection to him other than the name.

Chlorine is a greenish, poisonous gas, and it's one of the most useful chemicals in public health. Adding small amounts to drinking water kills germs and has dramatically reduced diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
But it also has a dark history. The German army first used it as a weapon on April 22, 1915, at the Second Battle of Ypres in the First World War. It was the beginning of chemical warfare. The same element that protects the water supply was turned into a weapon, which is a reminder that knowledge is neither good nor bad in itself. What matters is how we choose to use it.

In 1894 Lord Rayleigh noticed that nitrogen taken from the air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made from chemicals. The difference was small, but he trusted his measurements and kept investigating.
He and William Ramsay tracked down the difference to a previously unknown gas making up about 1 percent of the air. They named it argon, from the Greek for "lazy," because it won't react with anything. Light bulbs are often filled with it, to protect the filament. It's a fine example of how careful measurement can uncover something hidden in plain sight, since the air we breathe holds more than twenty times as much argon as carbon dioxide.

Potassium is a soft metal that reacts even more violently with water than sodium, and the hydrogen it releases ignites with a lilac flame. In nature it's always found combined with other elements.
In your body it works with sodium to carry nerve signals and keep your heartbeat steady. A banana has about 420 milligrams, but many other foods, including potatoes, beans and avocados, have more, and most people don't get enough. A diet that includes plenty of fruits and vegetables is the easiest way to get it. The banana is famous, but it's not the best source. Too little potassium is linked with higher blood pressure, and getting more of it from food can help bring pressure down, especially for people who also eat a lot of salt.

Calcium is the most abundant metal in the human body, and about 99 percent of it is stored in bones and teeth. The other one percent plays an important role in making muscles contract, nerves send signals and blood clot.
If you don't get enough in your diet, the body takes it from your bones to keep the blood level steady. That's why long-term shortages can lead to weak bones. Chalk, limestone and marble are all forms of calcium carbonate, often formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures long ago. Dairy foods are the best-known sources, but leafy greens, tofu and canned fish with soft bones also have plenty.

Scandium is a good example of Mendeleev's predictions. In 1871 he described a missing element beneath boron in his table, which he called "eka-boron," and said what it should be like.
In 1879 the Swedish chemist Lars Nilson found a new element in a Scandinavian mineral, named it after Scandinavia, and it matched. Another chemist, Per Cleve, noticed that it was the element Mendeleev had predicted. Today it's used in small amounts to strengthen aluminum in bicycle frames and aircraft parts. It's a good story about the power of a prediction. A gap in a table of elements led to a search, and the search found the missing piece.

Titanium is as strong as many steels but about 40 percent lighter, and it doesn't corrode. It's used in jet engines, in spacecraft and in high-end bicycles and golf clubs.
In the 1950s the Swedish surgeon Per-Ingvar Brånemark found by accident that bone grows right into titanium and holds it firmly in place, a property he named osseointegration. He had been using titanium chambers to watch blood flow in rabbits, and found that he couldn't get them out. That discovery led to dental implants and hip and knee replacements, and it's why those implants are made of titanium. Millions of people now have metal in their bodies thanks to a stuck rabbit chamber.

Vanadium is a hard, silvery metal that makes steel much tougher. It's named for Vanadis, a Norse goddess of beauty, because its compounds come in so many beautiful colors, including green, blue, yellow and violet.
Henry Ford used vanadium steel for the frame of the Model T because it was stronger and lighter than ordinary steel, which helped make the car affordable and durable. Today it's used in tools, springs and some batteries meant for storing electricity from the grid. It's an element few of us have heard of, but it's quietly part of the wrenches in our toolbox and the roads under our wheels.

Chromium is what makes stainless steel stainless. Steel with at least about 10.5 percent chromium forms an invisible, self-repairing layer of oxide on its surface that prevents rust. If you scratch it, the layer simply forms again.
The metal's name comes from the Greek word for color, because its compounds are so vivid, including the green in emeralds and the red in rubies. It's also the shiny coating on "chrome" car parts. Some chromium compounds are toxic, so factories that use them have to handle them carefully. The metal is a good example of how a small amount of one ingredient can change the character of another.

About 90 percent of the manganese mined goes into making steel, where it makes the metal harder and easier to work. Without it, steel would be brittle, and railways and bridges would not have been built the way they were.
In small amounts, it's an essential nutrient. It helps enzymes build bone and break down food. But too much, as workers in some industries have been exposed to, damages the brain, causing symptoms like those of Parkinson's disease. It's a reminder that the dose makes the difference. The same element that is needed by the body can harm it when the amount goes far beyond the normal.

Iron has shaped history. Earth's core is mostly iron and nickel, which generates the planet's magnetic field. And almost every large star ends its fusing life by making iron, which is why it's one of the most common heavy elements.
In your blood, hemoglobin uses iron to carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body, and it's what makes blood red. In the Middle East, the Iron Age began around 1200 BC, when people learned to make tools stronger than those of bronze. A shortage of iron in the diet is the most common nutritional deficiency in the world. It's the metal of tools, bridges and blood.

For centuries, cobalt has given pottery and glass a brilliant deep blue, and "cobalt blue" is still a favorite pigment. Medieval miners cursed the ore, because it was hard to smelt and gave off toxic fumes, and named it after the German word for a goblin, "kobold."
Today it's also an essential ingredient in the rechargeable batteries in phones and electric cars. About 70 percent of the world's supply comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and its mining has been linked to child labor and unsafe conditions. Companies and governments have been under pressure to trace where their cobalt comes from, and to find batteries that need less of it.

The name comes from German miners, who found an ore that looked like copper but yielded none. They blamed a mischievous spirit, "Old Nick," and called it Kupfernickel, which means "copper devil." The metal was isolated in 1751.
Today it's used in stainless steel, batteries and coins. The American five-cent coin, called a nickel, is actually 75 percent copper and 25 percent nickel. It's a bit of a joke that the metal that was named after a curse has ended up in our pockets. Nickel is also a common cause of skin allergies, so some jewelry is now labeled as nickel-free. Earth's core holds a great deal of it too, alloyed with iron, which makes meteorites a rich source of the metal.

Copper was one of the first metals people used, about 10,000 years ago, because it can be found in a pure form and is easy to hammer. The first copper tools and ornaments were made long before anyone learned to smelt it.
It conducts electricity almost as well as silver, so it's in nearly every wire in your house. It also kills many germs, and in 2008 the US Environmental Protection Agency approved copper alloys as the first solid surfaces that can claim to be antimicrobial. The ancients knew that water kept in copper vessels stayed fresher. It's a metal that has been useful to people for the whole of history.

Zinc is a bluish metal used to coat steel in a process called galvanizing, protecting it from rust even when scratched, since the zinc corrodes first and shields the iron beneath. Mixed with copper, it makes brass.
In your body, it's needed by hundreds of enzymes and plays a role in immunity and healing. Foods like oysters, beef and beans are good sources. Oysters have more zinc than almost any other food, by a wide margin. Some studies suggest that zinc lozenges might shorten a cold slightly if they're taken early, but the evidence is modest. The mineral is more useful as part of a regular diet than as a cure.

Gallium is a soft metal that melts at 29.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, so a lump of it will melt in your hand. It's a favorite of science teachers, who sometimes show a spoon made of it dissolving in a cup of hot tea.
In 1871 Mendeleev predicted it as "eka-aluminum," and in 1875 Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered it, and measured properties that matched. Mendeleev wrote to him to say that the density he had reported was a little off, and he turned out to be right. Today, compounds of gallium are used in blue and white LED lights and in some of the most efficient solar cells. It's a good example of a prediction that came true, to the decimal.

In December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at Bell Labs built the first working transistor, and its crystal was germanium. The transistor replaced bulky vacuum tubes that were hot, fragile and burned out, and it launched the age of electronics.
It won a Nobel Prize for them and for William Shockley, who led the group. Silicon later took over as the main material because it's cheaper and works at higher temperatures, but germanium is still found in some fiber-optic and infrared devices. Mendeleev had predicted it too, as "eka-silicon," and it was found in 1886 by Clemens Winkler, who named it for Germany, his homeland. So the element behind the first transistor was one of the table's successful predictions.
