For centuries, arsenic was the classic murder poison. It was odorless and tasteless, and its symptoms resembled those of common illnesses, so it earned the nickname "inheritance powder." Poisoners could get away with it because no one could prove what had happened.
In 1836 the chemist James Marsh devised a sensitive test that could detect even tiny traces in a body. It was the first time that courts had reliable forensic proof of arsenic poisoning, and it made such murders much harder to get away with. Today, arsenic is still a problem of a different kind. In parts of Bangladesh and India, well water naturally contains it, and millions of people have been exposed. Testing the water is the first step toward fixing it.

Selenium is a trace element that your body needs in tiny amounts to make antioxidant enzymes, but too much is toxic. The gap between enough and too much is narrow, which makes it a tricky mineral to take as a supplement.
Brazil nuts are unusually rich in it, and a single nut can contain more than a day's supply. Its name comes from Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon, chosen because it was found along with tellurium, whose name comes from the Latin for Earth. Soil in some parts of the world has little selenium, and people there can run short, while in other places, there's so much that it harms livestock. Most people who eat a normal diet get enough without thinking about it.

Bromine and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature. Bromine is a dark reddish-brown liquid that gives off a harsh, irritating vapor, and its name comes from the Greek for "stench."
Compounds of bromine have been used in photographic film, in fire retardants and in some medicines. Bromides were once a common sedative, and in the nineteenth century were given for nervousness and epilepsy. Their use faded when safer drugs came along. The element is found in seawater, and the Dead Sea is especially rich in it. Today, it's still used for disinfecting swimming pools and hot tubs, where a bromine compound does a job like that of chlorine.

For 23 years, the meter was defined by this gas. From 1960 to 1983, one meter was officially 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of the orange-red light given off by krypton-86 atoms. That was more precise and reproducible than the old metal bar kept in Paris.
In 1983 it was replaced by a definition based on the speed of light, which is even more precise. The name comes from the Greek for "hidden," because it makes up only a tiny trace of the air and was discovered by William Ramsay and Morris Travers in 1898. Superman's home planet shares its name, though the comics' fictional mineral has nothing to do with the real element. It's still used in some lighting and in high-speed photography flashes.

Atoms of rubidium can be made to flip between two energy states at an extremely precise frequency, so they make excellent timekeepers. Small rubidium atomic clocks are cheap and compact enough to be used in cell phone towers, in satellites and in telecommunications equipment, where accurate timing is vital.
The name comes from the Latin for deep red, from the color of its spectral lines. Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff discovered it in 1861, and it was one of the first elements found with the help of the spectroscope. The metal itself is soft and reacts violently with water, but the atoms in a clock are kept in a small sealed glass cell. It's the little cousin of the cesium clock, and a lot cheaper.

Strontium salts burn with a brilliant crimson color, and they're used in red fireworks and emergency flares. The next time you see a vivid red in a fireworks display, you're likely looking at strontium. It was named for Strontian, a village in Scotland where the mineral was first found.
It also has a more worrying form. Strontium-90, a radioactive isotope released by nuclear weapons tests and accidents, is dangerous because the body mistakes it for calcium and deposits it in the bones, where it irradiates the marrow for years. After the Chernobyl accident in 1986, it was one of the contaminants that people worried about. It's a clear case where a chemical lookalike lets a hazard slip into the body.
Ytterby: the village with four elements

Not far from Stockholm in Sweden, there's a village called Ytterby, and it has given its name to four elements: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium. The reason is a quarry there, which yielded a heavy black mineral that was found in 1787 by an army lieutenant, Carl Axel Arrhenius.
Over the next hundred years, chemists found that this one mineral was a mixture of many new elements, and several of them were named for the place. Yttrium compounds are used in LED lights, in lasers and in superconductors, and they also helped create the red in old television screens. Gadolinium, holmium and others from the same family also trace back to the quarry. No other place on Earth has so many chemical elements named after it.

Zirconium is remarkable because it barely absorbs neutrons, which makes it ideal for holding nuclear fuel. The fuel rods in most nuclear reactors are covered in a zirconium alloy, and it's also very resistant to corrosion and heat.
The mineral zircon is also the source of cubic zirconia, the sparkling diamond lookalike used in jewelry, which is made from zirconium dioxide. Zircon crystals themselves have been used to learn about the early Earth. Some tiny zircon grains from Western Australia are 4.4 billion years old, the oldest pieces of the Earth's crust ever found. Because the crystals are so tough, they have survived while almost everything else from that time has been destroyed.

Alloys of niobium and titanium become superconductors when cooled below about 10 kelvin, meaning they carry electricity with no resistance at all. They're used to make the powerful magnets in MRI machines and in particle accelerators, including the Large Hadron Collider.
The element was named for Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus in Greek mythology, since it's always found with tantalum and is chemically very similar. For a long time chemists confused the two, and some in the US called it columbium instead. The name niobium was officially adopted in 1950. Most of the world's niobium comes from a single large mine in Brazil, and it's added in small amounts to steel to make it stronger.

Molybdenum has one of the highest melting points of all metals, about 2,620 degrees Celsius, and it makes steel stronger at high temperatures. It's used in jet engines, in tools and in the pipelines that carry oil and gas.
It's also essential to life. Plants need it for the enzyme that turns nitrogen into forms they can use, and many enzymes in your own body contain it. It's named from the Greek word for lead, because it was once confused with it. In fact, the "lead" in a pencil is really graphite, and for a long time graphite and molybdenum were mixed up, too. It's a modest metal with a quietly large role in both industry and biology.

Technetium was the first element to be made artificially. In 1937 Emilio Segrè, an Italian physicist, got a strip of molybdenum that had been bombarded in a cyclotron at Berkeley, and with Carlo Perrier found the new element in it. The name comes from the Greek for "artificial."
It has no stable isotopes, so it's nearly absent in nature. One form, technetium-99m, is widely used in medicine. It's involved in about 40 million diagnostic scans every year. The "m" stands for metastable, and the isotope gives off a gamma ray and has a half-life of about six hours, which is short enough to be safe for patients and long enough to carry out a scan. Mendeleev had left a gap for it, so it was another piece that fit the table.

These three are among the platinum-group metals, rare and valuable cousins of platinum that tend to turn up in the same ores. Ruthenium was named for Ruthenia, the Latin name for Russia. The Russian-Baltic chemist Karl Claus identified it in 1844, from platinum ore from the Ural Mountains. It's used to harden platinum and palladium, and for tough electrical contacts.
Rhodium is one of the rarest and most valuable metals. About 80 percent of it goes to make catalytic converters, which turn the most harmful gases in car exhaust into less harmful ones. Its name comes from the Greek for rose, because many of its salts are pink or red. Palladium, which William Wollaston discovered in 1802 and named for the asteroid Pallas, can absorb hundreds of times its own volume of hydrogen. It too is used in catalytic converters. At times, rhodium and palladium have each been priced higher than gold.

Silver is the best conductor of both electricity and heat among all the metals. It tarnishes because it reacts with tiny traces of sulfur in the air, forming black silver sulfide. That's why old silverware turns dark, and why a piece kept in a sealed bag stays bright.
Silver compounds were once the light-sensitive part of all photographic film and paper, because they darken when exposed to light. Photography as it was practiced for a century and a half depended on it. It's also a natural antibacterial, which is why silver was used in medicine. Ancient people knew that water stored in silver vessels kept better, and today it's still used in some wound dressings. Its chemical symbol, Ag, comes from argentum, the Latin word for it.

Cadmium was used in rechargeable batteries and in pigments, but it's a poison. In the early 1900s, people in parts of Japan along the Jinzu River developed itai-itai disease, whose name means "ouch-ouch." It was a painful bone disease caused by mine waste containing cadmium that got into rice and water.
It led to stricter limits on cadmium, and today its use is much more limited. Cadmium builds up in the kidneys over many years, and cigarette smoke is one of the main ways people take it in. It's a story about how a pollutant can travel through the food chain, from a river to rice fields to the bones of people eating the rice. It's one of the reasons we monitor heavy metals in the environment.

Indium is a soft metal that, when combined with tin and oxygen, forms indium tin oxide, a coating that is both transparent and electrically conductive. That's the layer that senses your touch on the screen of almost every phone, tablet and flat-panel TV.
The name comes from the bright indigo line in its spectrum, which is how it was identified in 1863 by the German chemists Ferdinand Reich and Theodor Richter. Reich was colorblind, so he asked his assistant to look at the spectrum for him. It's a rare element and is mostly obtained as a byproduct of zinc mining. A small amount is spread across a very large number of devices, which has made people look for ways to recycle it.

Tin was one of the keys to early civilization. About 3300 BC people discovered that mixing tin with copper makes bronze, which is much harder than copper alone, and the Bronze Age began. Because tin was scarce, traders carried it great distances, and some of the earliest long-distance trade routes grew up around it.
When you bend a bar of pure tin, it makes a faint crackling noise called "tin cry," caused by the crystals inside it rubbing against each other. Tin is also what coats the inside of a "tin can," which is really made of steel. The thin layer keeps food from touching the steel. Its symbol, Sn, comes from the Latin word for it, stannum.

Antimony has been known since ancient times. In Egypt and elsewhere, a black powder from the mineral stibnite was ground up and used as kohl, an eye cosmetic. That makeup was used for beauty, and also for protection from the sun's glare.
The chemical symbol Sb comes from "stibium," the Latin name for the mineral. Today, antimony is used to make flame retardants and to harden lead in batteries. It was also once used to make type metal for printing, because it expands slightly as it cools, which makes sharp letters. A few medicines of the past contained it, though many were toxic. It's a reminder that cosmetics and chemistry have long gone together.

Tellurium is one of the rarest stable elements in Earth's crust, rarer than platinum. It's used in solar panels made with cadmium telluride, the second most common type of solar panel after silicon.
It was first isolated in 1782 by a Hungarian-Austrian mineralogist, Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein, and named by Martin Klaproth for the Latin word for Earth, tellus. People who've been exposed to a small amount sometimes develop a strong garlic smell on their breath that can last for weeks. It's an element that most people never hear of, but it turns up in thin-film solar cells that cover large fields. Because so little of it is mined, and most comes as a byproduct of refining copper, its supply is a worry for the solar industry.

Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make the hormones that regulate your metabolism. Without enough, it swells into a goiter. For much of history, whole regions far from the sea, where the soil is poor in iodine, had a high rate of goiter.
In 1924 Michigan began adding iodine to table salt, and the practice spread across the US, nearly eliminating goiter. Iodine deficiency is still a problem in parts of the world, and is a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability. It's one of the cheapest public health measures ever devised. A tiny amount of one element, added to the salt on the table, has protected generations from a harmful condition.

Xenon is a heavy noble gas, and its name comes from the Greek for "stranger." It was discovered in 1898 by William Ramsay and Morris Travers, in the same series of experiments that found neon and krypton.
It produces a bright, bluish-white light in car headlights and flash lamps. It's also used in ion engines for spacecraft, including NASA's Dawn mission to the asteroid belt, because its heavy atoms give more thrust. The engines give a very gentle push, but they can run for years. It's been used as an anesthetic as well, though it's too expensive for general use. A "stranger" that was once thought to be inert turned out to have many uses.

The length of a second is defined by cesium. Since 1967, one second has been 9,192,631,770 cycles of the microwave radiation given off by a cesium-133 atom. The ticking of a cesium atom has replaced the rotation of the Earth as our measure of time.
Atomic clocks based on it are accurate to within about a second over tens of millions of years. It's the reason your phone's time is right, and satellite navigation systems depend on that precision. The metal itself is one of the most reactive there is, and it's liquid just above room temperature, at about 28 degrees Celsius. The name comes from the Latin for "sky blue," after the bright blue lines in its spectrum.

Barium compounds block X-rays, so patients are given a "barium meal," a chalky drink, to make the digestive tract show up clearly on an X-ray image. The drink outlines the stomach and intestines in white, so a doctor can see any problem.
Barium salts also burn a bright green in fireworks. Although soluble barium compounds are poisonous, the one used for X-rays, barium sulfate, doesn't dissolve and passes through safely. It's a good example of how the exact form of a chemical matters. One barium compound is a medical aid, and another can be a poison, and that's why chemists pay such close attention to what a substance is, and not just to what element it contains.

Lanthanum is the first of the lanthanides, a row of 15 similar elements. Glass that contains lanthanum bends light strongly, which lets lens makers produce thinner and sharper camera and telescope lenses. It's also used in some batteries for hybrid cars. The name comes from the Greek for "to lie hidden," because it was hidden within other minerals when it was found in 1839.
Cerium is the most abundant of the rare earths, about as common in the Earth's crust as copper. When cerium is mixed with iron, it makes ferrocerium, the material in lighter flints: scrape it, and tiny hot particles fly off as sparks. It's also in catalytic converters and in some self-cleaning oven walls, where it helps break down grease. Both metals were found within minerals that were mined for other things, which is how the rare earths were hidden for so long.

For about forty years, scientists believed that "didymium," whose name means "twin," was a single element. In 1885 the Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach separated it into two. He called them praseodymium, "green twin," and neodymium, "new twin." Praseodymium gives glass and ceramics a yellow-green color, and is used in some strong magnets and welding goggles.
The neodymium-iron-boron magnet, developed in 1982, is the strongest type of permanent magnet commercially available. A small one can lift hundreds of times its own weight. You'll find them in headphones, computer hard drives, electric car motors and wind turbine generators. It's a nice irony that something once thought to be a single element, a twin, turned out to be a pair, and one of them now sits inside a lot of modern machinery.

Promethium has no stable isotopes, so it's extremely rare in nature, with only a tiny amount at any moment in Earth's crust. For decades, chemists searched for it among the rare earths and found nothing, because there was nothing there to find.
It was first identified in 1945 by scientists at Oak Ridge in Tennessee, from the fission products of uranium. It's named for Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire from the gods for humans, which fits for an element obtained from nuclear fission. It was once used to make luminous paint for watch dials, as a safer substitute for radium. It's also been used in small batteries for spacecraft and in some thickness gauges. Its story is a reminder that nature doesn't always have an element where the table says there should be one.
Europium and terbium: the rare earths that glow

Europium glows brightly red under ultraviolet light, and euro banknotes use it as a security feature. Under UV, the genuine notes show glowing marks and fibers that counterfeit paper lacks. The element was named by the French chemist Eugène-Anatole Demarçay in 1901 for the continent of Europe, so the choice of banknote is a neat coincidence.
Terbium is its green counterpart. When excited, it glows a bright green, which made it useful in the phosphors for fluorescent lamps and older color televisions. Europium supplied the red in those same screens, so between them these two rare earths helped paint the colors of the late twentieth century. Terbium is also used in some solid-state devices and in certain kinds of strong magnets. Neither element is bright when you hold it in your hand. It takes a jolt of energy to make them shine.
Samarium, dysprosium and holmium: the magnet metals

Samarium is a silvery metal named for the mineral samarskite, which was in turn named for a Russian mining official, Colonel Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets. That makes it the first element named, indirectly, for a person. Samarium-cobalt magnets stay strong at very high temperatures. A radioactive form, samarium-153, is used as a medicine to relieve pain from cancer that has spread to the bones.
Dysprosium is what keeps the strongest magnets working in hot conditions. A small amount added to neodymium magnets lets them keep their strength at high temperatures, which is important in electric car motors and wind turbines. The name comes from the Greek for "hard to get," because it took Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran more than 30 attempts to isolate it from holmium in 1886. Holmium has the strongest magnetic moment of any element, and it's used to concentrate magnetic fields in some of the world's most powerful laboratory magnets. Per Teodor Cleve, who found it in 1878, named it for Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm.
Gadolinium and lutetium: elements in the scanners

Gadolinium is strongly magnetic near room temperature. Compounds containing it are injected into patients as "contrast agents" to make MRI images clearer, because they change the magnetic signal from nearby water molecules. The element is named in honor of Johan Gadolin, the Finnish chemist who discovered the first rare earth mineral in that quarry in Ytterby.
Lutetium is the heaviest and hardest of the lanthanides. Crystals that contain it are used in PET scanners, where they detect the gamma rays that come from a radioactive tracer injected into the patient. A radioactive form of it, lutetium-177, is also used in a newer treatment for certain prostate cancers and tumors, carrying radiation directly to cancer cells. Between them, the two metals show how some of the least familiar elements end up in the hospital, helping to see inside the body and to treat disease.
Erbium, thulium and ytterbium: cables, lasers and clocks

Erbium is the secret behind much of the internet. In fiber-optic cables, light signals fade as they travel. Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers, developed in 1986 and 1987, strengthen the light directly, without converting it to electricity and back. They sit along the undersea cables that carry internet traffic across oceans. Thulium, the least abundant of the stable rare earths, is still more common than gold or platinum. It's used in some medical lasers and in a few portable X-ray devices, and Per Teodor Cleve named it in 1879 for Thule, the ancient name for the most northerly region of the world.
Ytterbium atoms are used in the most precise clocks ever built. Optical lattice clocks that use them are stable to about one part in 10 to the 18th power, which means that if one had been started at the Big Bang, it would be off by less than a second today. These clocks are so sensitive that they can detect the effect of a height difference of a centimeter on the speed of time.
Hafnium and tantalum: tiny parts in your pocket

Hafnium is excellent at absorbing neutrons, so it's used to make control rods that regulate nuclear reactors, including in some nuclear submarines. It also plays a role in computing. Starting in 2007, chipmakers like Intel began using hafnium oxide in place of silicon dioxide as the insulating layer in transistors, which let them keep making chips smaller without leaking current.
Tantalum is used to make tiny, reliable capacitors in phones and laptops, so there's probably some in your pocket. It's also extremely resistant to attack by body fluids, so it's used in surgical implants and in pacemakers. A lot of it comes from a mineral called coltan, and, as with cobalt, mining it in some regions has been linked to conflict and harm to workers. Neither metal is well known, but both sit inside devices that most of us use every day.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, 3,422 degrees Celsius, and the highest of all elements except carbon. That's why it was used for the glowing filaments in incandescent light bulbs for about a century. The filament can glow white-hot without melting, which no other practical material could do.
It's also very dense and hard. Tungsten carbide is used to make cutting tools and drill bits, and it can cut through steel. Its chemical symbol, W, comes from its other name, wolfram, which is the name still used in German. The name tungsten comes from the Swedish for "heavy stone." When you see an old light bulb glowing, it's the tungsten that you are looking at, running hotter than the surface of a small star.

Rhenium was the last stable element to be discovered, in 1925 by Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg in Germany. It's among the rarest elements in the Earth's crust, so finding it meant sifting through tons of ore for a tiny amount. They named it for the Rhine, the river that runs through their homeland.
It's used in superalloys for jet engine turbine blades, because it keeps its strength at extremely high temperatures, allowing engines to run hotter and more efficiently. Ida Tacke later married Walter Noddack, and the couple worked together for many years. She was nominated for a Nobel Prize more than once, though she never won. It's a rare element with an important job, and a good story of persistence.
Osmium and iridium: the heavy metals

Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element. A cubic centimeter weighs about 22.6 grams, roughly 22 times as much as the same volume of water. A volleyball-size lump would weigh over 200 pounds. Its name comes from the Greek word for smell, because one of its compounds, osmium tetroxide, gives off a strong, unpleasant odor, and it's also highly toxic.
Iridium is a very dense, corrosion-resistant metal that's rare in Earth's crust but much more common in asteroids and meteorites. In 1980 the physicist Luis Alvarez and his son Walter, a geologist, found a thin layer of clay rich in iridium in rocks around the world, exactly at the time the dinosaurs died out. It pointed them to the idea that an asteroid had struck the Earth. A faint line of heavy metal in a rock became evidence of one of the greatest disasters in the planet's history.

Platinum is a dense, rare metal that doesn't tarnish or corrode, and it's valued for jewelry and as a catalyst in car exhaust systems and chemical manufacturing. Its resistance to corrosion is what made it so useful for the one job that most people never think about, which is defining how heavy a kilogram is.
From 1889 until 2019, the international standard for the kilogram was a small cylinder made of an alloy of 90 percent platinum and 10 percent iridium, kept under three glass bells in a vault near Paris. Copies were sent around the world, and over the years they drifted very slightly from the original. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined in terms of a fundamental constant of physics, so it no longer depends on a lump of metal in a vault.

Gold is chemically inert, so it doesn't tarnish or rust, and ancient gold objects still look as bright as the day they were made. A mask from the tomb of Tutankhamun is more than 3,000 years old and shines as if it were new.
Most of its atoms were probably created in the collisions of neutron stars, and were scattered through space long before the Earth formed. It's incredibly malleable. A single gram can be hammered into a sheet about a square meter in size, so thin that light shines through it with a greenish tint. All the gold ever mined would fit into a cube about 22 meters on each side, which is smaller than you might think.

Mercury is the only metal that's liquid at room temperature, and its silvery blobs were fascinating to people for centuries. It was used in thermometers, in barometers and in dental fillings. Ancient doctors even gave it as a medicine.
But it's a potent poison. In the 1950s, in the Japanese city of Minamata, a factory dumped mercury waste into the bay, which contaminated the fish that people ate and caused severe neurological damage and birth defects. Thousands of people were harmed. Thermometers today use other liquids. A 2013 international treaty, named the Minamata Convention after the city, aims to reduce the use and release of mercury around the world.

Thallium is a soft metal whose salts have no taste or smell and cause a slow, mysterious illness that includes hair loss. That made it a favorite weapon of mystery writers, and it was once sold as a rat poison.
In Agatha Christie's 1961 novel The Pale Horse, a murderer uses it, and in 1977 a nurse in London who had read the book recognized the symptoms in a real patient, and the diagnosis saved a life. The patient was a young child who had been critically ill, and doctors had no idea what was wrong. It's one of the rare cases in which a detective story helped in a real medical emergency, and the book is sometimes cited in medical journals.

Lead has been used for thousands of years. The Romans made water pipes out of it, and its Latin name, plumbum, gave us the word "plumbing" and the symbol Pb. It's soft, easy to work and doesn't rust, so it has long been tempting to use.
But lead is a neurotoxin, especially harmful to children. After leaded gasoline was phased out in the US, average blood lead levels in Americans fell by about 78 percent between 1976 and 1991. It's one of the great public health successes. The change took decades of work, including by the scientist Clair Patterson, who showed how widespread the pollution was. Lead paint and old pipes can still be a risk in older homes, so it's worth testing if you're not sure.

Bismuth was long thought to be the heaviest stable element, but in 2003 scientists found that it's very slightly radioactive. Its half-life is about 20 billion billion years, over a billion times the age of the universe, so for all practical purposes it's stable.
It's the key ingredient in Pepto-Bismol, the pink stomach remedy, and it's unusual among heavy metals in being almost nonpoisonous. When melted and cooled slowly, it forms beautiful rainbow-colored stair-step crystals, and the colors come from a thin layer of oxide on the surface. They're a favorite of collectors, and some people grow them at home. It's a surprisingly gentle metal for one that is so heavy, and it was nearly the last stable element on the table.
Polonium and radium: the Curies' elements

Marie Curie discovered polonium in 1898, together with her husband Pierre, while searching a uranium ore for the source of its unusual radioactivity. She named it for her native Poland, then partitioned between other countries, as a political statement. It's intensely radioactive and highly toxic. In 2006, a former Russian intelligence officer, Alexander Litvinenko, died in London after being poisoned with it.
The Curies found radium the same year, and it glows faintly in the dark. After that, it was used in everything from luminous watch dials to supposed health tonics. In the 1920s, young women employed to paint watch dials with radium paint, who were told to point their brushes with their lips, developed severe illnesses. Their legal fight, as the "Radium Girls," led to workplace safety laws. Marie Curie herself died in 1934 of an illness that was probably caused by her years of exposure.
Astatine and francium: the rarest natural elements

Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth. Scientists estimate that less than 30 grams exist in the entire crust at any moment, because its most stable isotopes decay within hours. The name comes from the Greek for "unstable." It was first made artificially in 1940, and is being studied as a way to deliver radiation to cancer cells.
Francium is even more fleeting, with its longest-lived isotope lasting only about 22 minutes. The French physicist Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939 at the Curie Institute in Paris, and named it for her homeland. She was the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences. Only tiny amounts have ever been made, and it has never been seen as a visible sample. Between them, these two elements show that the table has places where matter barely has time to exist.

Radon is a colorless, odorless radioactive gas that seeps up through the ground as uranium in rocks decays. It can collect in basements and houses, and after smoking it's the second leading cause of lung cancer in the US, according to the EPA.
You can't see it, smell it or taste it, which is why testing is the only way to know. A home test kit costs only a few dollars, and if levels are high, a vent fan system installed under the house can reduce them. Levels vary a lot from one house to the next, even on the same street. It's one of the few household dangers where a small, cheap test and a modest repair can make a real difference to your health.

Actinium is a silvery radioactive metal that glows with a pale blue light in the dark, from the radiation it gives off. It's about 150 times as radioactive as radium, and its name comes from the Greek for "ray." One of its isotopes, actinium-225, is being tested in medicine, in drugs that deliver tiny particles of radiation directly to cancer cells.
Thorium is a radioactive metal that's about three times more abundant than uranium in Earth's crust. It has been studied as a possible fuel for nuclear reactors, which some say could be safer. It was discovered in 1828 by the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who named it for Thor, the Norse god of thunder. Protactinium sits between thorium and uranium. It was identified in 1913 by Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring, and its name means "before actinium," because when it decays, it turns into actinium.

Uranium is the heaviest element found in nature in large amounts. In December 1938 the German chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann bombarded uranium with neutrons and found that it split into lighter elements, to their surprise. They hadn't expected an atom to break in two.
Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained the process, which they called fission, in early 1939. Meitner had been forced to flee Germany earlier that year because she was Jewish, and she worked out the explanation from exile. Today nuclear power plants supply about 10 percent of the world's electricity. The same discovery that made nuclear energy possible also led to nuclear weapons, a reminder that science can bring benefits and dangers together.

Neptunium was the first element heavier than uranium to be made. In 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley, Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson bombarded uranium with neutrons, creating a new element. It was named for Neptune, the planet beyond Uranus, just as uranium was named for Uranus. Elements beyond uranium are called transuranic elements.
Plutonium was first produced in 1940 as well, by a team led by Glenn Seaborg at Berkeley, and it was named for Pluto, which was then considered a planet. It's the fuel in some nuclear weapons: the bomb dropped on Nagasaki in August 1945 was a plutonium device. Its isotope plutonium-238 produces heat as it decays, and that's used to power spacecraft, including Voyager and the Curiosity rover. The same element appears in both a terrible weapon and a quiet source of power for exploring the solar system.

Americium is in more homes than you might guess. Most ionization smoke detectors contain a tiny amount of americium-241, which ionizes the air in a small chamber so that a small electric current flows. When smoke enters, it disrupts the current, and the alarm sounds.
Seaborg's team made the element in 1944, and named it, like the element above it, europium, for a continent. The amount in a detector is about as much as a speck, and the alpha radiation it gives off can be stopped by a sheet of paper. It's an unusual thing, that a man-made element created in a wartime laboratory should end up on the ceiling of so many bedrooms, quietly guarding families.

Curium was made in 1944 by Glenn Seaborg's team at Berkeley and named for Marie and Pierre Curie, the pioneers of radioactivity research. One of its isotopes, curium-244, gives off alpha particles, which are used in instruments on several Mars rovers called alpha-particle X-ray spectrometers, to work out which elements are in rocks and soil.
Berkelium was first made in 1949 at the University of California, Berkeley, and named for the city. It's highly radioactive and can only be made in tiny amounts, in specialized reactors. In 2010, a batch of berkelium that was made at Oak Ridge National Laboratory was used to make the first atoms of element 117, tennessine. Californium, first made at Berkeley in 1950, emits a lot of neutrons, which makes it useful for starting up nuclear reactors, detecting explosives and finding gold and oil. Just a microgram of californium-252 can give off about two million neutrons per second.
Einsteinium and fermium: from the first hydrogen bomb

Einsteinium was discovered in an unusual place: the fallout from the first hydrogen bomb test, "Ivy Mike," in November 1952, in the Pacific. Scientists at Berkeley found it in the debris collected from the explosion. The discovery was kept secret for three years because of the Cold War. The element was named for Albert Einstein, who died in 1955.
Fermium was found in the same fallout. It's named for Enrico Fermi, who built the first nuclear reactor in 1942. It's the heaviest element that can be made by repeated capture of neutrons in a nuclear reactor. To make elements beyond it, scientists have to smash atoms together in particle accelerators. The explosion, in which uranium was hit by an enormous flood of neutrons, did in an instant what a reactor would take years to do.

Mendelevium was the first element to be made one atom at a time. In 1955 Albert Ghiorso and colleagues at Berkeley bombarded a tiny speck of einsteinium and detected just 17 atoms in total, one by one, across several experiments. It's named for Dmitri Mendeleev, who created the periodic table, and who had predicted undiscovered elements, so it was fitting.
Nobelium is named for Alfred Nobel, who founded the Nobel Prizes. Its discovery was disputed for years. A group in Stockholm claimed it in 1957, but others couldn't repeat the work, and labs in the US and the Soviet Union each made competing claims. Lawrencium is named for Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron, the type of particle accelerator that was used to discover so many new elements. It was first made in 1961 and lasts only hours, so studying its chemistry is very difficult.

Rutherfordium was the first of the superheavy elements, those beyond the actinide series. It's named for Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand-born physicist who discovered the atomic nucleus. It has no stable isotopes, and the longest-lived known ones last about an hour. During the Cold War, teams in the US and the Soviet Union both claimed to have made it first, and they disagreed over the name.
Dubnium is named for the town of Dubna in Russia, where the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research is located, and where a team created it. Its most stable known isotope lasts about 16 hours. In 1997 the international chemistry body settled the quarrel over names. Seaborgium honors Glenn Seaborg, who helped discover ten elements, including plutonium. It was controversial because he was still alive when the name was proposed in 1994. He lived to see it officially named, and died in 1999.

Lise Meitner, an Austrian-Swedish physicist, helped to explain nuclear fission in 1938, but was left out when her colleague Otto Hahn received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1944. Many consider this a serious injustice. She had worked with Hahn for thirty years, and it was she who worked out, with her nephew Otto Frisch, what had actually happened to the uranium.
Element 109 was first made in 1982 in Germany, and named for her in 1997. She's the only woman besides Marie Curie to have an element named for her. Meitner never took part in the building of the atomic bomb, and she refused to when asked. She said she wanted nothing to do with it. The element named for her is, like her, a reminder of how much credit can go astray.

A group of elements came out of a single German laboratory, the GSI near Darmstadt. Bohrium is named for Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist who explained the structure of the atom, and was first made in 1981 when the team fused atoms of bismuth and chromium together. Hassium is named for Hesse, the German state that includes Darmstadt, where it was first made in 1984. In 2001, chemists managed to study a few atoms of it, and showed that it forms a compound similar to that of osmium, as expected from its position in the periodic table.
Darmstadtium, first made in 1994, is named for the city, and its longest-lived known isotope lasts about ten seconds, which is long for an atom this heavy. Roentgenium, also first made in 1994, is named for Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays in 1895 and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. Only a few atoms of it have ever existed, so nobody has seen a sample, and its properties are mostly predicted.

Copernicium honors Nicolaus Copernicus, who proposed that the Earth moves around the Sun. It's fitting that an element at the very edge of the table should be named for a scientist who changed the way people saw their place in the universe. It was made in 1996 at the GSI lab, and officially named in 2010, on the anniversary of Copernicus's birthday.
Chemists have studied a few atoms of it and suggest that it behaves like a very volatile metal, and might be a liquid or even a gas at room temperature. If so, it would be a very unusual metal, and it would show an odd effect of relativity on the heaviest atoms. The electrons move so fast that they behave a little differently from what the usual rules would predict. It's a fine example of how extreme atoms test our theories.

Nihonium was the first element ever discovered in Asia. A team at Japan's RIKEN institute, led by Kosuke Morita, made three atoms of it, in 2004, 2005 and 2012, by firing zinc atoms at bismuth. The long wait between the first and the last atom shows how rare these events are. In nine years, only three atoms were seen.
"Nihon" is one of the Japanese names for Japan. The name was officially approved in 2016, and it was celebrated in Japan, where many saw it as the result of persistence. The team's patience was a point of national pride. It was the first time that the discovery of an element was credited to a laboratory in Asia.

Flerovium is named for the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna, Russia, which was named for the physicist Georgy Flerov. It was officially named in 2012. Scientists believe that it lies near an "island of stability," a predicted region where certain superheavy nuclei might live much longer than their neighbors, perhaps for minutes or even much longer.
Moscovium is named for the Moscow region, where Dubna is located. A team of Russian and American scientists first made it in 2003, by firing calcium-48 ions at americium. Livermorium is named for the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, which collaborated with the Russian scientists in Dubna to make it in 2000. Their atoms last a fraction of a second, so researchers can only make a few at a time and study how they decay. They were all named officially in 2012 and 2016.
Tennessine and oganesson: closing the seventh row

Tennessine was first made in 2010 by a team of Russian and American scientists. They needed a rare target, berkelium, which was made at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, and that's why it's named after the state. It sits in the halogen column of the periodic table, though it's not known how closely it behaves like the others.
Oganesson is the heaviest known element, and it completed the seventh row of the periodic table. It's named for the Russian nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian, who led the team that made it. He was still alive when it was named in 2016, making him only the second person honored that way after Glenn Seaborg. Only a handful of its atoms have ever been made, and each one lasts for a fraction of a second. With the naming of these two elements in 2016, the table, for now, has no more gaps.

In 1838 the botanist Matthias Schleiden suggested that all plants are made of cells, and in 1839 Theodor Schwann said the same of animals. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added the third part, that every cell comes from another cell. Together, the three ideas became the foundation of biology.
Before that, many people believed that living things could arise from nonliving matter, like flies from rotting meat. The cell theory ended that notion. A human body has around 30 trillion cells, and they all trace back to a single fertilized egg that divided again and again. Every cell in you is the descendant of a cell that was alive before it, an unbroken line stretching back billions of years.

Mitochondria are the small structures in your cells that turn food into usable energy. They have their own little ring of DNA, and you inherit them from your mother, because the egg supplies them and the sperm does not.
In 1967 the biologist Lynn Margulis argued that they began as free-living bacteria that were taken in by a larger cell, and the two ended up living together. Her idea was met with scorn at first. Most biologists now accept it, and it's called endosymbiosis. It also applies to plant chloroplasts, which are descended from captured photosynthetic bacteria. In a sense, every complex cell, including each one of yours, is a partnership that began more than a billion years ago.

Plants, algae and some bacteria capture sunlight and use its energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, giving off oxygen as a byproduct. It's the process that feeds almost all life on Earth, directly or indirectly.
The pigment chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green, so leaves look green. In the fall, when the chlorophyll breaks down, the yellow and orange pigments that were hidden underneath show through. Tiny algae in the oceans produce roughly half of the oxygen we breathe, which means a lot of every breath comes from the sea. The sugar a tree makes is built largely from carbon dioxide in the air, and so a tree is mostly made of air.

Your cells burn sugar with oxygen to make ATP, a molecule that works as the cell's energy currency. One molecule of glucose can yield about 30 ATP. It's the reverse of photosynthesis. The carbon dioxide you breathe out is the carbon from the food you ate.
The body uses ATP so quickly that it recycles about its own weight in it each day, rebuilding it again and again. It's the reason you need to keep breathing and eating. The supply of ATP in your cells lasts only seconds, so the machinery has to run all the time. When you hold your breath, you can feel the urgency, and that's your cells running low on the oxygen they need to make more.

In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published their model of DNA's structure in a one-page paper in Nature. It showed two strands twisted around each other like a spiral staircase. They noted, with some understatement, that the structure suggested a way for the genetic material to copy itself.
It was built using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling, and measurements by Maurice Wilkins. One of Franklin's images, known as Photo 51, was shown to Watson without her knowledge. Watson, Crick and Wilkins won the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958, and the prize isn't given after death. Many people today feel that her contribution didn't get the credit it deserved.

DNA is built from four letters, A, T, G and C. In 1950 Erwin Chargaff discovered that in any organism's DNA, the amount of A matches the amount of T, and the amount of G matches C. The amounts of the four letters differed from species to species, but the matching held.
Watson and Crick used this to see that the letters pair up, A with T and G with C, across the two strands. That means each strand holds the information to rebuild the other, which is how DNA can copy itself. When a cell divides, the strands separate, and each one serves as a template for a new partner. It's an elegant design, since the same structure that stores the information also gives the method for copying it.

Every baby is born with some brand-new changes in their DNA that neither parent had. A study in Iceland in 2012 counted about 60 new changes per person on average. They arise mostly from small errors in copying the genetic material when the egg and sperm are made.
Most land in parts of the DNA that don't matter. A few may be harmful, and a very few help. Over many generations, these random changes are the raw material that natural selection works on. The study found that the number of changes rose with the father's age, by about two per year. So in a very real sense, each of us is a little bit new, and the human species is a vast experiment that has been running for a very long time.

Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian monk in what is now the Czech Republic. In the 1850s and 60s, he crossed thousands of pea plants and carefully counted the traits, such as tall versus short, in the offspring. It was patient work, and it took years.
He found consistent ratios, often about 3 to 1, and concluded that traits are passed on in distinct units, which we now call genes. His 1866 paper was ignored until 1900, years after he died. Three scientists independently rediscovered his results around that time, and the field of genetics began. Mendel is a good example of a careful experimenter who was ahead of his time, and who never knew how important his garden had been.

DNA is read in words of three letters, called codons. There are 64 possible codons, and they spell out the 20 amino acids that are strung together to make proteins, plus signals for start and stop. Since there are more codons than amino acids, several codons can mean the same thing.
The code was worked out in the 1960s by Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and others. The code is almost the same in every living thing, from bacteria to humans, which is strong evidence that we share a common ancestor. A human gene can even be put into a bacterium, and the bacterium will read it correctly and make a human protein. That's how insulin is made for people with diabetes today.

Bacteria have an immune system that cuts up the DNA of invading viruses, called CRISPR. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that this system could be reprogrammed to cut DNA at any chosen spot, making gene editing much easier and cheaper than before.
They won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In late 2023, the UK and the US approved the first medicine based on CRISPR, for sickle cell disease. It's a rare case of a basic discovery about bacteria turning into a treatment within about a decade. Gene editing also raises serious ethical questions, especially when it comes to changes that could be passed to children, and scientists around the world are still debating where the lines should be.

Your cells all carry the same DNA, yet a liver cell is very different from a neuron. The difference lies in which genes are switched on, and chemical tags on the DNA and its packaging help control that. These tags are called epigenetic marks.
Diet, stress and age can alter them. Some people claim these changes can be inherited by grandchildren, such as the effect of famine on later generations. Evidence for that in humans is limited and debated, though a few animal studies support it. So the idea is real in a narrow sense, since marks do shape how genes work, and uncertain in the broad sense that is often claimed. It's an exciting field, and one where headlines tend to run ahead of the evidence.

Sometimes unrelated species end up with similar features because they face similar challenges. Eyes have evolved independently dozens of times. Dolphins, which are mammals, and sharks, which are fish, have similar streamlined bodies. Birds, bats and insects all developed wings separately.
It's strong evidence that natural selection is a powerful force, and that certain solutions work again and again. If you gave the same problem to evolution many times, it would often come up with similar answers. At the same time, the details usually differ. A bat's wing is made of stretched skin over long fingers, a bird's of feathers, an insect's of thin membranes. They fly in the same way for the same reasons, but they were each built in their own way.

Look at the skeleton inside a human arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper. The same bones, a single upper bone, two lower bones, wrist bones and fingers, appear in all three, though used for very different purposes. A person can lift a cup, a bat can fly and a whale can steer.
Charles Darwin saw this as strong evidence of common descent: different jobs, same blueprint, modified over time. It's a bit like the same recipe adapted for different meals. If each had been designed from scratch, there would be no reason for a whale to have finger bones. The pattern makes sense if all three came from a shared ancestor that had a limb with those bones, and each descendant modified it in its own way.

It's common to imagine evolution as a ladder, with humans at the top. But natural selection only fits creatures to their local conditions. It has no goal, and it doesn't plan ahead. What works in one place and time may be a disadvantage somewhere else.
Cave fish living in total darkness have lost their eyes, and tapeworms have lost their guts, and both are perfectly suited to their lives. The biologist Stephen Jay Gould argued that life is better pictured as a bush with many branches. Bacteria, which are the oldest life, are still the most common form of it, and by many measures they're the most successful. Humans aren't the end of the story. We're one twig on a huge tree.

Bacteria reproduce so fast that they can evolve resistance to drugs within years. Each time antibiotics are used, they kill the vulnerable bacteria and leave the resistant ones to multiply. It's natural selection at work in a very short time, and in a very practical setting.
A 2022 study estimated that drug-resistant bacterial infections directly caused 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019. Using antibiotics only when needed, and completing the course, slows the process. Antibiotics don't work against colds or the flu, which are caused by viruses, so taking them for those only adds to the problem. New antibiotics are hard to develop, and the old ones are precious. Preserving them is a shared responsibility, and each of us has a part in it.

On the Galápagos Islands, Peter and Rosemary Grant spent four decades measuring finches. They caught, measured and banded thousands of birds on a small island called Daphne Major. In 1977 a severe drought killed most of the small, soft seeds, leaving mainly big, hard ones.
Birds with larger beaks could crack them and survived better. The next generation had measurably larger beaks. It showed natural selection at work within a single human lifetime, not just over millions of years. When the rains returned, and the seeds changed again, the trend later reversed. The Grants' work is some of the clearest evidence of evolution in action, and it shows that the process is continuing around us today.

In 1988 the biologist Richard Lenski started twelve separate populations of E. coli bacteria in flasks in his lab. Every day since, a sample has been moved to fresh food. The flasks have been going for more than three decades, through tens of thousands of generations, which, if they were human generations, would stretch back about three quarters of a million years.
After more than 30,000 generations, one population suddenly evolved the ability to feed on citrate, which E. coli normally can't do. The experiment, still running, shows evolution as it happens, and it can be replayed with frozen samples to see whether it would happen again. It is a patient, simple and beautiful piece of science, and it has answered questions about how chance and necessity shape evolution.

All the life on Earth that we know of, from bacteria to blue whales, shares DNA, the same genetic code and similar basic cell machinery. That points to descent from a single ancestral population that lived somewhere between 3.5 and 4 billion years ago.
A formal statistical test in 2010, by the biologist Douglas Theobald, found that this common-ancestry idea fits the data better than the alternatives. The differences between species are just branches of one tree. It's a humbling and beautiful thought that you share a distant ancestor with every oak, mushroom and fish. If you went back far enough, you would find a single population of microbes that is the great-great-grandparent of everything alive today.

When scientists compared our genome with the chimpanzee's in 2005, they found that, where the sequences line up, about 98.8 percent of the letters are the same. That figure counts single-letter differences, and you might see it quoted as "we're 99 percent chimp."
When you include stretches that are inserted or missing, the difference is larger, about 4 to 5 percent. Either way, our closest living relatives are chimpanzees and bonobos, and our lines split roughly six to seven million years ago. Small changes in how genes are turned on, early in development, seem to matter more than the number of differences. A tiny difference in the plan can produce a very large difference in the animal.

In 2010 the Swedish geneticist Svante Pääbo and his team published a draft of the Neanderthal genome, pieced together from tiny fragments of ancient bone. It was an astonishing technical feat, since the DNA was thousands of years old and badly broken.
It showed that people whose ancestors lived outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA. That means our ancestors met Neanderthals and had children with them. Some of the inherited genes affect things like the immune system and skin. Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Medicine for this work. It overturned the old picture of Neanderthals as a separate and vanished branch. In a small way, they're still with us.

For a long time, we thought that modern humans emerged about 200,000 years ago. In 2017 researchers reported fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, which they dated to roughly 300,000 years ago, with features of both modern humans and earlier forms.
The finding suggests that our species didn't appear in a single place and time. It evolved across the whole of Africa, in pieces, over a long period. Our species spread through Africa and left in waves, and the main migration out was about 60,000 years ago. The picture is still changing as new fossils and DNA come in. We know much more than we did a generation ago, and there are probably more surprises to come.

Bacteria are living single-celled organisms, and many are harmless or helpful, while a few cause disease. Viruses are much smaller and aren't cells at all. They're packets of genetic material that can only reproduce by hijacking a host's cells.
Antibiotics target bacteria, so they do nothing against colds or the flu, which are caused by viruses. For viruses, we use vaccines and, in some cases, antiviral drugs. It's a distinction that matters in daily life, since many people expect an antibiotic every time they're sick. Most of the bacteria in and on your body do you no harm, and some, such as those in your gut, are valuable. You carry roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones.

In 1928 the Scottish doctor Alexander Fleming came back from vacation to find that a mold had contaminated one of his bacteria dishes, and the bacteria around it had died. He noticed something that many people would have thrown in the trash.
He'd noticed the effect, but turning it into a drug took a decade of work by Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their team at Oxford, who made it in the early 1940s. The three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Penicillin saved many thousands of lives in the Second World War, and it has been one of the most important medical advances in history. It's a lasting lesson that discoveries need both the lucky observation and the hard work.

In 1966 the ecologist Robert Paine experimented on the rocky coast of Washington state by removing all the starfish from a patch of shore. Without them, mussels took over and crowded out other species, and the variety of life dropped sharply.
A single predator turned out to be holding the whole community in balance. He called such species keystone species, like the stone at the top of an arch, which holds all the others in place. Sea otters, which keep sea urchins from destroying kelp forests, are another example. It's a way of seeing that not all species matter equally to an ecosystem, and that the loss of one may have effects far beyond what we'd expect.

Wolves were removed from Yellowstone National Park by the 1920s and brought back in 1995. Some of the effects are well documented, such as fewer elk in some areas, and the elk behaving more warily. They avoid places where they are easy to ambush.
A popular story says that the wolves also changed the courses of the rivers, by letting trees grow back along the banks. That part is debated, since the effects on plants vary and other factors matter. Scientists have found that willows grew back in some places, but not in all, and the connection to the rivers is less clear. So the wolves are a real success story with a more modest effect than the legend suggests.

Energy is lost at each step up a food chain. A plant captures sunlight, a rabbit eats the plant, and a fox eats the rabbit. At each step only about a tenth of the energy gets passed on, since most is used for living and moving, and given off as heat.
That's why there are far fewer lions than zebras, and why food chains rarely have more than four or five links. The real figure varies between about 5 and 20 percent. The rule also explains why eating plants directly is a more efficient use of land than eating animals that have eaten plants. It's a simple idea from the ecologist Raymond Lindeman, and it explains a good deal about how nature is arranged.

About 252 million years ago, the biggest mass extinction in Earth's history happened at the end of the Permian period. Massive volcanic eruptions in what's now Siberia pumped out huge amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases, and changed the climate and the chemistry of the oceans.
An estimated 80 to 96 percent of marine species, and about 70 percent of land vertebrates, died. It took millions of years for life to recover. The survivors then gave rise to a new set of animals, including the dinosaurs. It's a reminder that life on Earth has come close to ending, and that a large, fast change in the atmosphere can be deadly. The planet recovers, but on a timescale much longer than a human life.

The largest known living organism by area is a honey fungus, Armillaria ostoyae, in the Malheur National Forest in Oregon. Most of it is underground, spreading through the soil and the roots of trees as thin threads.
It covers about 2,400 acres, an area as big as well over a thousand football fields. It may be thousands of years old, and the part that you see is just a few mushrooms in the fall. The fungus is a parasite that slowly kills the trees it grows on. It's one single individual, with all of the same DNA. A walk through that forest is, in a way, a walk across the body of one very large and very old living thing.

Popular books have described forests as having an underground "wood wide web," in which trees share food and send warnings through fungi connected to their roots. It's a beautiful idea, and it has been repeated in films and talks, so many people believe it.
But in 2023 a team led by Justine Karst reviewed the research and found that the evidence for forest-wide sharing of nutrients and signals is far weaker than the stories suggest. Fungi do connect to roots, but what they do with the connection is less clear. Some of the best-known claims rest on a small number of experiments. It's a fine example of an appealing idea that has run ahead of the science, and of why it's worth asking how well something has been shown.

Have you noticed a houseplant bending toward a window? That's phototropism. In 1880 Charles Darwin and his son Francis experimented with grass seedlings, covering different parts of them, and found that the tip senses the light and sends a signal to the part below, which bends.
The signal turned out to be a plant hormone, which was later named auxin. It was one of the first plant hormones to be identified. The side of the stem that's away from the light grows faster, and so the plant curves toward it. A simple experiment with a few seedlings and some bits of foil led to the discovery of one of the chemical messengers that control how plants grow, and it came from the same man who wrote On the Origin of Species.

When a honeybee finds a good source of flowers, it returns to the hive and dances on the honeycomb. The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch decoded the dance in the 1940s. The angle of the straight run shows the direction of the food compared with the sun, and how long it lasts shows the distance.
The other bees follow the dancer in the dark, feeling the movements, and then fly off to the flowers. It's one of the few cases in nature of animals passing detailed, abstract information to one another in a kind of symbolic language. He won the 1973 Nobel Prize for it, one of the few Nobels in the study of animal behavior. Many people were skeptical at first, but later experiments confirmed his reading.

An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills and one through the body. Its blood is blue, because it carries oxygen with copper instead of iron. Its body plan is utterly unlike ours, and yet it's very intelligent.
About two-thirds of its neurons are in its arms, and each can taste, touch and even make simple decisions on its own. Octopuses have been seen solving puzzles, opening jars and escaping from tanks. Their ancestors split from ours more than 500 million years ago, so their intelligence evolved on a separate path. Meeting an octopus is as close as we can come to meeting an intelligent alien on Earth.

Tardigrades are microscopic animals, less than a millimeter long, nicknamed water bears. They look like tiny plump creatures with eight legs, and you can find them in a clump of moss.
They can survive being dried out for years, frozen near absolute zero, heated above boiling and exposed to high radiation. In 2007 a European Space Agency experiment exposed them to the vacuum and solar radiation of space for ten days. Some survived and even laid eggs after returning to Earth. When they dry out, they curl up into a state called a tun and suspend their metabolism almost completely. Add water, and they get going again, as if nothing had happened.

Naked mole rats are small, hairless rodents that live underground in colonies in East Africa. They live about 30 years, far longer than mice of similar size, which live about three. They also rarely get cancer.
One reason may be that their cells make an unusually thick, sugary substance that stops cells from crowding together and forming tumors. They also live in colonies with a queen, rather like bees, which is unusual among mammals. Researchers study them for clues about aging and cancer. They're odd-looking animals, but they may have a few things to teach us about how to stay healthy for a long time.

The Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate we know of. In 2016 a team in Denmark used radiocarbon dating on proteins in the lens of the eyes of 28 sharks and estimated that the biggest was about 392 years old, give or take 120 years.
These sharks grow very slowly, only about a centimeter a year, and are thought to reach maturity at about 150 years of age. They live in the cold, deep water of the North Atlantic, where everything runs at a slow pace. A shark born in the 1600s might still be swimming today. The estimates have a wide margin of error, but even the lowest ones show an animal that lives for at least two hundred years.

Turritopsis dohrnii is a tiny jellyfish that, when it's injured or stressed, can turn back into an earlier stage of life. The adult reverts to a polyp, a kind of larval form, and starts its life cycle again.
In theory, it could do it indefinitely. In practice, most of them still get eaten or die of disease, so none of them is truly immortal. But they are a subject of intense study in aging research, because they seem to be able to reset the clock of the cell. The jellyfish is only about the size of a fingernail, and it lives in oceans around the world. It reminds us that aging, which seems a law of nature, may not be as fixed as it appears.

In a 2010 study, John Marzluff and his colleagues at the University of Washington wore a rubber mask while they trapped and banded wild crows. For years afterward, crows scolded and swooped at anyone wearing the same mask, though not at people in other masks.
Even young crows that had never seen the trapping joined in, which means that crows can pass on information about dangerous people. They learn from their parents and from other crows in the flock. The scolding went on for many years. It's a striking sign of how smart crows are, and of how well they can recognize people. If you're nice to a crow, it may remember that too.

Birds are not just related to dinosaurs. They are dinosaurs, the living descendants of a group of feathered, two-legged dinosaurs called theropods. That group also included Tyrannosaurus and Velociraptor, so a chicken is a cousin of the most famous predators who ever lived.
Since the 1990s, spectacular fossils in China have shown many dinosaurs with feathers of various kinds, some of them with wings, and some of them too small to fly. In that sense, a sparrow is a small dinosaur, in the same way that you are a mammal. The dinosaurs that we think of as extinct died out 66 million years ago. The ones in your backyard feeder are the survivors, and there are more than ten thousand species of them.

The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, bigger than any dinosaur. It can grow up to 30 meters long, and weigh around 150 tons. Its blow, the spout of air it breathes out, can rise about 30 feet into the air.
It's astonishing that such an enormous animal feeds mainly on tiny shrimp-like creatures called krill, and it can eat up to about four tons of them a day during the feeding season. It gulps a huge mouthful of water, then pushes it out through plates of baleen, which trap the krill. Blue whales were hunted almost to extinction in the twentieth century, but protection has let some populations begin to recover.

Dogs were the first animal people domesticated, long before farming began. Genetic studies suggest that their ancestors split from wolves some time between 15,000 and 40,000 years ago, though experts debate exactly when. The date is hard to pin down, because the DNA of ancient animals is so scarce.
Dogs have evolved a talent that wolves, and even chimpanzees, lack: the ability to read human gestures such as pointing and to look to our faces for guidance. A puppy will follow where you point, even without training. It's a sign that dogs have been shaped by living with us for a very long time, and that in some ways we have shaped each other. They are, in a sense, a partnership between two species.

Earth has four main layers. There's the thin outer crust that we live on, a thick, slowly flowing mantle, a liquid outer core of molten iron and nickel, and a solid inner core. The crust is thinner, compared with the planet, than the skin of an apple.
The Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann discovered the inner core in 1936, by noticing that some earthquake waves bounced off something solid deep inside the planet. It's about as hot as the surface of the Sun, but it stays solid because of the immense pressure. No one has ever been near it, since the deepest hole ever drilled reaches only about 12 kilometers, and the center lies about 6,400 kilometers down. Everything we know comes from the way earthquake waves travel through.

In 1912 the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined together and have slowly moved apart. He pointed to the way South America and Africa fit together, and to matching fossils and rocks on both sides of the ocean.
Geologists mocked him because he couldn't explain what could move continents. He died in 1930 on an expedition across Greenland, long before he was proved right. In the 1950s and 60s, discoveries about the seafloor provided the answer, in the theory of plate tectonics. The continents ride on large plates that move at about the speed that fingernails grow. It's a good example of an idea that was rejected because of a missing mechanism, and accepted once the evidence was found.
Earthquakes: the Ring of Fire and the magnitude scale

Around the edge of the Pacific Ocean lies a horseshoe-shaped zone of volcanoes and earthquake faults, 40,000 kilometers long, known as the Ring of Fire. About 90 percent of the world's earthquakes, and about 75 percent of its active volcanoes, occur there. The reason is that several tectonic plates meet along the Pacific's edge, where one plate slides under another.
The numbers used to describe earthquakes are logarithmic, so each whole step up means about 32 times more energy released. A magnitude 7 earthquake releases roughly 32 times as much energy as a magnitude 6, and about 1,000 times as much as a magnitude 5. The strongest earthquake ever recorded was a magnitude 9.5 in Chile in 1960. That's why a small difference in magnitude can be a very large difference in damage.
Krakatoa and Tambora: volcanoes that changed weather

On August 27, 1883, the volcano Krakatoa in Indonesia exploded. The sound was heard on Rodrigues Island, 4,800 kilometers away, and is considered the loudest sound in recorded history. The giant tsunamis it generated killed more than 36,000 people. The ash and sulfur it pushed high into the atmosphere dimmed sunsets around the world and lowered global temperatures for several years.
Sixty-eight years earlier, in April 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia had the largest eruption in recorded history. It threw a huge cloud of ash and sulfur into the atmosphere, blocking some sunlight. In 1816, the following year, snow fell in New England in June and frosts came through the summer, and crops failed and food ran short across Europe. It was known as the "year without a summer." The weather of a whole planet can be changed by a single mountain.

Rocks are constantly being recycled. Magma that cools becomes igneous rock. Wind and water wear rocks down into sediment, which gets pressed into layers of sedimentary rock. Heat and pressure transform either type into metamorphic rock.
Any of the three can be melted, buried, uplifted or worn down to become another, over millions of years, in a slow cycle with no beginning or end. Marble is limestone that has been cooked and squeezed, and sandstone is old beach sand. The rock under your feet has been through many lives. It's a useful way of seeing that the ground isn't permanent. It is a slow-moving river, and the Earth is always remaking it.

In 1788 the Scottish farmer and geologist James Hutton studied rock layers at a place called Siccar Point and realized that they showed the same processes we see today, slow erosion and deposition and uplift, repeating over and over. Tilted layers of old rock were overlain by flat layers of younger rock, and it must have taken a very long time.
He wrote that he found "no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end." It made people realize that the Earth is vastly older than the thousands of years that had been assumed. His friend John Playfair, who went there with him, wrote that the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time. We now know that the planet is about 4.5 billion years old, and Hutton's insight was the first step toward that number.

Imagine all 4.5 billion years of Earth's history squeezed into 24 hours. The planet forms at midnight, and the first life appears around 4 a.m. For most of the day, nothing more than microbes lived here.
Dinosaurs arrive around 10:40 p.m., and they die out at about 11:40 p.m. Modern humans show up only in the last six seconds before midnight. Written history would be a flicker in the last fraction of a second. The comparison is useful because it puts our short time into perspective. Everything people have ever done, every war, every invention and every poem, happened in a sliver of the day, and the planet was very busy long before we came along.

In 1812 the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs created a scale for the hardness of minerals, from 1 for talc, which you can scratch with a fingernail, to 10 for diamond. A harder mineral scratches a softer one, and that's the whole test.
Your fingernail is about 2.5, a steel knife about 5.5 and quartz is 7. The scale shows order only, since the steps aren't equal. Diamond is far harder than corundum, which is 9, a bigger gap than between all of the minerals below it. It's still a handy tool. A geologist in the field can identify many minerals with only a coin, a nail and a pocketknife, by seeing what scratches what.

Oceans hold about 97 percent of Earth's water, and it's salty. Of the remaining 3 percent that's fresh, most is locked up in glaciers and ice sheets, so only about 1 percent of all the water is fresh water that's easy for us to reach.
Of the liquid fresh water, most is underground, and rivers and lakes hold only a tiny fraction. If all the water on Earth were gathered into a ball, it would be much smaller than you'd expect, about 1,400 kilometers across. Our planet looks blue from space, but the film of water on its surface is thin, and the part we can drink is thinner still. It's a good reason to value what we have.

We know more about the surface of the Moon than about our own seafloor. In 2023, the Seabed 2030 project, which is working to map all of it, reported that about a quarter of the ocean floor had been mapped to high resolution.
The deepest known point is Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 kilometers down, deeper than Mount Everest is tall. Only a handful of people have ever been there. The sea floor isn't flat, either. It has mountain ranges, canyons and volcanoes, including the longest mountain chain on Earth, the mid-ocean ridge, which winds around the globe. It's a surprising fact that so much of our own planet is still unexplored.

The atmosphere is made up of layers. The lowest, the troposphere, reaches about 12 kilometers up and holds most of the air and almost all weather. Commercial jets fly near its top, which is why the air outside is so cold, about minus 55 degrees Celsius.
Above it is the stratosphere, which holds the ozone layer that absorbs harmful ultraviolet light. Space has no sharp edge, but by convention, it starts at the Kármán line, 100 kilometers above the surface. If Earth were the size of an apple, the atmosphere that holds nearly all our air would be about as thin as the skin of that apple. We live at the bottom of a very thin layer, and everything we breathe is in it.

In the 1980s scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica, caused by chemicals called CFCs, used in aerosol sprays and refrigerators. Without the ozone layer, much more harmful ultraviolet light would reach the ground, which would raise the risk of skin cancer and damage crops.
In 1987 countries signed the Montreal Protocol, banning them. It worked. The UN reported in 2022 that the ozone layer is on track to recover to 1980 levels by about 2066 over Antarctica, much sooner elsewhere. It's one of the few cases in which the world acted together on an environmental threat and succeeded. The agreement is often cited as a model for what international cooperation can do, and a reason to believe that other global problems can be solved.

Gases in the atmosphere, such as carbon dioxide, water vapor and methane, trap some of the heat that Earth radiates, keeping the planet warmer than it would otherwise be. Without any greenhouse effect, the average temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius, and the oceans would be frozen.
John Tyndall measured it in the lab in 1859, and in 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated how much extra carbon dioxide would warm the planet. The basic physics has been understood for well over a century. The effect itself is natural and necessary for life. The concern is about what happens when we add more of the gases, in the same way that a thicker blanket would make a bed warmer.
