Before the Industrial Revolution, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air was about 280 parts per million. Today it's over 420. That's a rise of more than 50 percent, in about two hundred years.
Ice cores, which trap ancient air in bubbles, show that for 800,000 years before industrialization, it stayed between about 180 and 300. Burning coal, oil and gas, and clearing forests, account for the recent rise. A tell-tale sign is the chemistry of the carbon itself, which shows that the extra carbon dioxide comes from fossil fuels. Careful measurements on a mountain in Hawaii have been tracking the climb since 1958.

Earth's average surface temperature has risen by about 1.1 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s. The 2021 report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change states that it's unequivocal that human influence has warmed the planet.
Most of the increase has happened since about 1970, and the last decade has been the warmest on record. It may not sound like much, but the average temperature of the whole planet is hard to move. The difference between today and the last ice age, when ice covered much of North America, was only about five or six degrees. A change of one degree in the global average is a big shift, and it brings more heat waves and heavier rains in many places.

For the last couple of million years, Earth has swung between long ice ages and warmer interglacial periods. The Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković worked out that slow changes in Earth's orbit and tilt, in cycles of about 100,000, 41,000 and 23,000 years, alter how much sunlight reaches different latitudes and trigger the cycles.
The last glacial maximum was about 20,000 years ago. At that time, ice sheets covered Canada and northern Europe, and the sea was about 120 meters lower than it is today, so that people could walk from Asia to North America. A study of seafloor sediments in 1976 gave strong support to Milanković's idea. The ice ages show how sensitive the planet is to small changes in the sunlight it receives.

Hurricanes need warm ocean water, at least about 26.5 degrees Celsius, as fuel. The warm water gives them heat and moisture. When a hurricane moves over land or cooler water, it loses its fuel and weakens quickly.
The Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes from category 1 to 5 by their wind speed, with category 5 starting at 157 miles per hour. That's why the hurricane season peaks in late summer, when the sea is warmest. Hurricanes are called typhoons in the western Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean, but they're the same kind of storm. In the Southern Hemisphere, they spin the other way, clockwise.

A rainbow forms when sunlight enters raindrops, bends, reflects off the back and bends again as it leaves, spreading into colors. The red light always exits at an angle of about 42 degrees from the direction directly opposite the Sun.
Every raindrop sends colored light in many directions, but you see only the drops at the right angle. So no two people see exactly the same rainbow, and you carry yours with you as you move. The rainbow is also a full circle, though the ground cuts it off. From an airplane, you can sometimes see the whole circle. It's a lovely fact that something so shared and so familiar is, in a way, a private view.

A snowflake starts as a tiny ice crystal, and because of the shape of water molecules, it has six sides. As it falls, the shape it grows into depends on the temperature and humidity along the way, so each flake has its own history.
Wilson Bentley, a farmer in Vermont, began photographing them with a microscope camera in 1885, and took more than 5,000 images. The saying that no two are alike is probably true for the larger, more complicated ones, since there are so many possible paths. Simple, small ones can be identical. Each flake is a record of the weather it has passed through on its way down, written in ice.

Because Earth spins, moving air and water curve to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern. This is the Coriolis effect, and it's why storms rotate counterclockwise in the north and clockwise in the south.
But it's far too weak to decide which way water swirls down a sink or toilet, which depends on the shape of the bowl and any currents in the water. The effect only matters over large distances and long times, such as a hurricane, a long-range artillery shell or the great ocean currents. The old story about drains in the two hemispheres is a popular myth, and you can happily ignore it.

Every two to seven years, the surface of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean warms, trade winds weaken, and weather patterns shift around the world. This is called El Niño, the Spanish for "the boy," a name given by Peruvian fishermen who noticed the warm water around Christmas.
It can bring floods to Peru, droughts to Australia and Indonesia and milder winters in parts of North America. Its cooler opposite phase is called La Niña. The cycle is one of the largest natural patterns in the climate, and forecasters watch it closely, since it affects crops, fisheries and storms across many countries. It's a reminder that the weather in one place may depend on the temperature of water thousands of miles away.

The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a liquid is, from 0 to 14, with 7 neutral, like pure water. The Danish chemist Søren Sørensen introduced it in 1909, while working at the Carlsberg brewery's laboratory, where the acidity of beer mattered.
Each step is a tenfold change, so lemon juice, at about pH 2, is 100,000 times more acidic than water. Lye is at the other end, about 13. Your blood is kept very close to 7.4, and even a small shift can be dangerous. The scale is logarithmic, so it's good to remember that a change of one unit is a big deal. A few numbers are enough to describe everything from stomach acid to household bleach.

A soap molecule has two ends: one that's attracted to water and one that's attracted to grease. When you wash, the grease-loving ends stick into oil and dirt, and the water-loving ends face outward, so that water can carry the oil away.
Soap can also break apart the fatty outer envelope of some viruses, including coronaviruses, which is why handwashing works so well. It doesn't matter whether the soap is antibacterial, since regular soap does the job, as long as you scrub for about twenty seconds. The soap and the friction pull germs off the skin, and the water rinses them down the drain. It's a simple chemical trick that has saved countless lives.

Dissolving salt in water lowers the temperature at which it freezes. Seawater freezes at about minus 2 degrees Celsius, and a saturated salt solution won't freeze until about minus 21. That's why roads are salted in winter, so that ice melts and doesn't form.
The same trick is used in old-fashioned ice cream makers, where salt added to ice makes the mixture colder than freezing, so the cream freezes. It stops working well when it gets extremely cold, below about minus 10 degrees Celsius, when other chemicals are used. Salt also damages roads, cars and streams, so some cities now use alternatives, such as sand or beet juice, to protect the environment.

Atoms are far too small to count one at a time, so chemists count them in huge groups called moles. A mole is 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd particles, known as Avogadro's number. It's about as many as the number of grains of sand on all the beaches of the Earth, many times over.
It's set up so that a mole of carbon-12 atoms weighs 12 grams. That lets chemists, by weighing, count atoms. A mole of water is 18 grams, about a tablespoon, and it holds that vast number of molecules. Since 2019, the number has been fixed as an exact value, and the mole is now defined by it. The idea is named for Amedeo Avogadro, an Italian scientist who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gases hold equal numbers of molecules.

In a chemical reaction, nothing is created or destroyed. In 1789 Antoine Lavoisier carefully weighed everything before and after burning things in sealed vessels and showed that the total mass didn't change.
When something burns, it gains the weight of the oxygen it combines with. A log seems to lose most of its weight when it burns, but that's because the gases escape into the air. If you could catch every bit of the smoke and the ash, the weight would be the same. His work ended the old theory that burning releases a substance called phlogiston. Lavoisier is often called the father of modern chemistry, though he lost his head to the guillotine in 1794.

If you squeeze a gas into half the space, its pressure doubles, as long as the temperature stays the same. Robert Boyle worked this out in 1662, with air trapped in a bent glass tube and mercury. He poured mercury in the open end and watched the trapped air get smaller.
It explains why a bicycle pump heats up when you use it, and why your ears pop in an airplane when the pressure of the air around you changes. It's also how your lungs work. When your chest muscles expand your chest, the pressure inside falls, and air flows in. It's among the oldest laws of chemistry, and it applies to everything from a scuba tank to a syringe.

In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown noticed that tiny grains of pollen in water jiggle around constantly. He couldn't explain it, and he checked that it wasn't due to the pollen being alive, since dust from rocks did the same.
In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that it happens because invisible water molecules are bumping into the grains from all sides. The French physicist Jean Perrin confirmed it with experiments in the following years, which also convinced skeptics that atoms and molecules really exist. Until then, some distinguished scientists had doubted that atoms were real. A simple jiggle seen through a microscope became strong evidence for the unseen world of molecules.

In 1907 the Belgian-American chemist Leo Baekeland invented Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, from phenol and formaldehyde. Earlier plastics were made from natural materials, such as cellulose. Bakelite was made from scratch.
Unlike earlier plastics, it didn't melt once it was set, so it could be used for things that got hot, like telephone housings, radios and electrical parts. It was nicknamed "the material of a thousand uses." Baekeland had already become rich from inventing a photographic paper, and he did the work in a laboratory he had built behind his house. The material started the age of plastics, and its descendants are now everywhere. Today we make hundreds of millions of tons of plastic a year, and disposing of it has become one of the great environmental problems of our time.

PFAS are a large family of man-made chemicals that were used for decades in non-stick pans, waterproof fabrics and firefighting foam. They're called "forever chemicals" because their carbon-fluorine bonds, among the strongest in chemistry, mean they don't break down, so they build up in the environment and our bodies.
High levels have been linked to health problems including some cancers and reduced immune response. They have been found in rain, in water supplies and in the blood of nearly everyone tested. Regulators have been setting limits for them in drinking water, and manufacturers have been phasing out the worst ones. Cleaning them up is difficult. It's a case of a chemical that was useful in the short term and unexpectedly troublesome in the long term.

A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself. Enzymes are the catalysts of living things, making the reactions of life happen fast enough at body temperature. In a car's exhaust system, the catalytic converter uses platinum and related metals to turn harmful gases into less harmful ones.
Without catalysts, many reactions in your cells would be too slow to keep you alive. A single enzyme can do its job millions of times a second. Industry depends on them, too. The Haber-Bosch process, which makes fertilizer, uses an iron catalyst, and oil refineries rely on them all day long. A catalyst doesn't change what is possible. It only changes how fast it happens, and that can make all the difference.

Fire needs three things: fuel, heat and oxygen. Take away any one, and it goes out. That simple idea is the basis of every way of fighting a fire, from the smallest to the largest.
Water cools a fire, removing heat. A fire blanket or lid cuts off the oxygen. A firebreak removes the fuel. Fire safety experts now often use a fire tetrahedron, which adds a fourth element, the chemical chain reaction that keeps a flame going. Knowing this, you can choose the right method. For a grease fire in a pan, for example, put a lid on it, and never throw water, which would spread the burning oil.

Rust is what happens when iron slowly reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide, which is flaky and weak. Unlike the thin oxide layer on aluminum, which protects the metal below, rust flakes off and exposes fresh metal to the air, so the damage keeps going.
Salt speeds up the process, which is why cars rust faster where roads are salted, and near the sea. Stainless steel resists rust because the chromium in it forms a thin, invisible protective layer. The damage from corrosion costs the world's economies trillions of dollars a year. Paint, oil and coatings of zinc all work by keeping water and air away from the iron, and a small scratch left alone can eventually become a big problem.

Many ancient peoples used a mark to hold an empty place in a number, so that 305 could be told from 35. But treating zero as a number in its own right, one you can add and multiply, came from India. It was an idea that took a long time to arrive, and it changed the way people could calculate.
The Bakhshali manuscript, a birch-bark text carbon-dated to somewhere between the 3rd and 4th centuries, uses a dot for zero. In 628 the astronomer Brahmagupta wrote down rules for arithmetic with zero, including what happens when you add it to or subtract it from other numbers. From India the idea traveled through the Arab world to Europe. Without it, our whole way of writing numbers would be impossible.

Chinese mathematicians were working with negative numbers around 2,000 years ago. The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art used red counting rods for positive numbers and black ones for negative, which is the opposite of the way accountants use red ink today.
European mathematicians were much slower to accept them, and for centuries many called negative answers "absurd" or "fictitious," since you can't have less than nothing of something. They only became standard in the 1600s and later. It's a good reminder that ideas we find obvious were once hard to swallow. A debt, a temperature below freezing and a position below sea level are all things we now describe easily with a minus sign.

Pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159, and the digits go on forever with no repeating pattern. Every circle, big or small, has the same ratio. It's one of the few numbers that people of every culture have discovered for themselves.
In 1761 Johann Lambert proved that it can't be written as a fraction. In 1882 Ferdinand von Lindemann proved the stronger result that it's transcendental, not the solution of any ordinary algebraic equation. That showed that the ancient puzzle of "squaring the circle" with a compass and straightedge is impossible. The Greeks had tried for two thousand years, and the answer was that no one ever could.
How many digits of pi do we need?

You might think space navigation would need thousands of digits of pi, but NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory says that it uses 15 for its most exacting calculations. Fifteen is more than enough for any spacecraft.
They've calculated that even for a circle with a radius of about 15 billion miles, farther than Voyager 1 has traveled, 15 digits would put the circumference off by only about an inch. Computers have calculated 100 trillion digits, for the sheer fun of it. Such records don't help with engineering. They're done as a test of computers and of programmers' skill, and because people are curious. For everyday work, 3.14 is plenty.

The number e, about 2.71828, appears wherever things grow or decay continuously. Jacob Bernoulli found it in 1683 while asking a question about money. If a bank pays 100 percent interest, what happens if it's compounded more and more often, every month, every day, every second?
The amount doesn't grow forever. It approaches e. If you start with one dollar and compound continuously for a year at 100 percent, you end up with about $2.72. The number turns up in population growth, radioactive decay and the bell curve. It's as basic as pi, but it's less well known, perhaps because its story starts with a puzzle about interest.

Euler's identity is e raised to the power of i times pi, plus one, equals zero. It joins five of the most fundamental numbers in mathematics, e, i, pi, 1 and 0, in a single short equation using addition, multiplication and exponents. Each number came from a different branch of mathematics, and yet here they are together.
It comes from a formula discovered by Leonhard Euler in 1748. Many mathematicians consider it the most beautiful equation, and in a survey of readers of a mathematics magazine, it was voted that. The beauty is a matter of taste, but the surprise is real. Nobody would guess, looking at those five numbers, that they had anything to do with each other.

The square root of minus one can't be an ordinary number, since any number times itself is positive. Yet in 1545 the Italian Girolamo Cardano found that using such "impossible" numbers in the middle of a calculation could give correct, real answers, though he thought they were useless.
Rafael Bombelli worked out the rules for them in 1572. Today, mathematicians write the square root of minus one as i, and use such numbers for alternating current, signal processing and quantum mechanics. The name "imaginary" was meant as an insult, but it stuck. They are no less real than any other number. They're a tool that lets us describe things that go in circles, like waves, and that's why they are so useful.

A prime number is divisible only by one and itself. Around 300 BC the Greek mathematician Euclid proved that there are infinitely many. His argument is short: suppose you had a complete list of all the primes. Multiply them together and add one. The result isn't divisible by any prime on your list, so there must be another prime, and the list wasn't complete after all.
It's still a model of an elegant proof. Even so, the biggest primes we know are enormous. The largest found as of October 2024 has more than 41 million digits. A former NVIDIA engineer, Luke Durant, found it by running software on graphics processors in cloud computers across many countries. It's two raised to the power 136,279,841, minus one, a kind of number called a Mersenne prime. Such records are usually broken every few years, with the help of volunteer computing.

In 1742 the mathematician Christian Goldbach wrote to Leonhard Euler suggesting that every even number greater than two is the sum of two primes. For example, 10 is 3 plus 7, and 28 is 5 plus 23. You can try it for yourself, and it always seems to work.
Computers have checked it for every even number up to about four quintillion, and it's never failed. But nobody has found a proof, and it remains one of the oldest unsolved problems in mathematics. It's a striking thing, that a statement a child can understand has defeated the best mathematicians for nearly three hundred years. It's a reminder that "obviously true" and "proved" are not the same.

In 1202 Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, published a book that included a puzzle about how many pairs of rabbits there would be after a year, if each pair has a new pair every month. The answer gave the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, where each number is the sum of the two before it.
Indian mathematicians had noticed the sequence earlier. Pine cones, sunflower heads and pineapples often show spirals that count in Fibonacci numbers, such as 8 spirals one way and 13 the other. The reason is that the arrangement packs the seeds efficiently as the plant grows. The book itself did something more important. It introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals, 0 through 9, to Europe, where people were still using Roman numerals.

The golden ratio, about 1.618, is the number you get when a line is cut so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer is to the shorter. It's the limit of the ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers, which get closer to it the further you go.
Many people say it's the secret behind the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa and beauty itself, but those claims are mostly myth and wishful measuring. You can draw a rectangle on almost anything and find the ratio, if you aren't particular about where the edges are. The number itself is genuinely interesting, and it turns up in pentagons and in some plant growth. It's a lovely number without needing the legend.

In any right-angled triangle, the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two. If the two short sides are 3 and 4, the long one is 5, since 9 plus 16 is 25. It's the basis of how we measure distance.
A Babylonian clay tablet from about 1800 BC, known as Plimpton 322, lists number sets that fit the rule, so people knew it a thousand years before Pythagoras. Pythagoras's name is attached to it because the first proofs known to us came from the Greek tradition. More than 300 different proofs have been found since, including one by a US president, James Garfield, in 1876. Builders have used the 3-4-5 triangle for thousands of years to make square corners.

The diagonal of a square with sides of length one is the square root of two, and it can't be written as a fraction. The ancient proof is a clever argument by contradiction. Suppose it were a fraction p over q, in lowest terms. Then you can show that both p and q would have to be even, which contradicts "lowest terms."
A legend says that the Pythagoreans, who believed all numbers were ratios, were deeply disturbed by the discovery. According to one version of the story, a member who revealed it was thrown from a boat, though no one knows whether it is true. What is certain is that the discovery was a shock, because it showed that some lengths can't be measured exactly by whole numbers and their ratios.
Infinity comes in sizes: Cantor and Hilbert's hotel

It sounds absurd, but there are different sizes of infinity. In 1874 and again in 1891, the German mathematician Georg Cantor showed that you can't make a complete list of all the real numbers, the decimals, even an infinite one. Whatever list you offer, you can build a new number by changing one digit in each entry, and it can't be on the list. So the real numbers are a bigger infinity than the whole numbers. Some contemporaries thought he was mad.
The mathematician David Hilbert used a thought experiment to illustrate how strange infinity is. Imagine a hotel with infinitely many rooms, all full. A new guest arrives. No problem: ask each guest to move to the room with double their number, which leaves all the odd-numbered rooms empty. With infinite sets, a part can be as big as the whole, which is bizarre, and yet it follows from the rules.

Around 450 BC the Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea argued that the fast runner Achilles could never catch a tortoise with a head start. By the time Achilles reaches where the tortoise was, it's moved on a bit, and so on forever. Every time he gets to where it was, it has moved a little further.
The puzzle bothered thinkers for two thousand years, until mathematicians showed that an infinite series of ever smaller steps can add up to a finite total, so that Achilles does catch up. If a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on are added up, they come to exactly one. It's an example of how a simple paradox can lead to deep ideas about infinity, and about how to add up an endless list of numbers.

Calculus is the mathematics of change. It rests on two ideas: finding the slope of a curve at a point, which tells you the rate of change, and finding the area under a curve, which adds up many small pieces. The two turn out to be opposites of each other, and that's the central fact of the subject.
Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz developed it independently, between the 1660s and 1680s, and their followers carried on a bitter dispute over who deserved the credit. It underlies physics, engineering and economics. Anything that changes, such as a falling stone, a growing population or a cooling cup of coffee, can be described with it. Leibniz's notation is the one that most students still learn today.

The city of Königsberg, now Kaliningrad, had seven bridges that connected two islands and the banks of a river. Residents wondered whether you could walk through the city and cross each bridge exactly once. No one could find a way, but no one could prove it was impossible, either.
In 1736 Leonhard Euler showed that you could not. He simplified the map to dots and lines, which created graph theory. The key was to count how many bridges lead to each land mass. It now helps describe networks of all kinds, from roads to the internet to friendships. It's a good example of how the right simplification, throwing away most of the details, can reveal a deep truth.

Take a long strip of paper, give it a half twist and tape the ends together. You get a Möbius strip, a loop with only one side and one edge. August Möbius and Johann Listing described it independently in 1858.
If you draw a line along the middle until you return to the start, you'll find you've covered what looked like both sides. If you cut it down the middle, you don't get two loops. You get one longer loop. It's a classic example of a surface with surprising properties, and you can make one in a minute. Conveyor belts are sometimes made as Möbius strips, so that both sides wear evenly.

Topology is a branch of mathematics that studies shapes in terms of what stays the same when you stretch, bend or squash them, without tearing. To a topologist, a coffee cup and a doughnut are the same shape, because each has exactly one hole, and one can be smoothly deformed into the other.
It might sound like a game, but topology has real uses in physics, biology and data analysis. It helps describe how DNA tangles, how the universe might be shaped and what the structure of a large data set is. The subject grew out of Euler's solution of the bridge problem. Its main idea is that for many questions, the exact distances don't matter, and only how things are connected does.

In 1852 a mapmaker's observation raised a question: can any map be colored with just four colors, so that no neighboring regions share a color? It seems like it should be easy to settle, and yet for over a century, nobody could prove it.
In 1976 Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken did, with the help of a computer that checked nearly 2,000 cases, using over 1,200 hours of computer time. It was the first major theorem proved with a computer, and some mathematicians were uneasy about that, since no person could check every step by hand. Since then, the use of computers in proofs has become more accepted, and the theorem has been verified in other ways.

Around 1637 the French lawyer and mathematician Pierre de Fermat scribbled in a book margin that no whole numbers satisfy a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n for n above two. He added that he had a marvelous proof, but the margin was too small.
Nobody found a proof for 357 years. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in 1994, after seven years of working in secret in his attic, using mathematics that didn't exist in Fermat's day. An error was found and fixed in 1995, with the help of a former student, Richard Taylor. Most mathematicians doubt that Fermat's own proof, if he had one, was right. The story shows how a single line in a margin can drive a search for centuries.

In 1931 the young logician Kurt Gödel proved something startling. In any consistent system of rules rich enough to include arithmetic, there are true statements that can't be proved within the system. He was only 25 years old.
It ended the dream of David Hilbert and others of finding a complete and consistent set of rules for all of mathematics. It showed that there are built-in limits to what proof can do. The proof works by constructing a statement that says, in effect, "this statement can't be proved." If it could be proved, it would be false, which would be a contradiction. So it's true and unprovable. The result is among the most profound in the history of logic.

In 1936 Alan Turing asked whether it's possible to write a program that can look at any other program and tell, in advance, whether it will eventually stop or run forever. He proved that it can't be done, using a clever self-referring argument.
It's a real limit on what computers can do, not just a limit of today's technology, and it was one of the first such results in computer science. It means that there will always be questions about programs that no program can answer. Turing worked this out before the first electronic computer had been built, by thinking about an imaginary machine. His abstract machine is still used to define what it means to compute.

Some problems, like solving a big Sudoku or finding the best route through many cities, are hard to solve but easy to check once someone shows you an answer. The question of whether every problem whose answer can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly is called P versus NP.
It's one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a million-dollar prize. Most experts believe the answer is no, that some problems really are harder to solve than to check, but nobody has proved it. If it were yes, it would transform the world. Codes used to protect online banking would be breakable, and many tasks in science and industry could be done much faster. It's one of the deepest open questions in all of science.

In 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute named seven of the deepest unsolved problems in mathematics and offered $1 million for the solution of each. They were chosen to echo the famous list of problems posed by David Hilbert in 1900.
Only one has been solved so far: the Poincaré conjecture, by the Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman, in 2002 and 2003. He declined the prize and the other honors, including the Fields Medal, saying that he wasn't interested in money or fame. The rest, including the Riemann hypothesis and P versus NP, remain open. Anyone who can solve one will have solved a question that has stumped the best minds for generations.
Two surprising patterns: Benford and Zipf

In many real collections of numbers, like river lengths, populations and stock prices, about 30 percent of them begin with the digit 1, and fewer than 5 percent begin with 9. Simon Newcomb noticed in 1881 that the early pages of logarithm tables were more worn than the later ones, and Frank Benford rediscovered it in 1938. Auditors use it to catch fraud, since invented numbers tend not to follow the pattern.
Another strange regularity applies to words. In nearly any large body of text, the most common word appears about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, and so on. The linguist George Zipf described it in 1935. In English, "the" makes up about 7 percent of words. Strikingly similar patterns appear in the sizes of cities and the traffic to websites, though no one fully understands why.
The bell curve and why it appears

Many measurements, such as heights, test scores and measurement errors, cluster around an average and thin out symmetrically on either side, in what's called the normal distribution. About 68 percent of values fall within one standard deviation of the average, 95 percent within two, and 99.7 percent within three. Carl Friedrich Gauss used it in the early 1800s to handle errors in astronomical measurements.
Why does this shape show up so often? The central limit theorem says that if you take the average of many independent random things, the result tends to form a bell curve, whatever the shape of the original distribution. A general version was proved by Pierre-Simon Laplace in 1810. It explains why so many things in nature look bell-shaped, and it is one of the main reasons that statistics works.

If you flip a fair coin only a few times, you might get seven heads in ten. But as the number of flips grows, the share of heads gets closer and closer to a half. This is the law of large numbers, proved by Jacob Bernoulli, and published in 1713.
It's why casinos always win in the long run. A casino may lose to a lucky player in a single night, but over millions of bets, the small edge in its favor adds up with certainty. It's also a warning that small samples can easily mislead. A hot streak in a few games, or a surprising result from a small survey, doesn't tell you much. The law works only when there are many trials. It doesn't mean that luck will "even out" in the short term.

In 1654 the French mathematicians Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat exchanged letters about a gambling problem. How should the stakes be divided fairly if a game of chance is interrupted before it's finished? A nobleman who liked to gamble had put the question to Pascal.
Their solutions laid the foundations of probability theory. Before then, people had played games of chance for thousands of years but had no mathematics to describe them. The approach they took, to count the possible outcomes and see how many favor each player, is still the basic method. It's a nice case of a practical problem leading to a whole new branch of mathematics. Today, probability is the basis of insurance, genetics, weather forecasts and much else.

The number of ways to arrange a deck of 52 cards is 52 factorial, which is about 8 followed by 67 zeros. That's so large that every time you properly shuffle a deck, you almost certainly create an order that has never occurred before in the history of the world.
If every person on Earth shuffled a deck every second since the start of the universe, they'd barely scratch the surface. The number grows so fast because each card you add multiplies the possibilities by the size of the deck. It's a striking example of how quickly combinations can grow. The same fact is the reason why a good password, built from many characters, is very hard to guess.

The idea that a monkey hitting keys at random on a typewriter would eventually type the complete works of Shakespeare goes back to Émile Borel in 1913. It's true in theory, if given infinite time. Any particular string of letters has a definite chance, however small, of turning up.
But it would take far longer than the age of the universe for any realistic number of monkeys. The chance of even a short phrase, such as a line of a sonnet, is astronomically small. The theorem is really about the nature of large numbers and chance, not about literature. It's a reminder that "possible" and "likely" can be very far apart, and that a very rare event is not the same as an impossible one.

A logarithm turns multiplication into addition. In 1614 the Scottish mathematician John Napier published tables of them, which saved astronomers and navigators years of tedious arithmetic. To multiply two big numbers, you looked up their logarithms, added them, and looked up the answer.
Around 1622 the English minister William Oughtred used the idea to invent the slide rule, two sliding scales marked with logarithms. For about 350 years it was a standard tool, and engineers carried them in their pockets. Apollo astronauts carried slide rules as a backup. Pocket calculators replaced them in the early 1970s. Many quantities are still measured on logarithmic scales, including earthquakes on the Richter scale, sound in decibels and acidity in pH.

A legend says the inventor of chess asked a king for a reward of one grain of rice on the first square of the board, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time. The king agreed, thinking it modest. It sounded like a few bags of rice at most.
By the 64th square, the amount would be about 18 quintillion grains, more rice than has ever been grown. The first half of the board adds up to a manageable pile, and it's in the second half that the numbers become huge. It's a classic illustration of exponential growth, which can look slow at the start and then suddenly overwhelm everything. That's the pattern of an epidemic, a bank balance with compound interest, and a chain reaction.

Pick any positive whole number. If it's even, halve it. If it's odd, triple it and add one. Keep going. The conjecture is that you'll always eventually reach 1. Try it with 7: it goes 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Lothar Collatz posed it in 1937, and computers have tested it for every number up to nearly 300 quintillion, but there's no proof. The mathematician Paul Erdős said that mathematics may not be ready for such problems. It's a deceptive puzzle. It's so simple that a child can try it, and yet it has defeated the world's best mathematicians for almost a century.
How we count: binary and base sixty

Computers use the binary system, where there are only two digits, 0 and 1, instead of our ten. In 1703 the German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz wrote about it, and was fascinated that all numbers could be made from just those two symbols. Each digit is a bit, and eight bits make a byte. Any number, letter, picture or sound can be written in binary, which suits machines that have switches that are either on or off.
We divide hours into 60 minutes and minutes into 60 seconds because the ancient Babylonians counted in base 60. It's a handy number: 60 can be divided evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, so fractions are easy. We still use it for time, and the 360 degrees of a circle probably also come from the Babylonians. The numbers we count in are a human choice.

Around 300 BC the Greek mathematician Euclid wrote the Elements, a textbook that built all of geometry from a handful of simple assumptions, called axioms, by logical proof. Each result was supported by those that came before it.
It was used for over 2,000 years and became one of the most influential books ever written. Abraham Lincoln is said to have studied it as a young lawyer, to learn how to argue and prove a point. The book's lasting influence is the method more than the content. The idea that you can start from simple, clear assumptions and reason your way to surprising conclusions is the basis of mathematics, and of much of science and philosophy.

Euclid assumed that, given a line and a point not on it, there's exactly one line through the point that never meets the first. For centuries, mathematicians tried to prove this, until in the 1820s and 30s, Gauss, János Bolyai and Nikolai Lobachevsky showed that you can build consistent geometries without it.
On a curved surface, the angles of a triangle add up to more or less than 180 degrees. Think of a triangle drawn on a globe, with one corner at the North Pole and two on the equator, where each angle is 90 degrees. A century later, Einstein used these ideas to describe curved spacetime. It's a good example of how pure mathematics, explored for its own sake, can become the language of physics.

A fractal is a shape that looks similar at every scale, like a coastline, a fern or a snowflake edge. The mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot named them in 1975. He asked a famous question in 1967, "How long is the coast of Britain?" and showed that there's no single answer: the more finely you measure, the longer it gets.
Fractals help describe many natural shapes, such as clouds, mountains, lightning and the branching of blood vessels and lungs. They're also used in computer graphics to make realistic landscapes. A fractal can be generated from a very simple rule repeated over and over. That's the secret of its beauty, since the simple rule creates a complicated and endlessly detailed picture.

In 1961 the meteorologist Edward Lorenz was running a weather simulation on a computer. To save time, he restarted a run in the middle, typing in 0.506 instead of the full figure, 0.506127. The tiny difference grew until the forecast was completely different.
It showed that small changes can lead to large differences later, and it's one reason that weather can only be forecast about ten days to two weeks ahead. The name comes from a talk in which Lorenz asked whether a butterfly flapping its wings in Brazil could set off a tornado in Texas. The point wasn't about butterflies. It was that some systems are so sensitive that long-term prediction is impossible, even when the rules are perfectly known.

In this method, you assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show that it leads to an absurdity, so the assumption must be false. It's used to prove that the square root of 2 is irrational, and that there are infinitely many primes.
The English mathematician G. H. Hardy wrote that it "is one of a mathematician's finest weapons." It's like checking a door by assuming it's open and finding you'd walk through a wall. It's also a useful way to think in everyday life. If someone's claim leads to a result that can't be true, the claim has to be wrong, and you don't need to look at every detail to say so.

According to a well-known story, when Carl Friedrich Gauss was about ten, his teacher asked the class to add up the numbers from 1 to 100, hoping to keep them busy. Gauss gave the answer in moments. He saw that 1 plus 100 is 101, 2 plus 99 is 101, and so on, making 50 pairs of 101, which is 5,050. The tale may have been embellished in the retelling, but the method is real and useful.
The same sum can be proved another way, by induction, a way of showing that something is true for all whole numbers. First show that it's true for the first case. Then show that, if it's true for any case, it must be true for the next one. It's like a line of dominoes: if the first falls, and each one knocks over the next, then they all fall. It proves that the sum of the first n numbers is n times n plus one, divided by two.

In September 1999 NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter, which had traveled nine months to reach Mars, approached the planet too low and was lost. The cause was a mix-up in units. Software built by one team gave the thrust in pound-force seconds, which is the English system, and the navigation team expected newton-seconds, which is metric.
The $125 million spacecraft probably burned up in the atmosphere. A pound-force is about 4.45 newtons, so every correction to the course was off by that factor. It's a vivid reminder that a number without its unit is meaningless. The investigation found that the problem could have been caught, and the lesson led to stricter checks on how teams share data. Even the best engineers can fail on something as basic as units.

Honeybees build their wax cells as hexagons, and a mathematician explains why: it's the most efficient shape. The honeycomb conjecture, which goes back to the ancient Greeks, says that dividing a flat surface into equal-area cells with the least total boundary is best done with a hexagonal grid.
Thomas Hales proved it in 1999. Bees use the least wax to store the most honey. Wax is costly for a bee to make, since it takes roughly six to eight pounds of honey to produce a pound of wax. Circles would leave gaps, and squares or triangles would need more wall. The bees don't know any mathematics, of course. Over a long time, natural selection has favored the colonies that saved wax.

In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether proved a result that physicists consider one of the most beautiful and important. Every symmetry in nature leads to a conservation law. If the laws of physics are the same at all times, energy is conserved. If they're the same everywhere in space, momentum is conserved.
Noether worked for years at the University of Göttingen without pay or a formal position, because she was a woman. When she died in 1935, Einstein wrote that she was the most significant creative mathematical genius since women were admitted to higher education. Her theorem is a pillar of modern physics, and it explains why the conservation laws hold. They aren't a coincidence. They follow from the symmetry of the world.

In the eastern United States, some cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground and then emerge together in huge numbers. Both numbers are primes. One hypothesis is that prime-numbered cycles make it hard for predators or other cicada broods with shorter cycles to line up with them.
If a cicada came out every 12 years, a predator with a cycle of 2, 3, 4 or 6 years would often catch up with it. With a 17-year cycle, an overlap with shorter cycles is rare. It's an elegant idea, but it's a hypothesis, and not all biologists are persuaded. The mathematical argument is attractive, but the evidence is not conclusive. Still, the emergences are a spectacle, with billions of insects coming up at once, and a neat puzzle.

Pi Day is celebrated on March 14, because 3.14 are the first digits of pi. The physicist Larry Shaw organized the first celebration at the Exploratorium museum in San Francisco in 1988, with a march around a circular space, followed by fruit pie.
March 14 is also Albert Einstein's birthday. In 2019 UNESCO proclaimed it the International Day of Mathematics. The celebration is playful, but it brings a lot of people together to think about numbers, and many schools and museums hold events. It's a good reminder that mathematics can be fun. If you want to join in, you can bake a pie, recite as many digits as you can, or just measure a circle and divide.

These are three ways of saying "typical," and they can give very different answers. The mean is the usual average, found by adding everything up and dividing. The median is the middle value when you line them all up, and the mode is the most common one.
If Bill Gates walks into a bar, the average wealth of the people in it shoots up, but the median hardly moves. For things like income or house prices, where a few huge values pull the mean, the median is usually the more honest summary. When you read that the "average" family earns some amount, it's worth asking which average is meant. A different choice can paint a very different picture of how people are doing.

The average on its own doesn't tell you how spread out the numbers are. The standard deviation does. Karl Pearson gave it its name in 1893, and it's one of the most widely used numbers in all of statistics.
Imagine two classes that both average 70 on a test. In one, the standard deviation is 5, so almost everyone scored between 60 and 80. In the other it's 20, so you have students at 30 and others at 100. The averages match, but the classes are very different places to teach. Whenever you see an average, it's worth wondering about the spread around it, since a number with a wide spread tells you much less about any one case.

Studies often report a "95% confidence interval." It sounds like there's a 95 percent chance the true value is inside the range, but that's not quite what it means. It means that the method used would capture the true value in 95 percent of repeated studies.
The difference is subtle, and surveys have found that many researchers get it wrong, including trained scientists. A practical reading is that the interval shows the range of values the data can't rule out. A narrow interval means a precise estimate, and a wide one means a lot of uncertainty. When a result is reported as a single number with no interval, it's fair to ask how much it could vary.

News stories about polls often mention a margin of error, usually about plus or minus 3 percentage points for a poll of around 1,000 people. It reflects only random chance in picking the sample.
It doesn't cover badly worded questions, or people who didn't respond, which can matter more. If a poll shows 52 percent to 48 percent with that margin, the two sides are statistically tied, even if the headline says someone's ahead. Note that the margin applies to each number separately, so the gap between two candidates has an even larger margin. The next time you see a close poll, it's good to remember that it can't tell you who is leading.

In 1936 the magazine Literary Digest mailed out ten million ballots and got back more than 2.4 million, and predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt in a landslide. Roosevelt won in one of the biggest landslides in history, carrying all but two states.
The magazine had drawn its sample from its own readers and from telephone and car-owner lists, which in the Depression skewed richer. George Gallup, polling a much smaller but representative sample, got it right. The lesson is that how a sample is chosen matters far more than how big it is. A huge sample that's biased is worse than a small one that's fair, and no amount of data can fix a lopsided way of collecting it.

A study can find that something "works" and still tell you nothing about how much. Effect size measures how large the difference is. Jacob Cohen suggested rough benchmarks for a standardized difference: 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium and 0.8 is large.
A "statistically significant" result with a tiny effect may be of no practical use, particularly in large studies where even trivial differences can be detected. For example, a diet that makes people lose a few ounces over a year might be "significant" with enough participants, but nobody would care. So when you read about a finding, it's good to ask two questions. Is it real? And how big is it? The second question is the one that tells you whether it matters.

A study with too few participants may fail to detect a real effect. That's low statistical power. A 2013 review of neuroscience studies estimated that the typical study had a power of only about 21 percent, which means it would miss most real effects.
Worse, low power also means that the results that do cross the threshold of significance tend to exaggerate the true effect. A small study that finds a big result is more likely to be a fluke or an overstatement than a large study. It's one reason why many findings from small studies don't hold up when they're repeated. If a surprising result comes from a few dozen people, it's wise to wait for a bigger one.
How to make music make you younger

In 2011 Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn published a paper claiming that listening to the Beatles song "When I'm Sixty-Four" made people nearly a year and a half younger. It was absurd, and it was done on purpose.
It was a deliberate demonstration of how researchers, by making flexible choices about which data to include and which tests to run, can find "significant" results in nonsense. They then proposed rules to stop that kind of p-hacking, such as stating in advance how many participants you will use. The paper was a landmark in the movement to make research more reliable. It showed that a result can be statistically significant and still be completely meaningless.

In 2009 the neuroscientist Craig Bennett put a dead Atlantic salmon in an fMRI brain scanner, showed it photographs of people in social situations, and asked it to determine their emotions. Without correcting for the thousands of statistical tests involved, the analysis found brain activity in the dead fish.
It was a joke with a serious point. If you run enough tests, some will come out "significant" by chance alone, and you have to correct for multiple comparisons. The study won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012, an award for research that makes you laugh and then makes you think. Since then, brain-imaging researchers have taken the issue much more seriously. It's a good story to remember whenever someone says they found a link after testing many things.

In pre-registration, researchers publicly record their hypotheses and methods before collecting data. That stops them from quietly changing the question after they see which results turn out well. It's like calling your shot before taking it.
A 2021 comparison of studies found that 44 percent of those published in a "registered report" format found a positive result, compared with 96 percent of standard published papers. It suggests that the usual literature is skewed toward positive findings, since negative results rarely get published. It's an important change, and one that makes it easier to trust the results. A finding that was predicted in advance is much more convincing than one that was noticed afterward.

A meta-analysis pools the results of many studies on a question to give a clearer overall picture. The psychologist Gene Glass coined the term in 1976, when he combined hundreds of studies of psychotherapy to see whether it worked.
A larger body of evidence gives more precise answers than any single study. But it can only be as good as the studies it includes, and if negative results were never published, even the pooled answer can be biased. Good meta-analyses look for this problem, and they judge the quality of the studies they include. When you hear that "one study found" something, it's worth asking whether there's a meta-analysis, since a single study can mislead.

A headline says a drug "doubles your risk," which sounds alarming. But if the risk was tiny to begin with, doubling it may mean very little. A very small number doubled is still a very small number.
In 1995 the UK government warned that a new type of contraceptive pill doubled the risk of blood clots. The actual risk went from about 1 in 7,000 women to about 2 in 7,000. Many women stopped taking the pill, and there was a rise in unwanted pregnancies and abortions. The harm from the scare was larger than the harm from the pill. It's a good reason to ask, whenever you see a percentage change in risk, "From what to what?"

One helpful way to express how well a treatment works is the number of people who need to take it for one person to benefit. If a drug cuts a risk from 2 percent to 1 percent, you could call that a 50 percent reduction. It sounds impressive.
But 100 people have to take it for one to be helped, and the others get the costs and side effects. The number makes the trade-offs clearer. A treatment with a number needed to treat of 5 is much more valuable than one with 500. It doesn't tell you whether to take a drug, but it gives you a fair way to weigh the benefit against the downsides. It's a question worth asking your doctor.

Any medical test can make two kinds of error. Sensitivity is how good it is at finding people who do have the condition, and specificity is how good it is at correctly clearing people who don't. A test can do very well on one and badly on the other.
A very sensitive test catches nearly everyone who's sick but may also flag many healthy people, which is why a positive result often needs a follow-up. When a condition is rare, most positive results can even be false alarms, even with an accurate test. That's an important reason why doctors don't screen everyone for everything. A positive result isn't the end of the story, and it's often worth asking, "How sure is this test?"

Screening tests find diseases earlier, and the apparent survival time after diagnosis gets longer. But that can be an illusion. Suppose a cancer is found at age 63 without screening and the patient dies at 70, which is 7 years of survival.
With screening, it's found at 60, and the patient still dies at 70, so survival after diagnosis is 10 years, but the person didn't live any longer. All that has happened is that the clock started sooner. The fairer test of screening is whether fewer people die of the disease. That's why researchers look at deaths in the whole population, and not only at survival after diagnosis, when they judge whether a screening program helps.
Always plot your data: Anscombe and the Datasaurus

In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe made up four small sets of numbers that have almost identical averages, spreads and correlations. Yet when you plot them, they look completely different: one is a neat line, one is a curve, one has a single outlier pulling the line, and one is a vertical stack of points. His point was that you should always graph your data, because summary numbers can hide what's really going on.
Decades later, the idea got a modern twist. In 2016 the data visualizer Alberto Cairo made up a data set that, when plotted, looks like a dinosaur, yet has the same averages, spread and correlation as a random scatter of dots. In 2017 researchers Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice built on it, showing a dozen other shapes, including a star and a bullseye, that all share the same summary statistics.

A bar chart is supposed to show quantities in proportion to the height of the bars. If the vertical axis starts at 95 percent instead of zero, a difference between 97 and 99 can look like the second bar is several times as tall.
It's a common way to make small differences look dramatic, sometimes by accident. Always check where the axis starts. Edward Tufte called misleading graphs a violation of graphical integrity. For line charts, it's often acceptable not to start at zero, since the trend matters more than the size, but for bars it's a distortion. A quick glance at the numbers on the side of a chart can save you from being misled.
The law of truly large numbers

When there are enough chances, even extremely unlikely things are bound to happen. The statisticians Persi Diaconis and Frederick Mosteller pointed out that if an event has a one-in-a-million chance on a given day, then with hundreds of millions of people in America, it should happen to hundreds of people every day.
So coincidences aren't strange. They're expected, when you consider how many opportunities there are. A person who dreams of a friend and gets a call the next morning feels something uncanny, but among millions of dreamers, it will happen to many. That doesn't make it any less memorable for the person it happens to. It just means that you can't take a rare event as proof of anything, if it could have happened to any of a million people.

In 1898 the Russian-Polish statistician Ladislaus Bortkiewicz looked at records of how many Prussian cavalry soldiers were killed by horse kicks each year, in 14 army corps over 20 years. The numbers were small, and each death seemed like a random accident.
He showed that the numbers fit a mathematical pattern known as the Poisson distribution, which describes rare events that occur independently at a steady average rate. It's a classic example of how even odd accidents follow statistical laws. The same pattern describes the number of calls arriving at a switchboard, the number of typos on a page and the number of meteorites that land in a field. Randomness, it turns out, has a shape.

In the 1920s, at an English country research station, a woman claimed that she could tell whether the tea or the milk had been poured into a cup first. The statistician Ronald Fisher turned this into a famous experiment: eight cups, four of each kind, presented in random order.
If she's just guessing, the chance of getting all eight right is 1 in 70. The example became a model for randomization and significance testing. It shows the logic of a good experiment. Decide in advance what would count as evidence, take away every chance of bias by randomizing, and then ask how likely the result would be by luck alone. According to the story, she got all of them right.

When a website wants to know which version of a page works better, it can show version A to some visitors and version B to others, chosen at random, and compare the results. It's the same logic as a medical trial.
It lets companies settle arguments with data instead of opinions. In 2009 Google reportedly tested 41 shades of blue for a link bar, and a designer left the company partly because he felt that such testing was replacing design judgment. The case shows both sides. Testing can find what works, and it can also push toward small, safe changes. It's a powerful tool, but it only answers the questions you ask, and some of the best ideas are the ones nobody thinks of testing.

The chance of winning the Powerball jackpot is about 1 in 292 million. With three drawings a week, if you bought a ticket for every single drawing, you'd expect to wait nearly two million years to win once.
On average, a ticket is worth less than what you pay for it. People still play, and most of the pleasure is in the daydream. That's fair enough, as long as you think of it as the price of an entertainment and not as an investment. It helps to remember that you're far more likely to be struck by lightning than to win. If you do play, small amounts you can afford to lose are the sensible way.

If you're offered a bet that's in your favor, how much of your money should you put on it? John Kelly, a physicist at Bell Labs, published a formula in 1956 for the answer. It tells you the fraction of your money to wager, based on your edge and the odds.
Bet too much, and a bad run can wipe you out, even though you have an edge. Bet too little, and you waste the edge. Many professional gamblers and investors use half the Kelly amount, to be safer, since the formula assumes you know your odds exactly, and in real life you don't. The idea is a good reminder that, in a favorable game, the most important thing is to stay in the game long enough for the edge to work.

When something is scarce, its price tends to rise. When it's plentiful, it falls. The English economist Alfred Marshall drew the now-famous crossing curves of supply and demand in his 1890 textbook. One curve shows how much buyers want at each price, and the other shows how much sellers will provide.
The point where they cross is the price at which the amount that sellers want to sell equals the amount that buyers want to buy. It's a simple picture, but it explains a lot about how markets work. It's why umbrellas cost more in a downpour, why concert tickets rise when a show is popular, and why a bumper crop of apples brings down the price. Prices are signals that tell everybody what's scarce.

Water is essential for life but cheap, and diamonds are useless for survival but expensive. Economists puzzled over this paradox until the 1870s, when Carl Menger, William Stanley Jevons and Léon Walras each realized that value depends on the next unit, not the total.
Because you already have plenty of water, one more glass is worth little, while one more diamond is scarce. Decisions are made at the margin. It's a way of thinking that helps in everyday choices. Instead of asking whether something is good, you ask whether a little more of it is worth the cost. Is one more hour of work worth more than one more hour of sleep? The answer depends on how much of each you've already had.

In 1817 the economist David Ricardo showed something surprising: two parties can both gain from trade even if one is better at everything. Imagine a lawyer who also types faster than her assistant. She still comes out ahead by letting the assistant type, because her time is worth more spent on legal work.
The same logic applies to countries, and it's the main reason that economists generally favor trade. Each country does best by focusing on what it does relatively well, and trading for the rest. It doesn't mean that everyone benefits equally, or that nobody loses a job. The theory is about the total, and the losers can be real. But it explains why trade, on the whole, makes people richer and not poorer.
Adam Smith: the pin factory and the invisible hand

In The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, Adam Smith described a pin factory where the work was divided into about eighteen distinct steps. He said ten workers, each specializing in a few tasks, could produce about 48,000 pins a day, while a single worker doing everything might make one pin a day, or at most twenty. The division of labor makes everyone far more productive.
The phrase "invisible hand" is one of the best-known in economics, and Smith used it only once in the book. He argued that people pursuing their own interests may, without intending it, end up helping society. Yet he was no simple cheerleader for business. In the same book, he warned that merchants rarely meet together without it ending in a conspiracy against the public. Smith held both ideas, that markets work well and that they need watching.

Inflation means that prices in general are rising, so each dollar buys less. Many central banks aim for about 2 percent a year, which they consider a healthy level. A little inflation encourages people to spend and invest, and makes it easier for wages to adjust.
Even 2 percent adds up. At that rate, prices double in about 35 years. At 7 percent, they double in about 10. That's why money sitting in a drawer slowly loses what it can buy, and why a savings account that pays less than inflation is losing value in real terms. When you compare what something cost in the past with what it costs now, it's worth adjusting for inflation, since a dollar in 1980 bought far more than a dollar does today.

When a government prints too much money, prices can spiral out of control. In Germany in 1923, prices at one point doubled every few days, and people were paid twice a day and rushed to spend the money before it lost value. Wheelbarrows of banknotes were needed to buy a loaf of bread.
In Zimbabwe, in November 2008, monthly inflation reached an estimated 80 billion percent. When money stops working, people turn to barter or foreign currencies. Savings are wiped out, and the social order can be badly shaken. Hyperinflation is rare, and it usually follows war, collapse or reckless government finance. It's a stark example of how much we rely on money keeping its value, something we usually take for granted.

A central bank sets short-term interest rates to influence the economy: lowering them to encourage borrowing and spending, and raising them to cool down inflation. The US Federal Reserve was created in 1913, after a series of bank panics, especially one in 1907. It has what's called a dual mandate from Congress, to keep prices stable and to promote maximum employment.
The dollar bill in your wallet has no gold behind it, and it isn't worth much as paper. It's money because the government says it is and because everyone accepts it. That's called fiat money, from the Latin for "let it be done." Until 1971, the US dollar could be exchanged for gold at a fixed rate, and when President Nixon ended that, the world moved fully to fiat currencies. Most money today is just numbers in bank accounts.

"Don't put all your eggs in one basket" has a mathematical backing. In 1952 Harry Markowitz showed that if you combine investments that don't all move in the same direction at the same time, you can reduce your overall risk without lowering your expected return.
He won a Nobel Prize for it in 1990. It's often called the only free lunch in finance. A portfolio of many different stocks is much less risky than any one of them, because when one falls, another may rise. The benefit has limits, since in a severe crash nearly everything falls together. But over time, spreading your money across many kinds of assets is one of the most reliable ways to protect it, and it needs no special skill.

An index fund simply buys all the stocks in a market, rather than trying to pick winners. John Bogle founded the first one available to ordinary investors in 1976, at Vanguard, and he was ridiculed for it at the time. People called it "Bogle's folly," because settling for average seemed un-American.
Reports that compare funds, such as the S&P SPIVA scorecards, regularly find that over a 15-year period, around nine in ten professional stock funds do worse than the index they're trying to beat. Part of the reason is the fees they charge. An index fund is cheap, because it doesn't need anyone to do research. It's a sobering lesson that, for most people, the simplest strategy beats most of the experts.

Eugene Fama proposed in 1970 that stock prices already reflect all publicly available information, so it's very hard to consistently beat the market. If a stock were obviously a bargain, so many buyers would rush in that the price would rise until the bargain disappeared.
Other economists, like Robert Shiller, argued that markets can be driven by emotion and bubbles. In 2013 Fama and Shiller, with another economist, shared the Nobel Prize in economics, an indication of how both views have supporters. It's still debated. A reasonable position is that markets are hard to beat but not perfectly rational, and that anyone who claims to be able to predict them should be treated with caution.

In the 1630s tulip bulbs in the Netherlands sold at extraordinary prices, and the craze is retold as the classic example of a speculative bubble that ruined thousands. The story says that a single bulb could cost as much as a house.
Modern historians, like Anne Goldgar, who looked through the records, say it was much smaller than the legend. Few people seem to have been ruined, and the evidence is thin. The story has been told so many times that the myth became the lesson. It's a nice irony that a story about people being carried away by a craze has itself been repeated, for centuries, with little checking. Whatever happened, bubbles in other times were certainly real.

If you have a pile of money to invest, is it better to invest it all at once, or to spread it out over several months? A 2012 Vanguard study found that investing all at once did better about two-thirds of the time, simply because markets tend to rise more often than they fall.
Spreading it out makes you less likely to regret putting everything in just before a drop, so it's a trade-off. Averaging in is a way of buying peace of mind, and a modest price for it. The best choice depends on how much a sudden fall would hurt you. What matters most is not the method, but that you don't wait on the sidelines for the "perfect" moment, which no one can identify in advance.
The time value of money and Franklin's bequest

Would you rather have $100 today or $100 in a year? Most people say today, and they're right. You could invest the money and have more later, and prices will likely have risen. Economists "discount" future money to reflect this. It's the principle behind interest on loans and savings, and it's how the value of any investment or business is worked out.
When Benjamin Franklin died in 1790, he left 1,000 pounds each to the cities of Boston and Philadelphia, to be loaned out at interest and not fully used for 200 years. By 1990 the funds had grown to millions of dollars: about $5 million in Boston's fund and $2 million in Philadelphia's. It's a vivid example of the power of compound interest over a long time.

In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin described a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains by adding another cow, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, so the pasture gets destroyed. It's an image for many shared resources, such as fisheries and the atmosphere.
Elinor Ostrom, who won the 2009 Nobel Prize in economics, showed that many communities have managed shared resources well by creating their own rules. Swiss villages have shared alpine pastures for centuries, and Maine lobster fishermen have set their own limits. So the tragedy isn't inevitable. It tends to happen when there are no rules, no trust and no way to enforce an agreement, and it can often be avoided when people can talk and set limits.

Two suspects are held separately. Each is offered a deal to betray the other. Whatever the other does, betraying seems best for you. But if both betray, they do worse than if both had stayed quiet.
Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game in 1950, and Albert Tucker told the prison story. In Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments around 1980, the winning strategy was "tit for tat": cooperate first, then copy the other player's last move. It was simple and forgiving, and it did better than much more complicated strategies. It's a powerful lesson. In repeated dealings, being nice, but not a pushover, tends to pay.

A Nash equilibrium is a situation in which no player can do better by changing only their own choice, given what the others are doing. John Nash proved in 1950 that every game with a finite number of players and choices has at least one.
It describes stable outcomes, not necessarily good ones, as the prisoner's dilemma shows, where both players betraying is a stable result that's bad for both. Nash won the Nobel Prize in 1994, after decades of struggling with mental illness, a story told in the book and movie A Beautiful Mind. The idea is used to understand everything from auctions to arms races to traffic. It tells us where a situation might settle, and not where it ought to.

Some things become more valuable as more people use them. A telephone is useless if you're the only one who has one, and valuable if everyone you know does. That's a network effect. Social networks, payment systems and messaging apps all depend on it.
Metcalfe's law says that the value of a network grows with the square of the number of users, but studies of real networks suggest it grows more slowly. It helps explain why one social network or payment system can come to dominate. Once most people are on one, nobody wants to leave, even if a better one is available. It also explains why new services often give away a lot at first, in order to reach the point where the network takes off.

In 1970 the economist George Akerlof wrote a paper about the used-car market. Sellers know whether their car is good or a "lemon," but buyers can't tell, so buyers are only willing to pay an average price. At that price, owners of good cars won't sell, and the market fills up with lemons.
The paper showed how a lack of information can make markets fail. He shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for it. Akerlof's paper was rejected by several journals before it was published, because reviewers thought it was trivial or wrong. The idea has been applied to insurance, jobs and loans. It's the reason why warranties, inspections and reputations are valuable. They help the buyer trust something they can't check for themselves.

When someone else bears the cost of a risk, people tend to take more of it. A driver with full insurance may be a little less careful. A bank that expects the government to bail it out if it fails may place bigger bets.
Insurers try to limit it with deductibles and co-payments, so that the person still has something to lose. The term comes from the insurance business, where it was first used to describe policyholders who were careless because they were covered. The concept helps explain a lot of modern financial history, including the crisis of 2008. It's not that insured people are bad. It's that everyone, if they are shielded from the consequences, tends to behave a little differently.

An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on someone who didn't choose to take part. A factory's pollution harms people downwind, a negative externality. A neighbor's beautiful garden pleases passers-by, a positive one.
In 1920 the economist Arthur Pigou argued that a tax on the polluter can make the price of a product reflect its true cost to society. Many modern carbon taxes follow the idea. Without such a tax, the price of a product leaves out the harm done to others, so people buy too much of it. Externalities help explain why markets, left alone, don't always give the best result, and why some things, like clean air, need rules or prices to be protected.

Some things, like street lighting, clean air or national defense, benefit everyone, whether or not they pay. That creates a free-rider problem: if you can use it either way, why pay? Voluntary contributions tend to fall short.
That's the reason economists give for why governments usually pay for such goods with taxes, to make sure that everyone chips in. Street lighting is a classic case, since you can't easily stop a passer-by from using the light. Public radio and open-source software face the same problem and rely on donations from the people who care. It's a useful way to see why a few things, which markets can't easily provide, are paid for in common.

Ronald Coase argued in a 1960 paper that if people can bargain easily with each other, they'll reach an efficient arrangement no matter who starts out holding the legal rights. For example, a factory and its neighbors could settle the problem of smoke by negotiation, without a government rule.
In real life, the costs of getting everyone together and agreeing are often too high, so the theorem works best for small groups. Coase himself stressed that, and he thought the real lesson was that we should look at how costly it is to make deals. The idea has been influential in law as well as economics. It suggests that a good first step to a dispute is to ask whether the people involved could simply talk and make a deal.

Price elasticity is how much demand changes when the price changes. For things people need and can't easily replace, like gasoline in the short run, demand barely drops when the price goes up. That's low elasticity.
For things with lots of substitutes, like one brand of soda, a small price rise sends buyers elsewhere. That's high elasticity. Businesses and governments use it to predict how changes in price will play out. A tax on cigarettes, for example, raises more revenue if smokers don't cut back much, and reduces smoking more if they do. It's a handy idea for understanding why some price increases cause an uproar and others pass unnoticed.

Gross domestic product measures the total value of goods and services a country produces. Simon Kuznets, who developed the measure in the 1930s, warned in a 1934 report to Congress that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income.
GDP counts cleaning up after a disaster as growth, but it doesn't count unpaid housework, leisure or the health of the environment. A country can grow richer while its people become sicker or lonelier. That doesn't make GDP useless. It's a good measure of the size of an economy. But it's a poor measure of how well people are living, which is why researchers also look at health, education and happiness.

The Gini coefficient is a single number that measures how unequal an income distribution is, from 0, where everyone has the same, to 1, where one person has everything. The Italian statistician Corrado Gini introduced it in 1912.
It's handy for comparing countries. Scandinavian countries are around 0.25 to 0.28, and some other countries are above 0.6. It doesn't show where in the distribution the inequality lies, so two countries with the same number can look quite different. And it says nothing about how rich a country is overall. It's a rough but useful summary, and it's best used alongside other facts about how people live.
The minimum wage debate and natural experiments

Does raising the minimum wage cost jobs? In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger compared fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which had raised its minimum wage, with neighboring Pennsylvania, which hadn't. They found no loss of jobs in New Jersey. Other studies have found different results, so the debate continues.
Economists can't usually run controlled experiments on whole economies.
