But sometimes events create something close: a lottery for the military draft, a state border where laws differ or a sudden change in a rule. These are called natural experiments. In 2021 David Card, Joshua Angrist and Guido Imbens shared the Nobel Prize in economics for developing ways to learn about cause and effect from them.

A nudge is a small change in how choices are presented that steers people toward a better decision, without forbidding anything, such as making organ donation or saving for retirement the default. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularized the idea in their 2008 book.
A 2022 review found that, once publication bias is accounted for, the average effect shrinks to nearly zero, though some well-designed nudges clearly work. The lesson is that it's not enough to find a clever idea. It needs to be tested, again and again. Defaults seem to be among the strongest and most dependable, since doing nothing is easy. Other kinds of nudges, such as reminders and slogans, are less certain.

Normally, when a price goes up, people buy less. But for some luxury goods, demand can rise as the price rises, because the high price is part of the appeal. In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen wrote about "conspicuous consumption," buying things to show status.
Designer handbags, luxury watches and certain sports cars fit. Ordinary goods don't work that way. If a luxury brand cut its prices sharply, its customers might stop buying, because the thing they were buying was exclusivity. It's one of the rare exceptions to the rule that demand falls as price rises. Veblen was a sharp critic of the wealthy of his time, and his phrase "conspicuous consumption" is still in everyday use.

A company can show a profit on paper and still run out of cash. Profit counts sales when they're made, even if customers haven't paid yet. Cash flow is the money that's actually in the bank.
Many businesses that look healthy fail because customers pay slowly while suppliers and employees need to be paid right away. It's why experienced owners say "cash is king." A growing company can be especially vulnerable, since it has to buy materials and hire people before the money from new sales arrives. If you run a small business, or are thinking of starting one, tracking cash each week is one of the most useful habits you can build.

Margin and markup are easy to mix up. Markup is profit as a percentage of what the item cost you. Margin is profit as a percentage of the price you charge.
If you buy something for $60 and sell it for $100, the profit is $40, so the markup is about 67 percent and the margin is 40 percent. Confusing the two is a common cause of pricing too low. A shop owner who wants a 40 percent margin but adds a 40 percent markup ends up with a margin of only about 29 percent. The same dollars give two different percentages, so it's worth being clear about which one you mean.
Unit economics and the break-even point

Unit economics asks whether you make money on each individual sale, after counting everything it costs to make the product and to win the customer. Suppose it costs $50 in advertising to get a customer who brings in $30 of profit. Every sale loses $20, and growing faster just loses money faster. It's worth working out before you try to scale a business.
The break-even point is how much you need to sell to cover all your costs. You work it out by dividing your fixed costs, such as rent and salaries, by the profit you make on each unit. Below that number, you lose money, and above it, every additional sale adds to your profit. These are among the first numbers to know before starting a business or launching a product.

In 1997 the Harvard professor Clayton Christensen argued that successful companies can be overtaken by cheaper, simpler products that start at the bottom of the market, and improve until they threaten the leaders. Steel mini-mills and small disk drives were among his examples. It became enormously influential.
Critics, including the historian Jill Lepore in a 2014 article, said that his examples were chosen after the fact, and that many companies he called disrupted did fine. So it's better as a way of describing the past than predicting the future. The idea holds something true, that leaders can be blind to threats from below, but it isn't a law. It's a story that sometimes fits and sometimes doesn't.

A minimum viable product is the simplest version of a product that you can put in front of real customers to learn whether they want it. Eric Ries made the term popular in his 2011 book The Lean Startup.
The idea is to learn early, with little cost, before spending months building something nobody wants. It's about testing assumptions, not about shipping something poor. A founder might start with a simple page that describes a product and see if anyone signs up, before building any of it. The same approach works outside business. Before you commit a lot of time to a project, it's wise to find the smallest test that would tell you whether it's worth doing.

Money can be saved for later, but time can't. Every hour is spent on something, and spending it on one thing means not spending it on another. You can't earn more of it, and you can't put it in the bank.
That's why the question "Is this worth doing?" is a weak test, because nearly anything has some value. A better question is "What else could I do with this hour?" That brings the real cost into view. It's a way of seeing that saying yes to one thing is always saying no to something else, so protecting your time is the same as protecting what matters most to you.

Marie Sklodowska was born in Warsaw and moved to Paris to study, and she went on to a career that nobody has matched. She worked in poverty at first, and in a cold, cramped lab. In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel for their work on radioactivity, a word she coined.
In 1911 she won the Chemistry prize for discovering polonium and radium, which made her the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. In the First World War she helped equip vehicles with X-ray machines, which soldiers called "little Curies," and she drove some of them to the front herself. She died in 1934 of an illness that was almost certainly caused by her years of work with radiation. Her notebooks are still radioactive today.

In 1609 Galileo heard of a Dutch invention and built a better telescope himself, then turned it to the sky. What he saw was astonishing. There were mountains and craters on the Moon, four small moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus. All of this was evidence that not everything in the heavens circled the Earth.
He published his findings in 1610 in a short book, and he became famous. But he also became a target. In 1633 the Inquisition forced him to renounce the Sun-centered view, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest. Even then, he kept working, and he wrote one of his best books while confined. Galileo's lasting legacy is the habit of looking and measuring, instead of simply trusting an authority.

For more than a thousand years most people believed that the Sun and planets circled the Earth. It matched what anyone could see, and it was supported by the authority of ancient writers. Copernicus, a Polish astronomer and church official, worked out in detail a system with the Sun at the center.
His book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was printed in 1543, and according to tradition he was handed a copy on his deathbed. The idea wasn't entirely new, since an ancient Greek, Aristarchus, had suggested it, but Copernicus supplied the mathematics. He had waited decades to publish, perhaps from worry about how it would be received. The book started what we now call the Copernican revolution, a change in how we see our place in the universe.

Kepler, a German astronomer, had access to the careful naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe, and spent years trying to fit Mars's orbit to a circle. It wouldn't fit. The error was small, only about eight minutes of arc, but Kepler trusted the data and refused to ignore it.
Eventually he realized the orbit was an ellipse. He published three laws of planetary motion between 1609 and 1619, which Isaac Newton later used to arrive at his theory of gravity. Kepler also wrote an early work of science fiction about a trip to the Moon, called Somnium. It's a nice example of how a scientist can be both rigorous and imaginative, and of how a small discrepancy, honestly respected, can overturn a belief that had stood for two thousand years.

Darwin returned from his five-year voyage on HMS Beagle in 1836 with the beginnings of an idea. For more than twenty years, he gathered evidence and told only a few friends. He was a careful man, and he knew that his theory would be controversial.
In 1858 he received a letter from the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, who had independently come to the same idea. A joint paper was read to the Linnean Society, and Darwin's book On the Origin of Species came out in 1859. The first printing sold out in a day. He spent the rest of his life writing more, including books on orchids, earthworms and human emotion. He is buried in Westminster Abbey, near Isaac Newton.

Wallace was a self-taught naturalist who made a living collecting specimens in the Amazon and in Southeast Asia. He wasn't wealthy or well connected, and he sold beetles and birds to museums and collectors in order to pay for his travels.
In 1858, lying sick with a fever on an island in Indonesia, he thought of natural selection, wrote it up in a few days and sent it to Darwin. Darwin was alarmed to see his own theory, and the two agreed to publish together. Wallace also found that animals on either side of a line through Indonesia are strikingly different, now called Wallace's Line. He was generous about credit all his life, and he even titled one of his books Darwinism. Many consider him the unsung co-discoverer of evolution.

In the 1860s the French chemist Louis Pasteur showed that microbes, not "spontaneous generation," were responsible for fermentation and spoilage. He boiled broth in flasks with long swan-shaped necks, which let in air but trapped dust and germs, and the broth stayed clear.
That supported germ theory, the idea that germs cause disease. He went on to develop vaccines for animals, including chicken cholera and anthrax. In 1885 he gave a boy named Joseph Meister, who'd been bitten by a rabid dog, the first rabies vaccine, and the boy lived. Pasteur also invented a way of heating milk and wine to kill germs, which we still call pasteurization. He's a good reminder that the most useful science often starts with a practical problem.

In the 1860s surgeons in hospitals operated in street clothes and wiped their instruments on their aprons, and many patients died of infection afterward. Many surgeons took pride in their blood-stained coats. Nobody understood why wounds became infected.
The British surgeon Joseph Lister read about Pasteur's work on germs and began to clean wounds and tools with carbolic acid. In 1867 he reported that deaths among his amputation patients fell from about 45 percent to about 15 percent. He also sprayed the operating room with the acid, which later proved unnecessary, but the principle was right. The mouthwash Listerine was named after him, though he had nothing to do with it. Modern surgery depends on the cleanliness that he insisted on.

In 1847 the Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women giving birth in the hospital ward where doctors worked were dying of fever at a much higher rate than in the ward staffed by midwives. He puzzled over the difference, and when a colleague died after being cut during an autopsy, he saw a link.
He realized that doctors were coming straight from autopsies, and he told them to wash their hands in chlorine solution. Deaths fell from about 18 percent to about 2 percent. His colleagues rejected the idea, partly because it implied that doctors were killing their patients, and he ended his life in an asylum. Only after his death did germ theory vindicate him. His story is a lesson in how hard it can be to accept a truth that's uncomfortable.

In the 1790s the English country doctor Edward Jenner heard that milkmaids who'd caught cowpox seemed not to get smallpox. Smallpox killed and disfigured millions, and a way to prevent it would be a great gift. In 1796 he took matter from a cowpox sore and scratched it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps.
Later he exposed the boy to smallpox, and the boy didn't catch it. Jenner would not pass modern standards of research ethics, but his method worked. The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin word for cow, vacca. Smallpox was eventually wiped out worldwide, and the last natural case was in 1977. It is the only human disease so far to have been completely eradicated, and Jenner's experiment started the road to that victory.

Florence Nightingale is remembered as the "Lady with the Lamp," a nurse in the Crimean War, but she was also a brilliant statistician. She gathered data and drew striking charts, including a polar-area diagram, to show that far more soldiers died of disease than of battle wounds.
After sanitary reforms at the hospital at Scutari, the death rate dropped from over 40 percent to about 2 percent. She used her charts to persuade officials and the public, since a picture could succeed where a table of numbers could not. In 1858 she became the first woman elected to the Royal Statistical Society. She spent the rest of her long life as a reformer of nursing and public health, largely working from her bed.

Ada Lovelace was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, and she studied mathematics. Her mother, worried that she would inherit her father's wildness, made sure she had a thorough training in science and numbers.
She translated an article about Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer that was never completed, and added her own notes in 1843. They included a step-by-step method for the machine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, which is regarded as the first computer program. She also saw that such a machine could work with symbols and even music, not just numbers. That vision, of a computer as something more than a calculator, was a century ahead of its time.

In 1936 the young British mathematician Alan Turing described an imaginary machine that could carry out any calculation, a model of what we now call a computer. He was 24, and he made it up to solve a problem in pure logic.
In the Second World War, he worked at Bletchley Park and helped break the German naval Enigma code, work that is thought to have shortened the war. In 1950 he asked whether machines can think, and proposed a test. He was convicted in 1952 for being gay, and the British government pardoned him in 2013. He died in 1954, at the age of 41. The most important prize in computer science, the Turing Award, is named for him.

Grace Hopper was a mathematician who became a rear admiral in the US Navy. In 1952 she created one of the first compilers, a program that translates instructions into machine code, and she argued that programming should be done in words close to English, which led to the language COBOL.
In 1947, when a moth was found stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer, she taped it into the logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found." The term "bug" was already used in engineering, but the story helped make it famous in computing. She was known for handing out short lengths of wire, a nanosecond long, to show how far light travels in a billionth of a second. She was still on active duty in her late seventies.

Katherine Johnson was a mathematician at NASA who worked as a human "computer" at a time when Black women were segregated at the agency. She had been a gifted student, starting college at 15, and she brought exceptional skill to the job.
She calculated the flight path for Alan Shepard's 1961 mission. In 1962, before John Glenn's orbital flight, the astronaut asked for "the girl" to check the computer's numbers by hand, and he wouldn't fly until she had. President Obama gave her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015. She lived to the age of 101. Her story was told in the book and film Hidden Figures, which brought attention to the many women whose work helped put people into space.

The British chemist Rosalind Franklin was an expert in X-ray crystallography. In 1952 she and her student Raymond Gosling produced "Photo 51," a sharp X-ray image of DNA that showed a helical pattern.
Without her knowledge, a colleague showed it to James Watson, and it gave him and Francis Crick crucial information for their 1953 model. She was close to solving the structure herself. She died of ovarian cancer in 1958, at 37, and the Nobel Prize isn't awarded posthumously. Her work before DNA, on coal and viruses, was also important. Today she is widely recognized as one of the key figures in the discovery of the double helix.

Barbara McClintock studied corn, and from the 1940s she noticed that certain genes could move from one place on a chromosome to another, changing the color patterns of the kernels. It was a radical idea, since genes were thought to be fixed in place like beads on a string.
Most scientists didn't believe her, and she stopped publishing about it for years. Decades later, other researchers found similar "jumping genes" in many organisms, including humans. She won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Medicine, alone, at the age of 81. Her story shows the value of patient observation, and the courage to keep believing in what the evidence shows.

In the early 1900s, Henrietta Leavitt worked at Harvard College Observatory as one of the women hired to measure photographs of stars, for low pay. They were called "computers," and they did careful, tedious work that the male astronomers did not want to do.
Studying pulsing stars in the Magellanic Clouds, she noticed that the brighter ones took longer to pulse. That gave astronomers a way of measuring distances to faraway stars and galaxies. Edwin Hubble later used it to show that the Andromeda nebula is a separate galaxy. Leavitt died of cancer in 1921, and a Swedish mathematician who wanted to nominate her for a Nobel Prize learned that she had already died. She is a fine example of an overlooked person whose work changed the way we see the universe.

In 1925 Cecilia Payne, then a graduate student at Harvard, concluded in her PhD thesis that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, not of the same mix as the Earth, as scientists had assumed. It was a startling result, and it went against what everyone thought.
A prominent astronomer, Henry Norris Russell, persuaded her to describe the result as probably not real. Four years later, he reached the same conclusion by other means and published it, giving her credit. The astronomer Otto Struve called her thesis the most brilliant ever in astronomy. She went on to become the first woman to be a full professor at Harvard, and later the head of a department there.

Physicists believed that nature doesn't distinguish left from right. If you looked at an experiment in a mirror, the laws would look the same. In 1956 Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang suggested that it might not hold for the weak nuclear force and needed someone to test it.
Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American experimentalist at Columbia, ran a delicate experiment on cobalt-60 at very low temperatures and found that it did break the symmetry. Lee and Yang won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics, but she did not. Many physicists have said that she should have shared it. She was nicknamed the "First Lady of Physics," and she also worked on the Manhattan Project. Her careful experiment overturned an idea that had seemed beyond question.

In 1905, while working as a patent clerk in Bern, Switzerland, the 26-year-old Albert Einstein published four papers in a single year, now called his miracle year. He had a day job and did his physics in his spare time, with no university position.
The papers explained the photoelectric effect, which showed that light comes in packets. They proved the existence of atoms by explaining Brownian motion, and presented the special theory of relativity. And a short follow-up gave the equation E equals mc squared. Any one of them would have made a career. Ten years later, he completed the general theory of relativity. He became a household name in 1919, after an eclipse expedition confirmed one of its predictions.

In 1900 Max Planck was trying to explain the glow of hot objects, and found that the numbers worked only if energy came in tiny packets, which he called quanta. The old theory predicted that a hot object would give off an infinite amount of energy at short wavelengths, which was plainly wrong.
He thought of the packets as a mathematical trick and was uneasy about it. It took years for physicists, including Einstein, to realize that it described something real, and Planck's constant became a foundation of quantum theory. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics. He was a conservative and modest man, and he said later that he'd been forced into the idea as an act of desperation. It shows that great discoveries can come from people who didn't set out to overturn anything.

In 1913 the Danish physicist Niels Bohr proposed that electrons in atoms can only occupy certain fixed energy levels and give off light when they jump between them. It explained why hydrogen glows in specific colors, something that no earlier model had managed.
He later led the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, and his institute in Copenhagen became a gathering place for the world's best young physicists. During the Second World War, he helped Jewish scientists escape from Nazi-occupied Europe, and he escaped to Sweden himself in 1943, by boat, and then flew to Britain. After the war, he campaigned for open sharing of nuclear knowledge. He is remembered as both a great scientist and a man of principle.

In 1928 the British physicist Paul Dirac wrote down an equation that combined quantum mechanics and special relativity to describe the electron. To his surprise, it had solutions that implied a particle with the electron's mass but opposite charge, which he first thought was the proton.
In 1932 Carl Anderson found just such a particle, the positron, in cosmic rays. It was the first evidence of antimatter, and Dirac shared the 1933 Nobel Prize. Dirac was famously quiet, so much so that his colleagues joked about a unit of speech, a "dirac," meaning one word per hour. His equation was so elegant that he said that it was more important to have beauty in your equations than to have them fit the experiments. It's an unusual view, but in his case, it worked.

In the 1860s the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell wrote down a set of equations that described how electric and magnetic fields behave. He found that they predicted waves that travel at the speed of light, and he concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.
Later, Heinrich Hertz generated such waves, which led to radio. Einstein said that Maxwell's work was the most profound change in physics since Newton. Maxwell also demonstrated the first color photograph, in 1861, and he contributed to the theory of gases and to understanding Saturn's rings. He died at 48, of cancer. Every time you use a phone, a radio or a microwave oven, you are using a prediction he made on paper, 150 years ago.

Michael Faraday left school at 13 to work as a bookbinder's apprentice, and he read the books he bound. One of them, on chemistry, caught his interest, and he attended public lectures by the chemist Humphry Davy and wrote up careful notes.
He became assistant to Davy, and in 1831 he discovered electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field creates an electric current. That's how generators work. He also began the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people in 1825, which are still held every year. He turned down a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society, preferring to stay a plain Mr. Faraday. He had almost no mathematics, but he saw the invisible fields so clearly that Maxwell was able to put them into equations.

Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor who worked briefly for Thomas Edison. He had come to the United States in 1884 with almost no money, and a head full of ideas about electric motors.
He designed a practical alternating-current induction motor, which he patented in 1888, and the American industrialist George Westinghouse bought his patents. In the "war of the currents," Westinghouse and Tesla's alternating current beat Edison's direct current, because AC can be sent over long distances at high voltage. It's how electricity is still distributed today. Tesla had many more ideas, some brilliant and some impractical, and he died in a New York hotel room in 1943, in debt. Today, the unit of magnetic flux density bears his name.

Richard Feynman was a physicist who won the 1965 Nobel Prize for his work on quantum electrodynamics. He was also a gifted teacher, and his lectures on physics, given at Caltech in the early 1960s, are still in print and still admired.
After the Challenger disaster in 1986, he served on the investigating commission. At a televised hearing, he dropped a piece of a rubber O-ring into a glass of ice water and showed that it lost its springiness in the cold, which explained why the seals had failed on the cold launch morning. It took a few seconds and a cup of ice water to make clear what weeks of testimony hadn't. It was typical of his approach, which was to look for the simplest way of seeing the truth.

In 1937, as a master's student, Claude Shannon realized that electrical circuits could carry out logic, laying the foundations for digital computers. Some have called it the most important master's thesis of the century.
In 1948 he published "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," which founded information theory. It showed that any information can be measured in bits and sent through a noisy channel without error, if coded properly. It's behind everything from phone calls to the internet. Shannon was also playful. He rode a unicycle through the halls of Bell Labs while juggling, and built a mechanical mouse that could solve a maze. A man whose work underlies the digital world was, apparently, having a very good time.

John von Neumann was a Hungarian-American mathematician who made major contributions to quantum mechanics, game theory and the design of computers. As a child, he could divide eight-digit numbers in his head, and he'd tell jokes in ancient Greek.
The stored-program architecture used by most computers today, in which instructions and data live in the same memory, is still called the von Neumann architecture. His colleagues, many of them brilliant themselves, often said that he was the fastest mind they ever met. He worked on the Manhattan Project and later on the first hydrogen bomb. He died in 1957, aged 53, of cancer. Many believe that he did more to shape the world of computing than almost anyone else.

In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist at CERN in Switzerland, proposed a system for sharing documents through links over the internet. His boss wrote "vague but exciting" on the proposal. At that time, the internet existed, but it was used mainly by specialists and was hard to navigate.
In 1990 he built the first web browser and server. In 1993 CERN announced that the technology would be free for everyone to use, with no royalties, which is a big reason the web took off. Berners-Lee could have become very rich, but chose not to patent it. The web and the internet are not the same thing. The internet is the network of cables, and the web is one of the things that runs on it.

The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus created the system that scientists still use to name living things. In his Systema Naturae of 1735 and in Species Plantarum of 1753, he organized plants and animals into groups, and gave each species a two-part Latin name, a genus and a species.
Our own species name, Homo sapiens, means "wise human." Before this, names were long, descriptive phrases, and they differed from one country to another. Linnaeus's tidy system gave naturalists around the world a common language. He also sent his students on voyages to collect specimens, and a number of them died in the process. Today, every newly discovered species is still given a name in the form that he established.

The German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt traveled through Latin America from 1799 to 1804, measuring and collecting at every opportunity. He climbed volcanoes, measured the temperature of ocean currents and collected thousands of plants.
He saw nature as an interconnected web, in which climate, altitude and plants were all linked, long before the word ecology existed. He influenced Charles Darwin, who carried his books on the Beagle, and many others, including the writer Henry David Thoreau. In 1802 he climbed higher on Chimborazo, in Ecuador, than anyone had climbed before. He was probably the most famous scientist in the world in his time, and many places and species carry his name.

Mary Anning grew up poor in the English seaside town of Lyme Regis, where she and her family collected fossils from the cliffs and sold them. Her father died when she was young, and the family depended on what they could find.
Around 1811, when she was about twelve, she and her brother found the skeleton of a giant marine reptile, an ichthyosaur. Later she found the first complete plesiosaur. She was largely uncredited by the scientific community, and as a woman she couldn't join the Geological Society. Even so, scientists traveled to buy her fossils and to ask her advice, and she knew more about the anatomy than many of them. In 2010 the Royal Society included her in a list of the ten British women who most influenced science.

In 1960 Jane Goodall, then 26, went to Gombe in Tanzania to study wild chimpanzees. She had no university degree, and she was accompanied by her mother for the first few months, because the authorities wouldn't allow a young woman to go alone.
She watched one, whom she called David Greybeard, strip leaves from a twig and use it to fish termites out of a mound. It was the first observation of tool-making in animals other than humans. Her mentor Louis Leakey wrote that we must now redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as human. She gave her chimps names and described their personalities, which was unconventional at the time. Her research at Gombe is now the longest-running study of wild chimpanzees.

The American marine biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring in 1962, a book that described how pesticides such as DDT were poisoning birds and the food chain. The title imagines a spring without birdsong.
It was attacked by the chemical industry, but it changed public opinion. It helped lead to the US ban on DDT for agricultural use in 1972 and the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency. She wrote it while being treated for breast cancer, and died in 1964. Carson was also a gifted writer, and her earlier book on the sea, The Sea Around Us, was a best seller. She is a model of how clear writing can move a whole society.

The American agronomist Norman Borlaug spent years in Mexico breeding wheat that was high-yielding and resistant to rust disease. He worked in the field himself, in hard conditions, and crossed thousands of varieties.
In the 1960s his varieties were introduced in India and Pakistan, and yields nearly doubled in a few years, helping to prevent widespread famine. This was a key part of what became known as the Green Revolution. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. Some experts have estimated that his work saved hundreds of millions of lives, though that number is hard to pin down. He kept working into his nineties, and he argued that hunger was a problem that science could solve.

The German chemist Fritz Haber invented a way to make ammonia from nitrogen in the air, which made artificial fertilizer possible and now feeds billions. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it, and it is one of the most consequential inventions of the twentieth century.
But he also led the German chemical weapons program in the First World War, and personally oversaw the first major chlorine gas attack in 1915. His wife Clara, a chemist who opposed his work, took her own life that year. Haber was Jewish by birth, and he was forced to leave Germany in 1933 after the Nazis came to power. His life shows how science can be a source of both great good and great harm, sometimes in the same person.

In 1955 the American physician Jonas Salk announced that his polio vaccine was safe and effective, following a huge trial with 1.8 million children. At the time polio paralyzed and killed thousands every year, and people were jubilant. Church bells rang and factories fell silent.
When the journalist Edward R. Murrow asked who owned the patent, Salk reportedly replied, "Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?" He never earned money from the vaccine. In the US, polio cases dropped from tens of thousands a year to a few thousand by 1957, and to a few hundred in the early 1960s. Salk went on to found the Salk Institute in California, where research continues today.

Hedy Lamarr was a famous film actress in the 1930s and 40s who was also an inventor. She'd fled Austria and her first husband, an arms dealer, and she had picked up some technical knowledge from listening to his conversations.
In 1941 she and the composer George Antheil filed a patent for a system of "frequency hopping," in which a radio signal rapidly changes frequencies in a pattern known to sender and receiver, to prevent enemy jamming of torpedo guidance. It was granted in 1942. The Navy didn't use it at the time. The principle is related to technologies later used in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS, though they were developed independently. She was belatedly honored for her invention in 1997.

In 1977 the Kenyan environmentalist Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement, which paid poor rural women a small amount to plant trees, to restore forests, prevent erosion and provide firewood. She was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate.
Over the decades, the movement planted tens of millions of trees. She was jailed and beaten for her activism, since she also campaigned against corruption and land seizures. In 2004 she won the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman to receive it. She said that when she planted a tree, she was planting hope. Her story shows how a simple, practical idea can grow into a movement that changes lives.

In the late 1960s the Chinese government set up a secret project to find a malaria cure, and Tu Youyou led a team that searched ancient Chinese medical texts. Malaria was killing soldiers on both sides in the Vietnam War, and the existing drugs had stopped working.
A recipe for sweet wormwood gave her an idea. The instructions said to soak the plant in cold water, not boil it, and she realized that heat might destroy the active ingredient. The compound she extracted, artemisinin, has saved millions of lives. She won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Medicine. She had no doctorate and no foreign experience, and she was the first Chinese woman to win a Nobel Prize in science. She tested the extract on herself first, to make sure that it was safe.

Ramanujan was a clerk in Madras, India, who taught himself advanced mathematics from a single textbook. In 1913 he sent a letter with pages of formulas to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy, who recognized his genius and brought him to England.
Once when Hardy visited him in the hospital, he mentioned that his taxi had a boring number, 1729. Ramanujan replied that it's the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways. Ramanujan worked out thousands of results, many of them without proofs, and mathematicians are still proving them today. He died in 1920 at age 32. Hardy said that his greatest discovery in mathematics was Ramanujan.

Archimedes of Syracuse was the greatest scientist of the ancient world. He worked out the principle of the lever, found the rule for floating bodies and calculated the area of a circle. He is said to have claimed that, given a place to stand, he could move the Earth.
In the famous story, he stepped into a bath, realized how to measure the volume of a king's crown by the water it displaced, and ran through the streets shouting "Eureka." He was killed in 212 BC when the Romans captured his city. According to one account, he was absorbed in a diagram drawn in the sand when a soldier came upon him. His tomb was marked with a sphere and a cylinder, the result of which he was proudest.

Eratosthenes was the head of the great Library of Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. He'd heard that at noon on midsummer day, the Sun shone straight down a well at Syene in southern Egypt, while in Alexandria, a stick cast a shadow.
From the angle of that shadow and the distance between the two cities, he calculated Earth's circumference. His result was within a few percent of the true value, depending on which unit of length he used. He did it more than two thousand years ago, with a stick, a well and some arithmetic. It's a lasting reminder that educated people knew the Earth was round long before Columbus, and that measuring what's in front of you can reveal what you cannot see.

Hypatia was a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher in Alexandria, Egypt, in the late 4th and early 5th centuries. She taught students from various religions and was widely respected. She was the daughter of a mathematician, Theon, and she edited some of his works.
In 415 she was killed by a mob during a period of political and religious conflict in the city, and her death has been remembered as a symbol of the loss of ancient learning. Very little of her own writing survives, so most of what we know comes from letters by her students and from later accounts. Her story is a reminder of how fragile a tradition of learning can be.

Ibn al-Haytham, known in Europe as Alhazen, worked in Cairo around the year 1000. In his Book of Optics, he proved that we see because light enters the eye, and not because rays leave the eye, as many ancient thinkers believed.
He tested ideas with experiments, used the camera obscura to study light and insisted that claims should be tested. Some historians call him a founder of the scientific method. According to one story, he pretended to be mad in order to escape a promise to control the flooding of the Nile, which he had realized was impossible, and spent years under house arrest. During that time he wrote his greatest book. He's a good example of how much early science came from the Islamic world.

Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked in the House of Wisdom in Baghdad in the early 9th century. His book on solving equations, whose title included the word al-jabr, gave us the word algebra.
Another of his books introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals to the Arab world and, through Latin translations, to Europe. His name, in Latin form, gave us the word algorithm. So two of the most important words in mathematics and computing trace back to one man, who lived more than 1,200 years ago. He also made world maps and helped to calculate the positions of the stars. The House of Wisdom, where he worked, was one of the great centers of learning of its time.

Ibn Sina, known as Avicenna in Europe, was a Persian physician and philosopher. By his early twenties, he had become a well-known doctor, and he is said to have treated a prince of Bukhara.
His Canon of Medicine, completed around 1025, was a huge encyclopedia that described how infectious diseases can spread, recommended quarantine and set out rules for testing drugs. It was translated into Latin and used as a textbook in European universities for about six centuries, into the 1600s. He also wrote on philosophy, and his writings were studied in many countries. His influence on medicine lasted longer than that of nearly any other doctor in history.

The Indian mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata wrote a short, dense book in the year 499. In it he stated that the Earth rotates on its axis, and that this causes the apparent daily motion of the stars, a thousand years before Copernicus.
He also gave a value for pi, 3.1416, which is very accurate, and he explained eclipses as shadows, not as acts of demons. India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after him. He wrote the book when he was only 23, according to his own account. Like many ancient works, it was compressed into short verses to make it easy to memorize. A single, thin volume that held so much was a remarkable achievement.

Leonardo is famous as the painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, but he filled thousands of pages of notebooks with studies of anatomy, water, flight and machines. About 7,000 pages survive, and many were written in mirror image, from right to left.
He drew the valves of the heart and flying machines centuries before others. But he never published his notes, which were scattered after his death, so they had little influence on science at the time. They were rediscovered only much later. If he had published, the history of anatomy and engineering might have been different. His curiosity was endless, and that is perhaps his greatest gift to us.
Vesalius and Harvey: opening the body

For about 1,400 years, doctors relied on the writings of the Roman physician Galen, who'd mostly dissected animals. In 1543 the young Flemish anatomist Andreas Vesalius published De humani corporis fabrica, based on his own dissections of human bodies, and showed that Galen was wrong in many details. The book had magnificent illustrations, and it transformed the teaching of medicine.
In 1628 the English physician William Harvey published a book arguing that blood circulates around the body, pumped by the heart. He had made a simple calculation: the heart pumps out far more blood in an hour than the body could possibly manufacture, so it must be going around in a circle. It contradicted ancient teaching, and many doctors rejected it for years, but he was right.
Hooke and Leeuwenhoek: the first microscopists

In 1665 the English scientist Robert Hooke published Micrographia, a book with spectacular drawings of what he'd seen under his microscope, including a flea and a louse. Looking at a slice of cork, he saw little box-like compartments, which reminded him of monks' cells, and he called them "cells." He was also involved in famous disputes with Isaac Newton over credit for discoveries in optics and gravity.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a cloth merchant in Delft in the Netherlands who ground his own tiny lenses, some magnifying nearly 270 times, better than any microscope of his time. In the 1670s he looked at pond water, and the plaque on his own teeth, and saw swarms of tiny living things, which he called "animalcules." The Royal Society in London doubted him until Robert Hooke confirmed the observations.

Benjamin Franklin was a printer, writer and diplomat, and a serious scientist. He proposed in 1749 that a pointed iron rod could protect buildings from lightning, and the lightning rod was in use by 1752. It was one of the first practical results of the study of electricity.
He also invented bifocal glasses, made one of the first maps of the Gulf Stream and introduced the terms positive and negative for electric charge. His famous kite experiment is probably a mix of fact and legend, since it's not clear that he ever did it as the story is told. He refused to patent his inventions, writing that as we benefit from the inventions of others, we should be glad to serve others by any invention of ours.
Writing: from clay marks to the alphabet

Writing began in Sumer, in what is now southern Iraq, around 3400 to 3200 BC. It seems to have started out as a bookkeeping tool, with little clay tokens and marks pressed into clay to keep track of grain, sheep and beer. Over the centuries, the marks became wedge-shaped signs, called cuneiform, that could stand for sounds. Then people could write names, laws, letters and stories, and the oldest known literature was born.
Most of the world's alphabets descend from a different, later invention. Around 1800 BC, workers from Canaan in Egypt's Sinai turquoise mines adapted a few Egyptian hieroglyphs into a simple script, with a sign for each sound. The Phoenicians spread it around the Mediterranean, the Greeks added vowels, and the Romans passed their version on to us. A system of about two dozen signs was far easier to learn than hundreds, and it put reading within reach of ordinary people.

The first wheels weren't for carts. They turned the potter's wheel, and wheeled vehicles appear a little later, around 3500 BC. A wheel and axle found in the Ljubljana marshes in Slovenia has been dated to about 3150 BC, among the oldest known.
It seems odd that the wheel came well after boats and plows, but it's actually hard. The axle and the hole have to fit very closely, and that takes skilled work. A wheel that spins on a fixed axle, or an axle that turns with the wheel, needs careful carpentry. Many people in the ancient Americas never used wheeled carts for transport, even though they knew the idea, partly because they had no large animals to pull them.
Göbekli Tepe and the start of farming

In 1994 the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began to dig on a hilltop in southeastern Turkey, and found huge T-shaped stone pillars carved with animals, arranged in circles. It was built about 11,500 years ago, before farming, and before pottery. That overturned the idea that people first settled down in towns and only then built monuments. Perhaps the need to gather for such a place helped to start settled life.
About 11,000 years ago, in a region of the Middle East called the Fertile Crescent, people began to plant seeds on purpose. Wheat, barley, lentils and peas were among the first crops. Farming let people stay in one place, store food and support larger numbers, and that led to villages, then cities, kings and writing. It also brought new problems, such as crowded living and disease.

The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC as the tomb of the Egyptian king Khufu. It stood about 146 meters high, and it was the tallest human-made structure in the world for nearly 4,000 years, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England surpassed it in the 1300s.
The workers weren't slaves, as people used to think. Archaeologists found their town nearby, with bakeries and graves, which shows they were paid and fed. They were organized in gangs with humorous names, such as "Friends of Khufu." It's an impressive engineering feat, done with copper tools, ramps and teamwork. Each of the roughly two million blocks had to be cut, moved and set in place, and the pyramid is still the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that survives.

Around 1754 BC the king of Babylon, Hammurabi, had 282 laws carved on a tall black stone pillar, so that everyone could see them. It covered trade, property, family and crime. Punishments depended on the social rank of the victim and the offender, and many were based on "an eye for an eye."
It's one of the oldest long written law codes, and it reflects the idea that the king's role is to ensure justice. At the top of the pillar, the king is shown standing before the sun god, who is handing him the symbols of authority. The code was copied by scribes for more than a thousand years. Its value for us is that it shows what people worried about in a very ancient city, from lost cattle to rental disputes and bad builders.

For 1,400 years, nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs. The knowledge of how had been lost, and the pictures on temple walls were a mystery. In 1799 French soldiers digging near the town of Rashid, or Rosetta, found a stone slab carved with the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, a cursive Egyptian script and ancient Greek. It dates from 196 BC.
Using the Greek as a key, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced in 1822 that he could read hieroglyphs. His breakthrough was to realize that the signs could stand for sounds, as well as for things. It opened up three thousand years of Egyptian history, from temples and tombs to letters and stories. The stone is now in the British Museum, and it has become a symbol of the effort of decoding any unknown language.

By tradition, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BC at Olympia in Greece, in honor of Zeus. They took place every four years, and included foot races, wrestling, boxing and chariot races. A sacred truce was declared so that athletes could travel safely, even when cities were at war.
Only free Greek men were allowed to compete, and the Games continued for more than a thousand years. Winners received a wreath of olive leaves and great fame at home, though no medals. The early athletes competed without clothes. The Games were ended in the late fourth century AD, and they were revived in Athens in 1896. The modern Games are much larger, but they still follow the same four-year rhythm.

In 508 BC the Athenian leader Cleisthenes reformed the government, giving citizens a vote in an assembly that made the laws. Any citizen could speak and vote. Officials were often chosen by lot, so that rich and poor had an equal chance.
But citizens were only free adult men born in Athens, perhaps a fifth of the population. Women, slaves and foreigners were left out. It was a limited democracy, but it introduced the idea that ordinary people should decide. The word itself comes from the Greek for "rule by the people." Later democracies have been far wider, and they've grown from that early seed, along with a lot of arguments about who should be counted.

In 490 BC the Athenians defeated a much larger Persian army at the plain of Marathon, one of the most famous battles in history. The victory saved Athens, and gave its citizens confidence in the young democracy.
The popular story that a runner raced 26 miles to Athens with the news, shouting "Victory!" and then dropped dead, is a much later legend. What's better documented is that a runner named Pheidippides ran about 150 miles to Sparta to ask for help. The modern marathon race comes from the legend, and its length, 26.2 miles, was fixed at the 1908 London Olympics. It's a nice case of a story that's better known than the facts behind it.

Alexander became king of Macedon at the age of 20, in 336 BC, after his father was murdered. In just over a decade he conquered the Persian Empire, defeating King Darius, and led his army as far as the Indus River in India by 326 BC. His soldiers refused to go further.
He died in Babylon in 323 BC, at 32, and his generals divided up the empire. It spread Greek culture across much of Asia, and cities he founded, such as Alexandria in Egypt, became centers of learning. His tutor in boyhood was Aristotle. Alexander was a brilliant soldier, and often a cruel conqueror. Within a short life, he changed the map of the ancient world, and his legend lasted for many centuries.

In 221 BC King Zheng of Qin finished conquering the other states of China and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor. He standardized writing, weights and measures, and even the width of cart axles, so that wagons could run in the same ruts across the empire.
His tomb is guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers, the Terracotta Army, which was discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well. Each figure has a different face. The emperor was also a harsh ruler, who burned books and punished critics. His dynasty collapsed within a few years of his death, but the idea of a single united China lasted. The name China itself may come from his state of Qin.

One of the most popular facts is that the Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon, and it's not true. Astronauts say it's barely visible, if at all, even from low Earth orbit, because it's narrow and is similar in color to the land around it.
The claim appeared in print in the 1930s, decades before anyone went into space. China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said in 2003 that he could not see the wall from orbit. Cities, airports and large highways are much easier to see, especially at night. It's a good example of a widely repeated claim that turns out to be false, and of why it's good to check an assertion even when it sounds reasonable.
From Republic to Empire: Rome and the Ides of March

According to tradition, the Romans overthrew their last king in 509 BC and set up a republic, in which leaders were elected. Two consuls shared power for a year, and the Senate advised them. The Republic lasted nearly 500 years, as Rome grew from a city into the ruler of the Mediterranean.
On March 15, 44 BC, the Ides of March in the Roman calendar, Julius Caesar was stabbed to death in the Senate by a group of about 60 senators. They hoped to save the Republic from a man who'd had himself made dictator for life. But the killing led to another civil war, and within 17 years to the rule of Caesar's adopted heir, Augustus, as the first emperor, in 27 BC. The plotters' attempt to restore the Republic ended it.

The "Roman Peace" was a period of about 200 years, from Augustus in 27 BC to the death of Marcus Aurelius in AD 180, when the Roman Empire was relatively stable. Trade and travel flourished, with good roads and shipping across the Mediterranean.
The peace was kept by large armies on the borders, and the people conquered by Rome didn't always feel peaceful. But it was a time of prosperity, in which a traveler could go from Britain to Syria under the same laws and the same coins. Cities grew, aqueducts and baths were built, and Latin and Greek spread. The peace didn't mean that there were no wars. It means that, for most people inside the empire, war was far away.

The Silk Road wasn't one road but a network of trade routes linking China, India, Persia and Rome. The Han emperor sent an envoy, Zhang Qian, west around 138 BC to find allies, and that opened up the routes.
Silk, paper, spices and ideas traveled along them, as did religions. So did diseases. Most traders only carried goods part of the way, passing them to others, so a piece of silk might change hands dozens of times before it reached Rome. The name "Silk Road" was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen. It's a useful picture of how connected the ancient world already was, and of how much we owe to the traders who crossed the deserts and mountains.

The popular story is that the great Library of Alexandria in Egypt was destroyed in a single great fire. In fact, it declined over centuries. Funding was cut, scholars were driven out in political purges, and a number of fires damaged parts of it, including one set by Julius Caesar's troops in 48 BC that burned some storage warehouses.
Historians reject the idea of one dramatic loss. The library was founded in the 3rd century BC, and at its peak it may have held several hundred thousand scrolls. It was part of the Museum, a kind of research institute where scholars lived and worked. Its slow fading is a less dramatic story than the legend, but a sadder one, since it shows how a great institution can be lost through neglect.

The Chinese had paper by the 2nd century AD, and it was a thousand years before Europe took it up. The court official Cai Lun is traditionally credited with inventing it around AD 105, but archaeologists have found older fragments.
Arab papermakers learned the craft after 751, at the Battle of Talas, according to tradition, and it reached Europe in the 1100s, through Spain. Paper made printing and widespread literacy affordable. Before then, people wrote on parchment, which was made from animal skins, or on papyrus, which was costly and fragile. A cheap, light and smooth material for writing changed what was possible, from letters and books to government records and, eventually, newspapers.

In AD 79 Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum. A young man named Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and described the towering cloud in two letters to the historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, sailed toward the eruption to rescue people and died on the shore.
The ash preserved homes, shops, loaves of bread, paintings and graffiti so well that we can read about daily life in a Roman town. One wall has a scrawled complaint about a bad innkeeper, and another has an election slogan. Excavations that began in the 1700s are still going on, and new discoveries come up every year. It's a time capsule, made by a disaster.

In AD 325 the Roman emperor Constantine called bishops from across the empire to Nicaea, in what's now Turkey, to settle a dispute over the nature of Christ: whether the Son was created or eternal. The disagreement threatened the unity of the church, and so of the empire.
The council produced an early form of the Nicene Creed, which affirms that the Son is of one substance with the Father. A revised version is still recited in many churches today. It was the first time that the bishops of the whole church had met in an assembly of this kind. It also set the date for Easter to be reckoned in a common way. The council shows how closely the story of the early church was tied to the Roman state.

In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer removed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus, and didn't bother to replace him. That date is traditionally given as the end of the Western Roman Empire.
Historians now see it as a slow change over about a century, not a sudden collapse, as barbarian kingdoms took over provinces. Most people probably didn't notice that anything special had happened. The Eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, continued until 1453. The Roman Empire's decline has been the subject of debate ever since. Some blame economics, others politics or invasion, and many today speak of transformation rather than fall. Whatever the cause, the Latin language, Roman law and Christianity carried on, and they shaped the kingdoms that followed.

The great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, now Istanbul, was built in only five years, from 532 to 537, for the emperor Justinian. Its enormous dome, about 55 meters high, seems to float on a ring of windows.
For almost a thousand years it was one of the largest enclosed spaces in the world. When Justinian first walked in, he is said to have exclaimed that he had outdone Solomon, who built the first temple. It was later a mosque, then a museum, and in 2020 became a mosque again. The building shows how much skill the engineers of the sixth century had, and it has survived earthquakes, fires and many changes of rule.

The Islamic calendar counts years from AD 622, the year of the Hijra, when the Prophet Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina after persecution. The word means "migration."
The calendar is lunar, with twelve months of 29 or 30 days, so the year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year. This means that the Islamic months, like Ramadan, move through the seasons, falling about 11 days earlier each year. Over about 33 years, the month goes all the way around. It's a different way of keeping time, tied to the Moon and not to the Sun, and it's still used to set the dates of Islamic holidays.

In ninth-century Baghdad, the caliphs supported a center of scholarship known as the House of Wisdom. Scholars there translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, and added their own discoveries in mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Al-Khwarizmi, who gave us the word algebra, worked there.
Many ancient texts, including some by Aristotle and Galen, survived because they were translated. Some were later translated back from Arabic into Latin, and so they came to Europe. It was part of a wider movement of translation that lasted for around two centuries. The House of Wisdom was destroyed when the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258. It stands as a reminder that knowledge is passed down by people, and that it can be lost.

On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as Emperor in Rome. He ruled much of western Europe, and promoted education, setting up schools in monasteries.
His scribes also developed a clear and legible handwriting style, Carolingian minuscule, which later became the model for our lowercase letters. The letters you're reading now descend from the script of Charlemagne's court. He himself, according to his biographer, could read but had trouble learning to write, and kept tablets under his pillow to practice. He's often called the father of Europe, and his empire was split among his grandsons within a generation after his death.

About 500 years before Columbus, Norse explorers reached North America. At L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, archaeologists found the remains of buildings, and wood that had been cut with metal tools, which the locals didn't have.
In 2021 scientists used a solar storm recorded in tree rings to date the cutting precisely, to the year 1021. It's the earliest known European presence in the Americas. The Norse sagas tell of voyages to a land called Vinland, and this site is the only confirmed evidence of them. The settlement did not last long, perhaps because of conflict with the local people or the distance from home. The find shows how a single year can be read from the rings of a tree.

On October 14, 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English King Harold at the Battle of Hastings. Harold was killed, perhaps by an arrow in the eye, as the Bayeux Tapestry seems to show, though that's debated.
French became the language of England's rulers for around 300 years, and English absorbed thousands of French words, which is why we have both "cow" and "beef." The English peasants who raised the animals used the old English word, while the Norman lords who ate the meat used the French one. The Tapestry itself is a 70-meter strip of embroidered cloth. The Conquest changed English law, language and landholding more than any other event in the country's history.

In 1215 a group of English barons forced King John to put his seal to a charter limiting his power. It promised, among other things, that no free man could be punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land.
Most clauses later became obsolete. The Pope soon annulled the charter, and the barons and the king went to war. But the idea that even a king is under the law influenced many later constitutions, including the American one. It was reissued several times by later kings, and a few of its clauses are still part of English law. The document itself is a collection of very specific grievances, but its spirit has been taken as a promise of liberty.

Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and in 1206 took the title Genghis Khan, "universal ruler." He and his successors built the largest connected land empire in history. Under his grandsons, it stretched from Korea to Hungary.
It also protected trade along the Silk Road and spread ideas and technologies, though it was founded on terrible violence, and may have helped to spread the plague. Cities that resisted were often destroyed, and millions died. At the same time, the Mongols allowed religious freedom and promoted trade, and they set up a postal system that was among the fastest of its time. He's a figure of both great achievement and great destruction.

Mansa Musa ruled the West African empire of Mali in the early 1300s, and was famously wealthy. In 1324 he traveled to Mecca with thousands of attendants and camels laden with gold.
He gave away so much in Cairo that the price of gold there fell for years. Back in Mali, the city of Timbuktu became a renowned center of learning, with libraries and a university. Mali was one of the main sources of gold for the Mediterranean world, and the journey put it on European maps. A map from 1375 shows him seated on a throne, holding a gold nugget. He may well have been one of the richest people who ever lived.

The plague that swept through Europe between 1347 and 1351 killed perhaps a third or more of the population. It came along trade routes from Asia, spread by fleas on rats, and by people. Whole villages were emptied.
With so many dead, workers were scarce, wages rose and the old feudal order, in which peasants were tied to the land, weakened. It took Europe about two centuries to recover its population. The disease returned in waves for centuries. It's one of the worst catastrophes in human history, and it shows how a single microbe can change the course of civilization. It also led to changes in medicine and in attitudes toward the poor.

Around 1450 the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg developed a way to print with movable metal type. Before that, books had to be copied by hand, and a Bible might take a scribe months.
His famous Bible appeared around 1455. By 1500, more than 20 million books had been printed in Europe. Books became cheap, and ideas, from science to religion, could spread quickly. The printing press helped bring about the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and the rise of literacy. Gutenberg himself didn't get rich from it, and he lost his workshop to a creditor. It's among the most influential inventions in history, and the first great step toward the age of mass communication.

On May 29, 1453, the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, after a siege of 53 days. His army used huge cannons to batter the ancient walls.
The city became the Ottoman capital, Istanbul. Greek scholars who fled west carried manuscripts with them, which helped to feed the Italian Renaissance. The fall was the end of the Roman Empire, which had lasted, in one form or another, for about 1,500 years. For Europeans, the closing of old trade routes increased the push to find sea routes to Asia, which led to the voyages of exploration that followed. A single siege thus helped to set the Age of Discovery in motion.

In 1492 the Italian navigator Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, crossed the Atlantic and landed in the Caribbean. He believed he'd reached the edge of Asia. Millions of people already lived in the Americas, and his arrival began lasting contact between the hemispheres.
After that, plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions, and changed both sides of the ocean. Potatoes, tomatoes, maize and chocolate went to the Old World, and horses, wheat and smallpox went to the New. The historian Alfred Crosby named the process in 1972. Many of the foods that we think of as typical of European countries, like Italian tomatoes, came from the Americas. The exchange also brought disease, conquest and enslavement for many Indigenous peoples.

In 1519 five ships under Ferdinand Magellan left Spain to find a westward route to the Spice Islands. The voyage was long and harsh, with mutiny, storms and starvation. Magellan was killed in a battle in the Philippines in 1521.
Only one ship, the Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, completed the journey around the world in 1522, with 18 men of the original crew of about 270. It proved that the world could be circumnavigated. When they arrived, they found that their calendar was a day behind, since they had traveled westward against the Sun. The voyage was a triumph, but it was also very costly in lives.

In 1521 Hernán Cortés and his forces captured Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, now Mexico City. The Spaniards didn't do it alone. Thousands of Indigenous allies, who resented Aztec rule, fought with them, and smallpox, which the Europeans had brought, killed a huge part of the city's people.
The conquest had many causes, not just Spanish weapons and horses. Cortés also had help from an Indigenous woman, known as Malintzin or La Malinche, who translated and advised him. The city was larger than any in Spain at the time, with canals, markets and a great temple. The old story that a small band of Spaniards conquered an empire is now seen as much too simple.

In 1517 Martin Luther, a German monk and professor, wrote a list of 95 arguments against the sale of indulgences, which were pardons that people bought to reduce punishment for sin. According to tradition, he posted them on the church door at Wittenberg.
The printing press carried his ideas across Germany within weeks. The Reformation that followed split Western Christianity, and Luther later translated the Bible into German. His translation helped to shape the German language. Whether he nailed the paper to the door or simply mailed it to his bishop is debated, but the effect was the same. It started a movement that changed religion, politics and education across Europe.

The King James Version of the Bible was completed in 1611 by about 47 scholars, working from Hebrew and Greek texts. It built heavily on the earlier English translation by William Tyndale, who was executed in 1536.
Its rhythmic language shaped English literature and speech, giving us phrases like "the powers that be" and "the skin of my teeth." It was meant to be read aloud in church, so its sentences are made to be heard. For almost three centuries, it was the standard Bible for English speakers. Many people who've never read it use its phrases every day, and its language is still part of what we think of as grand and solemn English.

The Inca citadel of Machu Picchu, high in the Andes of Peru, was probably built around 1450 as an estate for the emperor Pachacuti. It was abandoned about a century later, around the time of the Spanish conquest, and the Spaniards apparently never found it.
In 1911 the American explorer Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention, although local farmers had known about it all along. The stonework is so precise that blades of paper can't be slipped between some of the blocks, and the Incas built without mortar. It sits at about 2,400 meters, on a ridge between two peaks. Today it's one of the most visited sites in South America, and it has become a symbol of Inca engineering.

The treaties signed in 1648 in the German region of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War, one of the most destructive wars in European history, which killed perhaps a quarter of the people in the German lands. Whole regions had been laid waste, and armies had lived off the land.
The agreements said that each ruler would control his own territory, without outside interference, an idea that's often seen as the beginning of the modern system of sovereign states. The war had started as a religious conflict, but it ended as a political one. After it, the principle that a country's borders and its internal affairs are its own business became the basic rule of how nations deal with one another.

In September 1666 a fire that began in a baker's shop in Pudding Lane burned for four days and destroyed about 13,000 houses and 87 churches, including St Paul's Cathedral. The city was made largely of timber, and a dry summer and strong wind helped the flames to spread.
Only six deaths were officially recorded, though the true number may have been higher, since the poor weren't always counted. The disaster led to new building rules, which required brick and stone, and to the first fire insurance companies. The diarist Samuel Pepys buried his wine and a wheel of cheese in his garden to protect them. The architect Christopher Wren designed a new St Paul's, which still stands, and the city that rose from the ashes was safer.

Why should we obey a government? Three philosophers gave different answers. In 1651 Thomas Hobbes argued that people give up some of their freedom in return for safety. Without a strong ruler, he said, life would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short."
In 1689 John Locke said that government exists to protect people's rights, and can be replaced if it fails to. In 1762 Jean-Jacques Rousseau said that legitimate government must express the general will of the people. Their ideas shaped the American and French revolutions and the way we think about political power. Each started from the same question of why free people would agree to be governed, and each gave a different answer.
Two Enlightenment ideas: separated powers and daring to know

In 1748 the French thinker Montesquieu published The Spirit of the Laws, in which he argued that liberty is safest when government power is divided among separate branches, so that each can check the others. His idea strongly influenced the framers of the US Constitution, who divided the government into executive, legislative and judicial branches.
In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered the question "What is Enlightenment?" in a short essay. He said that enlightenment is people's emergence from their self-imposed immaturity, which he defined as the inability to use one's own understanding without someone else's guidance. His motto was "Sapere aude," or "Dare to know," a phrase that he took from the Roman poet Horace. Together, the two ideas describe a world in which power is checked and people think for themselves.

On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, which stated that "all men are created equal." Thomas Jefferson wrote most of the text, and Congress edited it. It was addressed partly to King George III, and partly to the world.
At the time, the words didn't extend to enslaved people or to women. Later movements, from abolitionists to suffragists to civil rights leaders, used them to demand that the promise be kept. Abraham Lincoln, in 1863, said that the nation was "dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal." The document is a statement of an ideal that the country has been working to meet, imperfectly, ever since.

In the summer of 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia, in secret, to write a new framework of government for the United States. They kept the windows shut in the heat, to keep the debates from being overheard. They debated for about four months, and the final document is only about 4,500 words long.
It has been amended 27 times, with the first ten amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, added in 1791. It's the oldest written national constitution still in use. Its brevity and its method of amendment are often seen as the reasons it has survived. It sets out the structure of government and leaves much to later generations, who have applied its words to situations that its authors could never have imagined.

On July 14, 1789, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, a royal prison and a symbol of tyranny, and the French Revolution began. Later that summer, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen set out ideas of equality and liberty.
The revolution overthrew the monarchy and later descended into the Terror, in which thousands were guillotined, and then the rule of Napoleon. It spread ideas of equal citizenship and national sovereignty across Europe. France still celebrates July 14 as its national day. The revolution is both inspiring and dreadful, and a warning that great ideals can be turned to terrible ends. It changed the way people thought about government, whether they liked it or not.

In 1791 enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up, in what became the only successful slave revolt in history to found a nation. Led first by Toussaint Louverture, and after his capture in 1802 by Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they defeated French, Spanish and British forces.
Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804, becoming the first Black-led republic and the second independent nation in the Americas. France later demanded a huge payment in exchange for recognizing it, which burdened the country for generations. The revolution frightened slave-owners everywhere, and inspired many others. It deserves to be better known as one of the pivotal events of the age of revolutions.

On June 18, 1815, near the village of Waterloo in what is now Belgium, Napoleon's army was defeated by British and allied forces under the Duke of Wellington and by Prussian forces under Marshal Blücher. It was a close fight, and Wellington later called it "the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life."
It ended 23 years of nearly constant war in Europe. Napoleon was exiled to the remote island of St. Helena, in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821. Europe then enjoyed a relatively long peace, and the word "Waterloo" has since come to mean a decisive defeat. The battle is a reminder of how much depended, on a muddy field, on a few hours and a few decisions.
Steam: Watt's engine and the first railways

Steam engines existed before James Watt, but they wasted most of their heat. In 1769 Watt, a Scottish instrument maker, patented a design with a separate condenser, which made the engine far more efficient. With the help of his business partner Matthew Boulton, steam power spread to mills, mines and later to railways and ships, and powered the Industrial Revolution.
The Stockton and Darlington Railway in northern England opened in 1825, using George Stephenson's steam locomotive to haul coal and passengers. Within a few decades, railways spread across the world. By 1850 Britain had about 6,000 miles of track. Trains made it necessary to standardize time, since each town had previously kept its own local time. The unit of power, the watt, is named for the man who started it all.

In 1807 Britain banned its involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, and in 1833 it abolished slavery throughout its empire. The United States abolished it with the 13th Amendment in 1865. Millions of people had been taken from Africa and sold into bondage, and the trade had been one of the biggest sources of wealth of the age.
Campaigners like William Wilberforce, Olaudah Equiano and Thomas Clarkson used pamphlets, petitions and a boycott of slave-grown sugar to turn public opinion, and the enslaved people themselves resisted constantly. Hundreds of thousands of Britons signed petitions, in a time when most could not vote. It was one of the first great campaigns of ordinary people to change a law on moral grounds.
Two books on liberty: Mill and Wollstonecraft

In his 1859 book On Liberty, the English philosopher John Stuart Mill argued that society may justly limit a person's freedom only to prevent harm to others. A person's own good, he said, isn't enough reason to force them. He defended free speech even for opinions that are wrong, because a false idea may contain some truth, and because truth that's never challenged becomes a dead dogma.
In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, in which she argued that women appear to be less rational than men only because they're denied an education. She called for girls and boys to be taught the same things. It was widely criticized at the time, and later became one of the founding texts of feminism. Mill himself went on to write The Subjection of Women, in 1869.
The telegraph, the telephone and the light bulb

On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sent a message from the Capitol in Washington to Baltimore, 40 miles away: "What hath God wrought." Until then, news could travel only as fast as a horse, a train or a ship. The telegraph made communication almost instantaneous. By 1866, a cable laid under the Atlantic connected America and Europe.
